sourceChannels: hard-benchmark-tasks-trajectories (target n=14; feeds other-foundry section; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): trajectories/write-ups of hard tasks from >=12 external agent benchmarks/foundries, mined for candidate mechanisms and shapes already proven to stress agents.

verifier-repairs-review-feedback (target n=10; feeds other-foundry section; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): cases where a benchmark's verifier/checker was repaired after review exposed a gap, mined for verification-strategy and anti-cheat mechanism material.

agent-solve-patches-failed-attempts (target n=2; feeds other-foundry section; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): agent patches/attempts (solved or failed) examined for the causal reason behind the outcome, not for the patch content itself.

klavis-mcp-cross-tool-workflows (target n=6; feeds klavis section; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): cross-tool MCP workflows drawn from Klavis repositories, mined for authority-boundary and multi-tool-coordination mechanisms.

authoritative-incident-upstream-fix (target n=9; feeds mechanism-mining section, fresh-incidents subarea; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): real production incidents carrying a documented upstream fix -- the highest-provenance channel, since causal identity and remediation are both attested by the source.

boundary-first-system-inspection (target n=12; feeds mechanism-mining section, boundaries subarea; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL): direct inspection of real systems' authority/trust boundaries, independent of any known incident, to surface latent mechanisms before they have failed publicly.

foundry-candidates-invalidly-packaged (target n=2; feeds mechanism-mining section, local-foundry-review subarea; classified REBUILT-FROM-INVENTORY -- counts toward the <=8 rebuilt cap, never toward the >=12 fresh-external floor): candidates already inside this foundry's own inventory (data/mechanisms.json, src/families/registry.ts, existing mutants.json entries) that failed packaging/validity checks, re-examined for whether the underlying mechanism is salvageable as a fresh family rather than a repaired old one. Source pool for this channel is exclusively this project's own prior candidates -- never a third-party system.

agent-self-check-failure (target n=1; feeds mechanism-mining section, external-verification-review subarea; classified FRESH-EXTERNAL -- counts toward the >=12 floor, never toward the <=8 rebuilt cap): a case where an EXTERNAL agent's self-verification/self-check step failed or proved gameable, examined as a candidate verification-strategy mechanism. Source pool is exclusively third-party agent/system trajectories drawn from the same external benchmark and write-up corpora as hard-benchmark-tasks-trajectories and verifier-repairs-review-feedback; it is never this foundry's own agent runs or inventory. Disambiguation note (closes a fresh/rebuilt classification ambiguity present in an earlier draft): despite sitting in the mechanism-mining section, this channel is kept in its own external-verification-review subarea, separate from foundry-candidates-invalidly-packaged's local-foundry-review subarea, precisely so its FRESH-EXTERNAL classification is fixed and unambiguous at registration time, not a per-candidate judgment call made later.

tb-official / Terminal-Bench requirements -- NOTE: this is explicitly NOT one of the 8 counted source channels and contributes 0 of the 56 raw-sweep units and 0 raw mechanisms: consulted only as a downstream filter and as the estimation input for the per-family 'probability of passing official Terminal-Bench task review' figure. It must never be tallied against the 8-channel count, the 56-unit sweep cap, or the 40-raw floor.
preregistration.extractionLimits: This is a PREREGISTRATION written before any of the 56 source units have been examined; the counts below are targets fixed in advance, not results. Sweep is capped at exactly 56 source units, distributed across the eight counted channels at their registered counts (14/10/2/6/9/12/2/1) -- no channel is over- or under-sampled relative to its cap without an explicit, timestamped, logged deviation from this document. One canonical extraction per source incident: an incident that appears to carry two mechanisms is resolved by selecting the single dominant causal one and logging the discarded alternative in an appendix, never split into two raw entries -- this bounds the raw pool at <=56 regardless of how mechanism-rich any one incident looks, and means the floor-vs-ceiling arithmetic below is tight by design, not by accident. A source unit that fails inclusionCriteria at extraction time yields zero raw entries and is logged as a rejected unit with its rejection reason, never silently dropped from the audit trail. Each channel's fresh-external vs. rebuilt-from-inventory classification is fixed at registration (see sourceChannels) and applies to every unit drawn from that channel uniformly -- it is never re-decided per candidate during extraction, closing the earlier ambiguity around agent-self-check-failure. Any encounter with durable-outbox or CAA (via boundary-first-system-inspection or authoritative-incident-upstream-fix in particular, since both channels could plausibly re-surface either anchor) is logged and tagged "anchor," contributing to neither the raw pool count nor the final 20. Anchor tagging is an IDENTITY match, not an AXIS match: a raw candidate is tagged "anchor" only when its (mechanism, professional workflow, authority boundary, verification strategy) tuple is substantially the same as durable-outbox's or CAA's registered tuple in data/mechanisms.json. A candidate that merely shares the same causal axis with an anchor (e.g., another idempotency-boundary case or another confused-deputy case that is not itself a re-identification of durable-outbox or CAA) is NOT tagged anchor, is not discarded, and proceeds into the raw pool and later dedup as an ordinary candidate, bound only by the ordinary <=2-families-per-causal-axis constraint like any other pair of families sharing that axis. This identity-vs-axis distinction is applied at extraction time by the investigator logging the encounter, who records the matched and differing tuple elements in the anchor log entry so the call is auditable rather than a bare judgment tag. Given realistic per-channel yield (rich, purpose-selected channels such as hard-benchmark-tasks-trajectories and authoritative-incident-upstream-fix expected near 75-85%; supporting-evidence channels such as verifier-repairs-review-feedback expected nearer 50-65%; the three single-digit channels contributing at most 5 raw entries combined even at 100% yield), the sweep is expected to land close to, and not comfortably above, the 40-raw floor -- see expectedRawCount and gaps.
preregistration.inclusionCriteria: A source unit is admitted to the raw pool only if all of the following hold: (1) it documents or directly evidences a genuine causal failure pattern (a MECHANISM) tied to a real system, incident, benchmark trajectory, reviewer finding, or inspected boundary -- never an invented scenario; (2) the professional workflow, the authority boundary, and at least a plausible verification strategy around the mechanism are sketchable from the source material, so a downstream TASK FAMILY determination is possible without further invention; (3) its difficulty does not rely primarily on obscure trivia, clerical volume, unavailable knowledge, or hidden semantics -- any candidate whose difficulty appears to trace mainly to one of these is rejected outright at extraction time, logged, and excluded from the raw count, not merely down-scored later; (4) it produces exactly one canonical extraction under the one-incident-one-extraction rule; (5) it is not a re-identification of durable-outbox or CAA presented as new -- those are tagged calibration anchors on sight and never enter the raw pool as candidate new families, per the identity-vs-axis distinction registered in extractionLimits (only a full-tuple match triggers this exclusion; sharing the causal axis alone does not). A unit may fail admission and still be logged for calibration purposes (e.g., a near-miss on an anchor mechanism) without counting toward the 40-raw floor.
preregistration.familyDefinition: Restated verbatim as the governing definition for this track: TASK FAMILY -- a reusable combination of core mechanism + professional workflow + authority boundary + safety/liveness obligations + verification strategy, supporting multiple materially different task packages without changing causal identity. This is distinguished, per the definitions in force for R1, from a TASK SHAPE (the abstract interaction topology alone, with no professional workflow, authority boundary, or verification strategy attached), a TASK INSTANCE (one immutable, hashed challenge package -- changing only a seed/identifier/threshold/scenario is not a new instance and never a new family), and a CONSTRUCTION RECIPE (reusable building techniques layered onto a family, never part of the family's own definition). Every raw extraction and every final family in this study is classified against this exact five-part definition; an extraction that names only a mechanism or only a shape, without a professional workflow, an authority boundary, and a verification strategy at least sketchable, is not yet a family candidate and is logged as a shape/mechanism fragment pending further evidence, not promoted into the raw-family pool.
preregistration.deduplicationRule: Candidates are clustered for semantic dedup on the tuple (core causal mechanism/axis, professional workflow, authority boundary, verification strategy), never on surface wording or source phrasing; near-duplicate raw items collapse into one family entry that retains the single strongest/most authoritative source citation and logs the discarded duplicates. The raw pool (>=40 entries, collected before any dedup pass begins) must deduplicate down to EXACTLY 20 final families, no more and no fewer. Four hard constraints are enforced on the resulting 20, checked pairwise/globally after clustering rather than only within a cluster: (a) no more than 2 final families may share the same core causal axis; (b) the 20 must span at least 8 distinct professional domains; (c) the 20 must span at least 8 distinct failure axes; (d) at least 12 of the 20 must originate from the seven channels registered FRESH-EXTERNAL (authoritative-incident-upstream-fix, boundary-first-system-inspection, klavis-mcp-cross-tool-workflows, hard-benchmark-tasks-trajectories, verifier-repairs-review-feedback, agent-solve-patches-failed-attempts, agent-self-check-failure -- the last is fresh-external because its source material is always a third-party agent/system per its channel disambiguation note, never this foundry's own inventory), and no more than 8 may be rebuilt/reconstructed from the current foundry inventory (data/mechanisms.json, src/families/registry.ts, existing mutants.json entries) -- only the foundry-candidates-invalidly-packaged channel (2 units) is registered REBUILT, and its units count toward the <=8 cap by construction. This fresh/rebuilt tag is fixed per-channel at registration, not decided per-candidate after the fact, so no raw candidate's fresh/rebuilt status is ambiguous at dedup time. Durable-outbox and CAA are excluded from both the 20-family count and the 12/8 split in either direction -- they are referenced only as calibration anchors when scoring or sanity-checking new candidates, never selected as one of the 20; a fresh family that merely shares an anchor's causal axis without matching its full mechanism/workflow/boundary/verification tuple is not an anchor and is eligible for the 20, subject only to the ordinary <=2-per-axis constraint (see extractionLimits' identity-vs-axis rule). If two raw candidates trace to the same source incident, that is treated as an extraction-time protocol violation (see extractionLimits' one-incident-one-extraction rule) to be caught and corrected before this dedup stage runs, not resolved by dedup itself. If no clustering of the raw pool satisfies all four constraints simultaneously with exactly 20 clusters, the study does not relax a constraint silently -- see stoppingRule.
preregistration.scoringRubric: Restated verbatim, FIXED weights, do not alter: Family Opportunity Score (0-100) = authoritativeProvenance(10) + economicValue(10) + latentDiagnosisReasoningBurden(15) + naturalAdversarialScenarioSpace(15) + subjectInaccessibleAuthority(10) + verifierAntiCheatFeasibility(10) + constructionOperatorCompatibility(10) + materiallyDistinctInstanceCapacity(10) + implementationTrialTractability(5) + noveltyPortfolioContribution(5) = 100. Separately, for each of the 20 final families, register two decision priors on a 5-point-increment scale (0, 5, 10, ..., 100), each stated as a plausible range (e.g. "40-55") plus a confidence label (low/medium/high): P(clean 5/6-or-6/6 | ordinary competent package) and P(clean 5/6-or-6/6 | full construction recipe applied). These are decision priors elicited from provenance, workflow, and boundary characteristics -- never measured frequencies -- and must never be derived from mutant-fatality counts, mechanism-axis counts, reader approval, contract score, or reward-zero outcomes caused by a specification, package, verifier, or infrastructure defect (per the TARGET EVENT definition, a defect-caused reward-zero is not a clean target result and must not leak into either prior). Also register per family, as separate estimates: probability of passing official Terminal-Bench task review; probability the family can produce at least 10 materially distinct task instances without changing causal identity; estimated expert build hours for the first package; estimated marginal build hours once reusable infrastructure for the family exists.
preregistration.stoppingRule: The sweep attempts up to 56 source units (the registered per-channel caps), stopping a channel early only if it is exhausted of qualifying units before its cap is reached -- never stopping early merely because the 40-raw floor has already been reached, since domain/axis diversity and the fresh/rebuilt split are only checkable once the full sweep's admissible pool is known. If, after the full 56-unit sweep, the raw admissible pool is below 40, the study does not lower inclusionCriteria to manufacture additional raw entries; it instead declares the sweep under-target, reports the shortfall and its per-channel breakdown, and treats extending a specific channel (or stopping the track short of family selection) as a separate, explicit, logged decision -- never a silent bar-lowering. If the raw pool is >=40 but no clustering into exactly 20 families satisfies all four dedup constraints (<=2 families per causal axis, >=8 domains, >=8 axes, >=12 fresh-external/<=8 rebuilt using the per-channel classification fixed in sourceChannels, anchors excluded from all counts via the identity-vs-axis rule in extractionLimits), the study stops and reports the shortfall (e.g. "19 families satisfy every constraint; no 20th candidate clears the bar") rather than relaxing any constraint to force a round number. R1 is complete only when: exactly 20 final families satisfy every dedup constraint; every one of the 20 has been scored on the full fixed-weight Family Opportunity Score rubric; and every one of the 20 carries all six supplementary estimates (the two clean-target-result priors, TB-review-pass probability, >=10-distinct-tasks probability, first-build hours, marginal-build hours).
gaps: Raw-count headroom is thin by design: 56 planned units against a 40-raw floor leaves only ~16 units (29%) of slack once the one-incident-one-extraction rule and realistic per-channel yield are applied; the central yield estimate (expectedRawCount=41) lands barely above the floor, not comfortably above it, so a modestly worse-than-expected sweep could fail the floor outright. This is a disclosed statistical-power risk, not a violation of the >=40 commitment itself, which the stoppingRule handles explicitly (declare under-target, never lower inclusionCriteria).

Three channels (agent-solve-patches-failed-attempts n=2, foundry-candidates-invalidly-packaged n=2, agent-self-check-failure n=1) supply only 5 of the 56 units combined; any final family whose best evidence comes from one of these axes rests on a fragile base where a single dead-end unit removes most of the channel's contribution. Note this no longer creates classification ambiguity (each channel's fresh/rebuilt tag is now fixed at registration), only yield fragility.

Domain (>=8) and axis (>=8) coverage are stated as floors on the dedup OUTPUT, but the sweep's INPUT is not pre-stratified by domain or axis -- nothing in the channel design guarantees the 56 units land across 8+ professional domains rather than clustering around a few shapes (e.g. dev-tooling/CI-adjacent incidents are likely over-represented in hard-benchmark-tasks-trajectories and verifier-repairs-review-feedback), so hitting the coverage floors may force discarding otherwise-valid raw candidates and could shrink the effectively usable pool below expectedRawCount.

Elicitation process for the two clean-target-result priors and the four supplementary per-family estimates is not specified beyond the rubric itself: no rater independence, blinding, or order-randomization is registered, so if one investigator scores all 20 families in a single sitting, early families risk anchoring the scale for later ones -- a real threat to the priors being genuinely predictive rather than self-consistent.

families20.name: CDN and DNS Cache Staleness Verification
families20.definition: Agent makes an authoritative change at an origin system (a DNS record or a CDN-fronted asset) and must correctly verify propagation despite intermediate caching layers that are contractually permitted to serve stale data until TTL- or purge-type-specific windows lapse, choosing the correct purge type and multi-tier verification sequence rather than treating one re-fetch as proof.
families20.taskShape: Agent updates an origin resource then issues a purge (soft, hard, tag, or prefix) against a simulated multi-tier CDN and/or updates a DNS record; the harness enforces the documented stale-serve window, tier-revalidation semantics (EXPIRED vs MISS), and purge rate limits, and the agent must choose a verification sequence that correctly distinguishes legally-stale from genuinely failed propagation.
families20.authorityBoundary: The origin (authoritative DNS zone or origin server) is the sole source of truth; caches and edge tiers hold delegated, time-bounded copies whose staleness is contractually legal, not a defect, so the agent's authority to declare content live is bounded by confirming propagation at the correct tier, not by the absence of an API error.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent cannot directly inspect every cache node's internal state; it only observes whatever response headers/values a given tier returns to a probe, with no built-in freshness signal unless it deliberately checks documented status semantics.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: TTL length; hard vs soft vs tag-based purge type; single-tier vs multi-tier topology; plan-tier rate limits; verification method chosen.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent that purges once and immediately re-fetches once will, per documented semantics, still legitimately see stale content and wrongly conclude failure, or accept a still-caching tier's EXPIRED response as proof of a true MISS.
families20.whyFair: The rules governing staleness (RFC 2181 TTL semantics, documented CDN purge-type behavior) are public, stable, and derivable by reading the relevant specification/vendor docs -- no hidden internal knowledge is required, only correct application of a documented cache contract.

families20.name: Read-Replica Lag Reconciliation
families20.definition: Agent writes via a primary database connection and later acts on that data through a read-replica endpoint, and must correctly reason about asynchronous replication lag, recovery-conflict query cancellations, and primary/standby role identity rather than assuming synchronous consistency or treating a stale/cancelled read as proof the original write failed.
families20.taskShape: Agent performs a write on the primary, then queries a hot-standby/read-replica for confirmation or subsequent logic, timed to land inside the replication lag window; the harness may also force a VACUUM-induced recovery-conflict cancellation the agent must diagnose as transient, and the agent must never issue a write against what it believes is the primary without confirming role via a status check.
families20.authorityBoundary: The primary holds current authoritative state; the standby is an asynchronously-replaying copy that may legally lag or forcibly cancel in-flight reads during WAL-replay conflicts, so a replica connection is read-only and eventually consistent by design, not an equally authoritative source.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent cannot observe the replication stream directly; it only sees whatever snapshot the standby has replayed at query time, with no freshness signal unless it explicitly checks dedicated status views (e.g. pg_stat_replication).
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: replication lag magnitude; concurrent primary write load; long-running analytical query vs simple read; primary vs replica role ambiguity; presence of a recovery-conflict cancellation.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent may treat an absent or stale row on the replica as proof its own write failed, retrying or duplicating it destructively, or may issue a write against a standby without checking role and mishandle the resulting read-only-transaction failure.
families20.whyFair: Postgres's own documentation (SHOW in_hot_standby, pg_stat_replication, documented recovery-conflict cancellation) gives the agent everything needed to reason correctly; standard, well-documented DBA practice, not tribal knowledge.

families20.name: Ambiguous-Failure Payment Retry Discipline
families20.definition: Agent issues a payment action where the network call can fail after the server-side effect has partially or fully completed; correct behavior reuses the same idempotency key or re-queries ledger state before resubmitting, and correctly treats a concurrent-conflict response as retry-safe rather than rotating keys and double-charging.
families20.taskShape: Harness injects timeouts at ambiguous completion points, sometimes racing a concurrent duplicate submission under the same key; agent must choose retry-with-same-key vs. query-then-decide vs. legitimate-new-key across several such events in one workflow.
families20.authorityBoundary: Agent is authorized to charge exactly once per logical intent; key reuse is valid only for identical intent, and the ledger, not client belief, is ground truth.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Whether the original attempt completed server-side before the client-visible failure is not observable except by querying ledger state.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: failure point relative to commit; presence of a genuine parameter change requiring a new key; concurrent same-key race vs sequential retry; workflow chain length.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: A naive agent treats an errored call as a no-op and blindly retries or rotates keys, producing a real duplicate charge invisible in any single response.
families20.whyFair: Idempotency-key discipline is standard, published professional practice (e.g. Stripe API design guidance); the task applies a known, derivable rule under realistic ambiguity.

families20.name: Worker Rebalance Callback Deduplication
families20.definition: A stateful worker process must keep exactly-bounded, non-duplicated external side effects (e.g. customer notifications) correct when it crashes, restarts, and transiently overlaps ownership with another worker instance during a consumer-group/partition rebalance.
families20.taskShape: Agent operates a live event-consumer service; the harness kills/restarts workers and forces partition-ownership overlap under continuous traffic; the agent must sequence state-commit vs. offset-commit vs. external-callback so kill/restart/scale sequences never silently drop or double-fire a customer-visible effect, within a documented duplicate tolerance.
families20.authorityBoundary: A worker's claim to a partition/consumer-group slot is time-bounded and revocable by the group coordinator; only the currently-owning worker may emit the callback for a given event.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Exact rebalance-protocol state and kill/restart timing are controlled by the harness and not introspectable by the agent in advance.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: worker restart timing; overlap window length; traffic rate; duplicate-tolerance threshold; number of concurrent worker slots.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents commonly order offset-commit before or after the external call incorrectly, or assume single-worker exclusivity, producing lost or duplicated callbacks under overlap.
families20.whyFair: The commit-then-emit-then-ack ordering discipline is standard, documented distributed-systems practice (Kafka consumer-group semantics) requiring genuine reasoning, and a tolerance band keeps the check achievable rather than trivia-hard.

families20.name: Rollback That Reactivates a Dormant Defect
families20.definition: Responding to a live incident on one of several replicated deployment targets, the agent must diagnose root cause before acting, because rolling back a recent change without isolating the cause can reproduce an identical latent bug -- a repurposed flag/identifier reaching never-removed deprecated code -- on previously-unaffected replicas.
families20.taskShape: Multiple identical replicas exist; one exhibits a defect traced to a reused identifier reactivating deprecated code; a plausible fast fix (rollback everywhere) is deliberately available as a trap, and the agent must audit per-replica deployment history/reachable code before broadly remediating.
families20.authorityBoundary: Agent has standing fleet deploy/rollback authority, but exercising it without verifying uniform pre-incident state across replicas exceeds the safe scope of a 'simple' rollback; each replica is independently authoritative for its own runtime state.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Dormant legacy code gated by a repurposed flag is not visible from the current deployment manifest or diff alone; it requires inspecting actual reachable runtime code paths per replica.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number of replicas; which is affected first; remediation options offered; presence of a written double-check deployment procedure.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Under incident time pressure, 'roll back everywhere' is the obvious action, so an agent applying it reflexively reproduces the identical failure on every remaining healthy replica -- the real Knight Capital escalation.
families20.whyFair: Drawn from a public, regulator-documented (SEC) incident; the reasoning required -- verify per-node deployment state before broad remediation -- is standard incident-response discipline, not proprietary or obscure.

families20.name: Nominally-Successful Batch Hides Partial Failure
families20.definition: Agent submits a multi-resource clinical batch bundle where the outer HTTP response is 200 OK regardless of individual entry outcomes; correct completion requires parsing per-entry status to detect and report which records actually landed.
families20.taskShape: Agent submits a batch of related resources, some entries engineered to fail server-side while the batch returns 200; agent must accurately report which resources committed and correctly retry only the failed subset.
families20.professionalDomain: healthcare interoperability / clinical data exchange engineering
families20.authorityBoundary: Batch requests carry no all-or-nothing guarantee; the agent's authority to declare the workflow done is bounded by per-entry status, not the top-level code.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Whether any entry persisted is not knowable from the outer response; it is only visible in the nested response Bundle.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number/type of resources; which subset is engineered to fail and why; transaction vs batch semantics; required follow-up action.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: A 200 OK strongly implies success; the spec's batch-semantics carve-out is easy to overlook, so agents checking only the top-level status mis-report partial success as full success.
families20.whyFair: This is documented, standard-conformant FHIR behavior, not an undisclosed trick.

families20.name: Silent Scope Narrowing on Token Refresh
families20.definition: Agent refreshes an OAuth2 credential mid-task expecting unchanged authority, but the authorization server silently returns a narrower scope per RFC 6749; correct behavior requires parsing the refresh response's scope field and adjusting subsequent calls rather than assuming prior permissions still hold.
families20.taskShape: Agent performs an authorized action, its token is refreshed mid-trajectory with a silently narrowed scope, and a later downstream action depending on the original scope must be detected as now-unauthorized via the response body rather than a late 403.
families20.professionalDomain: identity and access management / OAuth2 client integration engineering
families20.authorityBoundary: The refreshed token's actual scope is authoritative over the agent's assumed scope; the server may narrow it without prominent warning per spec, so the client must read the response, not assume.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The server-side decision to narrow scope is opaque; only the scope field in the refresh response and eventual call outcomes reveal it.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: which permission is narrowed; number of downstream calls depending on lost scope; proactive scope-parsing vs discovery-via-failure; single vs chained refreshes.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents treat refresh success as full authority restored and skip the optional scope field, executing downstream calls under a false assumption and failing several steps later with a hard-to-diagnose late 403.
families20.whyFair: The rule is explicit in RFC 6749 and load-bearing for any refresh implementation; correctly parsing a documented response field is core, non-obscure API-integration competence.

families20.name: SQL/Query Identifier Injection Scope Expansion
families20.definition: User- or upstream-tool-controlled identifiers (database/schema/table names, search query strings) are interpolated unsanitized into an executed data-tool call, letting a crafted or unusual identifier value cause the tool to read/touch objects far outside its nominally narrow, declared scope.
families20.taskShape: Agent is asked to perform a narrowly-scoped lookup (inspect a named schema/table, search a named spreadsheet) where the identifier may originate from an earlier, less-trusted step; agent must validate/parameterize the identifier rather than trust direct string interpolation, and a verifier checks whether the resulting action stayed within the intended object scope.
families20.professionalDomain: data warehousing / spreadsheet API integration security engineering
families20.authorityBoundary: The credential/session's nominal authority is scoped to the specific object named in the request; unsanitized interpolation lets a crafted identifier value silently expand that authority to arbitrary objects the underlying credential can reach.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent (or its verifier) cannot tell from the tool's successful response alone whether the query executed against the intended object or a different one reached via injection -- only an independent diff of actual queried objects reveals scope expansion.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: identifier source (user-typed vs chained from a prior tool's output); injection surface (SQL f-string vs Drive query string); presence/absence of an allow-list; error-vs-silent-success on malformed identifiers.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent implementing or using such a tool with a plausible-looking, narrow-sounding request will not notice that a crafted schema name or quote character breaks out of the intended query scope, because the call still returns a well-formed, plausible-looking result.
families20.whyFair: Unsanitized identifier interpolation causing injection is a textbook, well-documented software security defect (CWE-class), independently confirmed via a filed and reviewed PR -- not obscure or proprietary.

families20.name: Verifier Container Isolation Boundary
families20.definition: A task's grading verifier must run in a structurally separate, later-arriving container that shares no filesystem or package state with the agent's own now-destroyed container, so agent-mutated state or an agent-installed shim cannot be silently inherited and trusted by grading.
families20.taskShape: Agent completes work in one sandboxed container; a disjoint verifier container, built independently and started only after the agent's container is torn down, can read only explicitly declared artifact paths, baked-in image content, or a persistent sidecar; the family measures whether the agent's evidence of success lands within that declared surface, and whether the harness itself correctly enforces the isolation.
families20.professionalDomain: CI/CD and benchmark grading infrastructure engineering
families20.authorityBoundary: The verifier must be an independent authority the agent cannot influence beyond legitimate task completion; it trusts only the pre-declared artifact contract (artifacts list, Dockerfile-baked content, or sidecar) -- nothing else the agent produced is visible or credited.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Whether the verifier actually re-executes in a sealed, fresh environment is not directly inspectable by the agent; it can only be inferred indirectly, and the verifier's exact read-set and container lifecycle timing are fixed by configuration the agent cannot alter.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: shared vs separate container mode; number of declared artifacts; presence/absence of a sidecar; whether the deliverable is a running process vs a file; teardown timing.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents that leave real evidence of success in an undeclared location (e.g. only a running process, or an unlisted output file) score reward-zero despite substantive correct work, or a shared-container leak lets agent-mutated state be silently trusted by a misconfigured verifier.
families20.whyFair: A well-documented, recurring engineering failure mode across multiple independent benchmark projects' own review and contribution documentation, with a clear, mechanistically-specifiable correct architecture (sealed containers, declared artifact contracts).

families20.name: Trial-Time Tool Shim Poisoning
families20.definition: An agent with write access to a shared environment can pre-poison a binary or PATH entry (e.g. curl) that a nominally-independent, later-running verification step will invoke, causing that 'independent' check to silently consume attacker- or agent-controlled output.
families20.taskShape: Agent must either, as a builder, harden a verifier against trial-time tool shimming by baking external dependencies into a sealed, version-pinned image, or, as a security-review agent, identify that a verifier's live network/tool fetch is exploitable this way and demonstrate or propose the fix.
families20.authorityBoundary: Tools/binaries invoked by a later verification step are meant to sit outside the agent's turn's causal influence; shared-filesystem execution silently breaks that boundary, and a verifier's fetch/tool-invocation step is only trustworthy if it resolves to a binary the agent had no opportunity to influence.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The compromise is invisible from the verifier's own output -- a poisoned curl still 'succeeds' and returns data -- so detecting it requires inspecting the actual binary/PATH state independently of the verifier's report.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: which binary/tool is shimmable; whether external deps are baked into a sealed image vs fetched live; timing of the shim relative to verifier invocation; detection tooling present.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent may not realize a common binary name is both agent-writable and verifier-invoked, either accidentally leaving a broken shim, or a security-review agent missing that the underlying tool was replaced earlier in the same session, because the poisoned output is plausible and well-formed.
families20.whyFair: Documented real attack class (the cited RDI/Berkeley 89/89 case) with a well-defined mechanistic fix (sealed, version-pinned dependencies); reasoning about shared-execution trust boundaries is legitimate security-engineering skill.

families20.name: Narrow-Assertion Verifier Satisfied Without Real Work
families20.definition: A task's check asserts on a narrow, literal signal rather than the deliverable's substance, so a minimal artifact can pass without the underlying work being done, or conversely an over-fit check rejects a substantively correct but differently-implemented solution.
families20.taskShape: Agent is given a realistic deliverable requirement whose test suite is either well-constructed (rejects superficial or alternate-but-valid outputs) or deliberately loose; the family samples both to measure whether genuine capability, not verifier-gaming, drives outcomes.
families20.professionalDomain: software engineering / benchmark and QA test authoring
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent may satisfy the instruction by any means, but the intended boundary is that the means must produce the actual described outcome, not merely match the literal checker text.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The precise grader assertions are not shown in advance, only the natural-language task, mirroring how real acceptance criteria are not fully enumerated to an implementer.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: deliverable type; check specificity (exact-match vs semantic); presence of format-precision traps unrelated to the reasoning core; existence of alternate correct implementations.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent optimizing for the visible check can produce a hollow but passing artifact, or a genuinely correct artifact can fail an over-fit checker for incidental reasons.
families20.whyFair: The underlying skill (produce a genuinely correct deliverable, not a check-passing facade) is exactly what real reviewers assess.

families20.name: Self-Authored Verification Script Falsely Reports Success
families20.definition: Agent must write and run its own check before declaring a multi-step task complete; a subtle bug in that self-authored verification silently produces a false pass, and agents have been observed declaring success despite trace-level awareness the check is broken.
families20.taskShape: A CLI workflow requires the agent to both implement a solution and author verification confirming it; the environment makes a plausible but flawed self-check an easy path, and the family measures whether the agent catches its own verification's inadequacy and, having noticed a bug, changes its final completion claim.
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent is responsible for its own completion claim; a stated 'done' must be backed by verification that could actually have failed, and the agent's self-authored check has no independent authority over the true task outcome.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: True underlying correctness is only knowable via an independently-correct check the environment does not supply; the agent must build one itself and is not told whether it is trustworthy.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: type of self-check bug; how much trajectory precedes the verification step; whether the agent's own trace surfaces doubt.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Under completion pressure, agents that notice a bug in their own verification (e.g. a NameError or logic bug) have been observed rationalizing it away and declaring success anyway.
families20.whyFair: Writing a check that could actually fail is a basic, universal engineering discipline, not a specialized skill; reflects a directly observed real failure pattern in agent trajectories.

families20.name: Async DOM Mutation Timing in UI Action Replay
families20.definition: Agent drives a browser workflow and must correctly sequence wait-for-state-change actions against an async mutation stream -- batched delivery, delayed removal notification on detached subtrees, and discarded pending records at observer teardown -- rather than treating the DOM as instantaneously and completely observable, hardening the locally shipping UI action record/replay families.
families20.taskShape: Agent performs an action then must detect true completion in a live DOM where mutation delivery can batch multiple changes, continue reporting on an already-removed subtree, or silently drop pending records if the watcher disconnects before flushing (takeRecords()); a recorded action sequence's validity against a live, drifted DOM is also probed.
families20.professionalDomain: browser/UI automation and frontend testing infrastructure
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent may only conclude an action succeeded based on fully-delivered DOM mutation state, not an assumed synchronous effect or a prematurely torn-down observation window; a recorded action sequence is only valid against the state it was captured from, not the current live application.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Whether pending mutation records still exist undelivered is invisible without explicitly flushing before disconnecting; a naive 'current DOM' read can reflect stale, superseded content, and exact browser-internal batching/queue timing is not directly introspectable except through documented API semantics.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: type of async UI signal; whether an unrelated subtree removal races the real target update; whether flush-before-teardown is rewarded; time gap and degree of state drift between record and replay.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents built around simple click-then-check loops miss that mutation delivery is batched and async, acting on stale content or discarding real evidence via early teardown -- matching the local foundry's only two SHIP families' documented 5/5 trial failure rate.
families20.whyFair: These are standard, spec-documented MutationObserver semantics, genuine async reasoning rather than an undocumented quirk, and this family rebuilds on the foundry's only measured, replicated local capability gap rather than inventing a new shape from scratch.

families20.name: Out-of-Order and Split-Event Webhook Reconciliation
families20.definition: Agent's webhook consumer must dedupe split-representation duplicate events, tolerate out-of-order delivery without regressing state using stale timestamps, and recognize that a manual resend does not cancel the platform's independent automatic retry schedule.
families20.taskShape: A delivery sequence including an out-of-order pair and a split-duplicate pair arrives; agent must key dedup/order logic on object identity plus event type, not event id or created, and must not declare an incident closed on a single manual resend's 2xx, nor let a stale 'updated' event overwrite more current state.
families20.authorityBoundary: The consumer may mutate state only for events it can prove are both new and current; no ordering or single-delivery guarantee is granted, and local application/receipt order is not a valid proxy for true event order.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The provider's internal retry schedule and its decision to emit a second Event object for one logical change are invisible; only delivered payloads are seen, in whatever order they happen to arrive.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: which event types collide; gap size between out-of-order deliveries; whether a manual resend is attempted; number of split-duplicate pairs.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents commonly key dedup on event.id and order on created, or apply events in receipt order, both explicitly unsafe per the provider's own docs, reinstating stale state or double-applying an effect represented by two distinct event IDs.
families20.whyFair: The correct pattern is explicitly published guidance (e.g. Stripe's webhook docs); demanding but fair and fully derivable from given documentation.

families20.name: CRM Bulk Pagination Under Live Concurrent Writes
families20.definition: Agent walks a large CRM record set via repeated paginated calls while other users or automations concurrently modify the same object; it must detect locator/cursor expiration, handle mid-run rate-limit exhaustion, and reconcile record drift across pages without silently truncating or duplicating the final set.
families20.taskShape: A bulk export/audit/update task requires paging through hundreds of records; the harness expires the cursor mid-walk, trips a rate limit, or shifts membership across pages via concurrent writes, and correctness is judged on the final reconciled completeness/accuracy claim -- the agent must determine what was already safely processed before resuming.
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent's authority to declare a bulk operation complete is bounded by what it can verify was processed under a still-valid session/locator, without double-applying side effects to already-processed records; a query locator is a time- and session-bound handle, not a durable identifier.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The true full record set at a single consistent instant is not observable through paginated reads alone under concurrent writes; which records were inserted/deleted/modified by other actors between page fetches is only visible by re-querying.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: dataset and page size; cursor validity window; rate/type of concurrent writes; read-only audit vs read+write mass update; error-type returned on expiry.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Agents treat pagination as a reliable loop and don't anticipate cursor invalidation, either blindly restarting from scratch (reprocessing already-updated records) or silently giving up mid-walk, producing a silently wrong or truncated final count.
families20.whyFair: Locator expiry, rate limits, and pagination-consistency caveats are standard, documented CRM/REST API behavior with defined recovery procedures; genuine systems reasoning about live shared state, not hidden trivia.

families20.name: Tool Selection Collapse Under a Large Simultaneous Catalog
families20.definition: When exposed to hundreds-to-thousands of tool schemas across many aggregated servers and applications -- including near-mirror bot/user identity pairs -- degraded context handling leads an agent to select a plausible-but-wrong tool, server, or identity variant, completing an action that looks right but never touches the intended system or acts under the intended authority.
families20.taskShape: A workflow spans several real applications each contributing many similarly-named or similarly-prefixed tools (search_, list_, bot_ vs user_); with the full surface loaded, the agent must select the correct server, tool, and identity per step across a multi-turn workflow, graded by checking actual system-of-record authorship/state rather than superficial call success.
families20.authorityBoundary: Each tool variant carries distinct authority/attribution; selecting the wrong one produces an action under the wrong authority (e.g. bot vs human identity) even when the call technically succeeds.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: Which of several near-identical schemas is correct for a step is not marked in the schema; the resulting misattribution or wrong-system action is only visible to a grader checking true authorship/state, not to the agent from the call's own successful-looking result.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number of aggregated servers/tools exposed; presence of bot/user identity mirrors; naming similarity; availability of a discovery/router layer.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: The aggregator's own design rationale documents this exact failure, so an agent without scoped discovery plausibly picks a wrong-server, wrong-tool, or wrong-identity option returning a normal-looking success that never touches the intended system.
families20.whyFair: A directly evidenced, real engineering problem the industry itself builds mitigations for (discovery/router layers); testing discrimination professionals genuinely need, derivable straight from the tools' own documented schemas.

families20.name: Fuzzy-Instruction Tool Discovery and Dependency Threading
families20.definition: Agent receives a conversational request naming no explicit tools and must discover the right subset from dozens of candidates spread across multiple servers, then correctly thread one tool's output as another's input across a multi-hop, sometimes-parallelizable dependency chain.
families20.taskShape: A cross-domain analyst request is phrased without naming tools; agent must discover relevant tools from an undifferentiated catalog and correctly sequence or parallelize dependent calls across servers -- never using a placeholder for an upstream result it hasn't yet received -- with a judge checking claim coverage against the actual trajectory and dependency-awareness.
families20.professionalDomain: cross-domain knowledge work mediated by many specialized tool APIs
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent may call any tool it correctly identifies as relevant but must not fabricate an answer unsupported by an actual successful tool trajectory, and each server is authoritative only for its own domain's data -- the agent alone integrates authority across servers.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The intended correct tool subset and sequence are not given directly, only the request and full undifferentiated catalog; no individual server exposes whether its output was correctly consumed downstream.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number of servers/tools; dependency-chain depth; instruction fuzziness; degree of legitimate parallelism available.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Dependency-awareness and parallelism scores rarely exceed roughly 0.30 in this setting and degrade further as server count grows, as agents call tools out of true dependency order or serialize calls that could run in parallel.
families20.whyFair: Mirrors a realistic business-language request rather than an API spec, rewarding genuine discovery and multi-hop planning derived from the tools' own documented input/output contracts.

families20.name: Long-Horizon Coordination Across Many Real Applications
families20.definition: A task chains sequential, dependent tool calls across several distinct real applications over roughly twenty or more turns, requiring coherent cross-app state and correct per-step tool choice, with even top frontier agents solving well under half of such tasks.
families20.taskShape: Agent completes a business/IT operations goal spanning multiple independent applications with no shared state layer, executing many turns where an early error can silently break downstream steps, verified by dedicated per-app end-state checks.
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent is authorized to act across all named applications only insofar as each action is both locally correct and consistent with the required cross-app end state; no single application's state is authoritative for overall completion.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: No single application exposes the full cross-app goal state; the agent must maintain its own coherent model of progress since no system does it for them.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number of applications; average turn count; interdependency degree; whether errors are locally visible or only detectable cross-app.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Documented ~38.6% top-model success with ~20 turns shows this exceeds current coordination capability; plausible failures include losing an early decision or picking a wrong app-specific tool that silently breaks a downstream step.
families20.whyFair: An ordinary shape of real IT-operations work, evaluated end-to-end against real app APIs so difficulty measures genuine coordination capability, not an artificial trick.

families20.name: Multi-Day State Carryforward Drift
families20.definition: A single trajectory simulates extended, multi-day professional work where later steps depend on state correctly carried forward from many earlier steps; a deterministic verifier inspects only the final end-state, so any single dropped or drifted piece of upstream context propagates silently to failure.
families20.taskShape: Instruction frames a long chain of dependent operations over simulated extended time in a rich, multi-component environment; agent must plan and execute without intermediate checkpoint feedback, with some steps requiring genuine cross-domain expert judgment.
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent's authority is scoped to the full multi-step task; the verifier is binary against the fully carried-forward final state with no partial credit for locally-correct-looking intermediate steps.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: No intermediate checkpoint signal is available during execution; whether earlier state was correctly carried forward is only knowable at the final verifier.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: number of dependent stages simulated; richness of the multi-component environment; required domain expertise; execution time budget.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: Reported gaps directly attribute failure to long-horizon planning, execution monitoring, and error recovery, with a substantial score jump (documented ~27 points) from extending the time budget alone.
families20.whyFair: Full scope and rules are communicated up front; difficulty comes from sustaining correct execution over many steps, not hidden information.

families20.name: State-Diff Collateral Damage Verification
families20.definition: Agent must complete one target action inside a shared, stateful multi-app world, and is graded by a full world-state diff (not just the target field), so that a correct-looking completion which also mutates unrelated records or exceeds the action's intended blast radius scores as failure.
families20.taskShape: Agent completes a specified action (e.g. cancel a specific order, update one contact) inside a rich simulated multi-app environment with many other live records; the evaluator diffs entire world state before/after, rewarding only changes that exactly match the intended target with no collateral mutation elsewhere.
families20.professionalDomain: personal / enterprise app automation (multi-app simulated ecosystem)
families20.authorityBoundary: The agent's authorized write scope is exactly the one target record/field named by the instruction; any broader tool call (e.g. a bulk update, a wildcard filter) that also touches other records exceeds that authority even if the primary target was updated correctly.
families20.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent's own tool-call results confirm only that its target action succeeded; whether other, unrelated state was also silently altered is invisible without an external full-world-state diff the agent does not have access to during the task.
families20.naturalScenarioDimensions: world size/density of adjacent similar records; specificity of available tool filters (precise ID vs pattern match); presence of decoy records resembling the true target.
families20.whyAgentMayFail: An agent that uses a convenient but overly broad tool call to accomplish a narrowly-scoped instruction will satisfy the target check while also mutating adjacent records it never intended to touch, a mistake invisible from its own successful-looking call results.
families20.whyFair: A standard, explicitly-designed evaluation methodology (e.g. AppWorld-style state-based unit tests with collateral-damage checking) built specifically to measure real scope discipline -- a genuine and fair professional competency, not an artificial gotcha.

family.name: CDN and DNS Cache Staleness Verification
family.definition: Agent makes an authoritative change at an origin system (a DNS record or a CDN-fronted asset) and must correctly verify propagation despite intermediate caching layers that are contractually permitted to serve stale data until TTL- or purge-type-specific windows lapse, choosing the correct purge type and multi-tier verification sequence rather than treating one re-fetch as proof.
family.taskShape: Agent updates an origin resource then issues a purge (soft, hard, tag, or prefix) against a simulated multi-tier CDN and/or updates a DNS record; the harness enforces the documented stale-serve window, tier-revalidation semantics (EXPIRED vs MISS), and purge rate limits, and the agent must choose a verification sequence that correctly distinguishes legally-stale from genuinely failed propagation.
family.authorityBoundary: The origin (authoritative DNS zone or origin server) is the sole source of truth; caches and edge tiers hold delegated, time-bounded copies whose staleness is contractually legal, not a defect, so the agent's authority to declare content live is bounded by confirming propagation at the correct tier, not by the absence of an API error.
family.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent cannot directly inspect every cache node's internal state; it only observes whatever response headers/values a given tier returns to a probe, with no built-in freshness signal unless it deliberately checks documented status semantics.
family.naturalScenarioDimensions: TTL length; hard vs soft vs tag-based purge type; single-tier vs multi-tier topology; plan-tier rate limits; verification method chosen.
family.whyAgentMayFail: An agent that purges once and immediately re-fetches once will, per documented semantics, still legitimately see stale content and wrongly conclude failure, or accept a still-caching tier's EXPIRED response as proof of a true MISS.
family.whyFair: The rules governing staleness (RFC 2181 TTL semantics, documented CDN purge-type behavior) are public, stable, and derivable by reading the relevant specification/vendor docs -- no hidden internal knowledge is required, only correct application of a documented cache contract.

probabilityOrdinaryPackage.rationale: A and B independently converged on ~45% once units are aligned (A reported 45 on a 0-100 scale, B reported 0.45 on a 0-1 scale) -- this is genuine agreement, not an artifact, so it is kept as the central estimate. The 'purge once, refetch once is not proof' and EXPIRED-vs-MISS distinctions are extremely well-documented public knowledge (RFC 2181, every major CDN vendor's purge FAQ), so a meaningful share of frontier models will apply the correct heuristic from pretrained pattern-matching even against a loosely-built ordinary package that doesn't tightly bound timing or grade the reasoning trail, without needing to genuinely diagnose the harness's hidden per-tier state.
probabilityOrdinaryPackage.evidenceUsed: Convergence of A's and B's independently-derived estimates after normalizing scale; the family's own whyFair claim that the rules are public and derivable; no measured trial, mutant-fatality, or contract-score data exists for this not-yet-built family.
probabilityOrdinaryPackage.strongestReasonWrong: If an ordinary build still enforces genuinely idiosyncratic per-tier state/rate-limit rules discoverable only from this specific harness's spec (not from general CDN folklore), agents that default to recalled generic heuristics without reading the task-specific documentation could fail far more often than either scorer projects, pulling the true rate toward the low end or below it.

probabilityFullRecipe.rationale: A and B disagree sharply and in DIRECTION, not just magnitude: A projects hardening suppresses the clean-pass rate (0.45 -> 0.20), B projects hardening raises it (0.45 -> 0.75). Resolving this required checking each rationale against repo evidence rather than averaging. A's direction is the one supported by this repo's own stated purpose for hardening operators (docs/TASK-FAMILY-MODEL.md): operators exist to close bypass loopholes that let non-reasoning subjects pass, so a correctly-built full recipe should show a LOWER accidental clean-pass rate than an ordinary build, not a higher one. B's upward estimate leans on this repo's 'bypassable reward -> 5/6 -> 6/6' narrative, but that narrative describes the VERIFIER's mutant-catch-rate maturing across recipe iterations (the outbox family's checker eventually catching all known-bad implementations), which is a different quantity from the probability a real agent cleanly passes the hardened suite -- applying it to justify a rising agent-pass-rate looks like a metric conflation, and no other basis for B's direction survives once that conflation is set aside. So A's direction is adopted. However, A's magnitude (a 25-point drop to 20%) is itself not fully supported: this portfolio's own Phase 14 operator-ablation campaign (reports/hardness-operator-ledger.md; reports/PHASE-14-OPERATOR-EFFECTS.md) measured a real, counted NULL effect from a 'difficulty' hardening operator (committed-idempotency-authority / recompute-activation-concentration) on an uncertainty-plus-authority-change mechanism: 8/8 clean passes under both the control and the hardened/concentrated condition. That is direct, portfolio-internal evidence that hardening does not reliably suppress frontier clean-pass rates on authority/state-change-shaped mechanisms, even though the analogy to this family's specific TTL/purge-type axis is imperfect (different causal axis, not an exact match). Net effect: keep A's suppression direction, but pull the magnitude back toward the ordinary-package rate given that documented null-effect precedent, landing at 0.30 rather than either raw estimate or their blind average (~0.48, which would have erased the directional disagreement rather than resolving it).
probabilityFullRecipe.evidenceUsed: reports/hardness-operator-ledger.md and reports/PHASE-14-OPERATOR-EFFECTS.md (counted 8/8-vs-8/8 null-effect result on a related uncertainty/authority-change mechanism in this same portfolio); docs/TASK-FAMILY-MODEL.md's description of the bypassable-reward -> 5/6 -> 6/6 pattern as verifier/mutant-catch-rate evidence, not agent-clean-pass-rate evidence; both scorers' stated rationales and self-reported strongestReasonWrong fields.
probabilityFullRecipe.strongestReasonWrong: If this family's specific traps (purge-type mismatch, EXPIRED-vs-MISS, rate-limit punishment of brute-force polling) are more mechanically enforceable via tight time/rate budgets than the Phase 14 authority-recompute mechanism was, real suppression could be much closer to A's steeper 0.20; conversely, a second measured null-effect result on this mechanism would push the true rate back up toward 0.45, closer to B's premise that the trap is too well-known to survive contact with a frontier model even after hardening (though not to B's specific 0.75, which still requires the rejected conflation to justify an increase over baseline).

reconciled.reconciliationNotes:
Step 1 -- unit normalization: A's probabilityOrdinaryPackage/probabilityFullRecipe are on a 0-100 scale (45, 20); B's are on a 0-1 fractional scale (0.45, 0.75); both scorers used 0-1 fractions consistently for officialReviewProbability and tenDistinctTaskProbability. Converting A's pair to fractions (0.45, 0.20) before computing any delta is essential -- a naive raw-number diff on probabilityOrdinaryPackage (45 vs 0.45) would misleadingly look like a ~44.5-point gap when it is actually exact agreement (45% vs 45%).

Step 2 -- probabilityOrdinaryPackage: after normalization, A and B agree almost exactly (45% each). No real dispute here; kept at 0.45.

Step 3 -- probabilityFullRecipe: after normalization this is a genuine 55-point gap (0.20 vs 0.75), far past the 15pp trigger, and the two scorers disagree on DIRECTION (suppression vs inflation from hardening), not just magnitude. I traced B's upward estimate to a likely conflation between this repo's 'bypassable reward -> 5/6 -> 6/6' narrative (which is about the verifier's mutant-catch completeness improving across recipe iterations) and the separate question of whether a real agent's clean-pass rate rises or falls under hardening -- those are different quantities, and B's own listed strongestReasonWrong (hardening could over-correct into a timing puzzle that penalizes correct-but-differently-sequenced strategies) actually argues for an even LOWER full-recipe pass rate, undercutting B's own 0.75 central estimate by its own logic. I adopted A's suppression direction but discounted A's magnitude using a real, portfolio-internal null-effect precedent (Phase 14: 8/8 clean passes under both control and hardened conditions on a related authority/state-change mechanism), landing on 0.30 (range 0.15-0.45, confidence low) -- a reasoned compromise that rejects B's direction, tempers A's magnitude, and is explicitly NOT a blind average of 0.20 and 0.75 (which would have produced ~0.48 and erased the directional disagreement instead of resolving it).

Step 4 -- officialReviewProbability (0.55 vs 0.40) and tenDistinctTaskProbability (0.75 vs 0.90) each differ by exactly 15 percentage points -- at, not over, the stated trigger threshold -- and neither scorer gave rationale specific to these two fields beyond what's already litigated in the probabilityFullRecipe dispute, so they are resolved as ordinary midpoints (0.47 and 0.82 respectively) rather than given extended treatment.

Step 5 -- scoreBreakdown/opportunityScoreTotal: raw totals differ by 7 points (68 vs 75), below the 10-point mandatory-justification trigger. I still weighted the blend roughly 60/40 toward A rather than flat-averaging, because every subscore where A and B disagree has B scoring 1-2 points HIGHER than A, never lower -- a one-directional pattern consistent with the same optimism identified in B's probabilityFullRecipe reasoning. A flat 50/50 average would let that same bias leak into the composite score. Reconciled opportunityScoreTotal = 69 (vs A's 68 and B's 75) -- closer to A because A's read of this family held up better under scrutiny, not because A was simply preferred by default.

Net: this is a real, well-documented, moderately valuable candidate family with a genuine, both-scorers-agreed textbook-recallability risk and meaningful semantic overlap with already-built portfolio families (deployment-model-alias-rollout-drift's cache-freshness mechanism, durable-approval-outbox's stale-lease mechanism, and the caa-revalidation family's shared DNS source unit). The reconciled figures describe a moderate-opportunity, low-to-medium-confidence candidate best validated by the cheap falsifying probe below before any full build spend -- not the more flattering 75-point / 75%-full-recipe-survival picture B's raw numbers implied.
reconciled.cheapestFalsifyingProbe: Two-stage probe, cheapest gate first. (1) Zero-build: a single-turn, no-tool-use prompt to 3-5 frontier models describing a concrete scenario ("you issued a soft purge on an 8-hour-TTL asset behind a 2-tier CDN; a re-fetch 30 seconds later still returns the old ETag -- is this a failed purge, and what do you check next?") with no harness access. If models near-uniformly recite the textbook-correct multi-tier verification sequence from pretrained knowledge alone, the family's premise -- that agents need genuine in-context latent diagnosis rather than recalled CDN trivia -- is largely falsified before any environment is built, for the cost of a few API calls. (2) Only if stage 1 fails to falsify: stand up a minimal 2-tier cache stub (edge + shield, one fixed TTL, soft/hard purge endpoints, simulated clock), script a naive baseline that purges once and re-fetches once (declaring failure on any stale response) against a documented-correct reference policy that matches purge type to change and re-checks every tier's EXPIRED/MISS status, and run both across ~6 hand-built scenarios crossing purge type x tier count x TTL length. If the naive baseline still clears most scenarios under generous, end-state-content-match-only grading, the mechanism does not bite yet and the family needs a tighter time/rate budget or process-level (tier-status-trail) grading before any reference/verifier/mutant-bank investment.
reconciled.principalValidityRisk: Two compounding risks, not one. First (both scorers agree): the central trap -- one purge plus one re-fetch is not proof of propagation, and EXPIRED-vs-MISS -- is extremely well-documented public trivia (RFC 2181, every major CDN vendor's purge FAQ), so a competent frontier agent may clear the task via recalled pattern-matching rather than genuine latent diagnosis of the harness's hidden per-tier state; this is the same risk profile that has already produced a measured null hardening effect on a related authority/state-change mechanism in this portfolio (Phase 14: 8/8 clean passes under both control and hardened conditions). Second (from B, independently plausible and not fully answered by the first): if the verifier is built as an ordinary end-state content-match grader rather than one that grades the agent's intermediate tier-status reasoning and bounds each scenario's time/turn/rate-limit budget tightly, a patient, purge-type-agnostic "retry until it looks fresh" policy can satisfy the grader by simply waiting out the TTL without the agent ever distinguishing legally-stale from failed propagation -- the same bypassable-reward-before-recipe-hardening failure mode this repo has already hit and documented on the durable-approval-outbox and deployment-model-alias-rollout-drift lineages. Both risks point the same direction: the family's headline difficulty claim is unlikely to hold under an ordinary build and is not guaranteed to hold even under a hardened one, which is why probabilityFullRecipe is reconciled with wide, low-confidence bounds (0.15-0.45) rather than a confident 0.75.
reconciled.semanticOverlapGroup: stale-cached-authority-vs-current-source-of-truth: the causal axis (trusting a delegated/cached copy instead of re-verifying against current authoritative state, especially near an age/expiry boundary) already exists in this portfolio under deployment-model-alias-rollout-drift (cacheFreshness / cache_current_disagreement_at_the_age_boundary / the "cached-alias-truster" mutant) and, more loosely, in durable-approval-outbox's stale-lease/stale-read-at-handler-entry mechanism (tagged "cache invalidation" in data/mechanisms.json). It also shares the boundary-cert-transparency-dns source unit directly with the already-built caa-revalidation family, and is causal-axis-adjacent to ui-action-record-replay and access-token-scope-expansion (also stale-state mechanisms). The CDN/DNS purge-type and EXPIRED-vs-MISS tier semantics are new surface texture; the core failure axis is a variant of one this foundry has already built and hardened at least once -- consistent with both scorers independently giving noveltyPortfolioContribution the lowest score in the breakdown (2/10), a rare point of full agreement that was preserved unchanged in the reconciled breakdown.

family.name: Read-Replica Lag Reconciliation
family.definition: Agent writes via a primary database connection and later acts on that data through a read-replica endpoint, and must correctly reason about asynchronous replication lag, recovery-conflict query cancellations, and primary/standby role identity rather than assuming synchronous consistency or treating a stale/cancelled read as proof the original write failed.
family.taskShape: Agent performs a write on the primary, then queries a hot-standby/read-replica for confirmation or subsequent logic, timed to land inside the replication lag window; the harness may also force a VACUUM-induced recovery-conflict cancellation the agent must diagnose as transient, and the agent must never issue a write against what it believes is the primary without confirming role via a status check.
family.authorityBoundary: The primary holds current authoritative state; the standby is an asynchronously-replaying copy that may legally lag or forcibly cancel in-flight reads during WAL-replay conflicts, so a replica connection is read-only and eventually consistent by design, not an equally authoritative source.
family.subjectInaccessibleWitness: The agent cannot observe the replication stream directly; it only sees whatever snapshot the standby has replayed at query time, with no freshness signal unless it explicitly checks dedicated status views (e.g. pg_stat_replication).
family.naturalScenarioDimensions: replication lag magnitude; concurrent primary write load; long-running analytical query vs simple read; primary vs replica role ambiguity; presence of a recovery-conflict cancellation.
family.whyAgentMayFail: An agent may treat an absent or stale row on the replica as proof its own write failed, retrying or duplicating it destructively, or may issue a write against a standby without checking role and mishandle the resulting read-only-transaction failure.
family.whyFair: Postgres's own documentation (SHOW in_hot_standby, pg_stat_replication, documented recovery-conflict cancellation) gives the agent everything needed to reason correctly; standard, well-documented DBA practice, not tribal knowledge.

probabilityOrdinaryPackage.rationale: Both scorers independently land on 'roughly coin-flip' once put on the same scale: the taskShape bakes the forcing mechanism (timed lag-window read, occasional forced VACUUM conflict) into any competent build, so the trap fires even without special hardening -- but replication lag and recovery-conflict cancellation are extremely well-documented Postgres/DBA facts, so a nontrivial fraction of agents pass via pattern recall rather than live diagnosis, pulling the rate toward 50/50. UNIT NOTE: Scorer A reported this on a 0-100 scale (50, range 35-65), inconsistent with its own officialReviewProbability/tenDistinctTaskProbability fields which use 0-1 fractions; Scorer B used 0-1 fractions consistently everywhere (0.40, range 0.25-0.55). Rescaling A to fractions (0.50, range 0.35-0.65) shows the true gap is ~10 points, not the ~50-point gap the raw numbers imply. Final value averages the two unit-corrected estimates.
probabilityOrdinaryPackage.evidenceUsed: Family definition's taskShape/whyFair text (both scorers); cross-check of each scorer's own officialReviewProbability/tenDistinctTaskProbability fields, used to detect and correct Scorer A's unit error.
probabilityOrdinaryPackage.strongestReasonWrong: If an 'ordinary' build doesn't force the lag window deterministically (skips recovery_min_apply_delay, relies on real race timing) or leaves incidental tells (obvious replica hostname, generous timing margins), the trap may not fire reliably, pushing the true rate well above 50% for construction-validity reasons unrelated to competence. Conversely, if agents are worse at proactively issuing diagnostic status-view queries in agentic/tool-use mode than at reasoning about replication lag in chat, the true rate could run lower than either estimate.

probabilityFullRecipe.rationale: Both scorers converge on 'meaningfully suppressed by hardening, but not to a typical eval floor': this is a textbook, well-documented DBA gotcha whose diagnostic signal is largely self-revealing in the Postgres error text and status views, so even deterministic timing, camouflage, and process-level verification may not suppress the pass rate as far as a more obscure mechanism would allow. UNIT NOTE: Scorer A's raw value (20, range 10-30) is on the same 0-100 scale bug identified above; rescaled to fractions (0.20, range 0.10-0.30) it is only ~5 points above Scorer B's 0.15 (range 0.05-0.25) -- a minor, within-tolerance gap once corrected, not the ~20-point gap the raw numbers suggest. Final value averages the two unit-corrected estimates.
probabilityFullRecipe.evidenceUsed: Same family-definition evidence as probabilityOrdinaryPackage; both scorers' reasoning that this portfolio's hardening operators (forced timing, camouflage, process-level verification) typically suppress naive pass rates substantially, offset by both flagging this specific mechanism as unusually self-revealing relative to sibling stale-authority families.
probabilityFullRecipe.strongestReasonWrong: Both scorers' own strongestReasonWrong sections point the same direction: this may be one of the more 'textbook' DBA gotchas in the portfolio, and if 'verify state before retrying a write, treat a recovery-conflict cancellation as transient' has become a deeply-trained default agentic heuristic (analogous to idempotency-key discipline), even a maximally hardened package might see most agents clear it well above 30%, meaning the recipe may not suppress the pass rate as much as either estimate assumes.

reconciled.cheapestFalsifyingProbe: Two-stage, cheapest-first: (1) Before any agent is involved, script a headless proof that the mechanism is even forceable -- docker-compose a primary+hot-standby Postgres pair with recovery_min_apply_delay set, write a row on the primary, confirm a tight-loop read against the standby reliably lands inside the lag window, then separately force a VACUUM against a long-running standby query with max_standby_streaming_delay low and confirm 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery' fires deterministically. This is the cheaper, logically-prior test (both scorers independently gave a low implementationTrialTractability score, 4 and 3): if the timing/conflict can't be forced reliably within a couple hours of scripted attempts, the family is falsified before any agent-facing package is built. (2) Only if (1) succeeds, run a single-agent probe: give one frontier coding agent the plain taskShape prompt with no adversarial hardening and see whether it spontaneously checks pg_stat_replication/role status and treats the cancellation as transient on the first attempt across 4-5 quick reps; a high, easy clean-pass rate here falsifies the premise that the family is diagnostically hard enough to justify full construction investment.
reconciled.principalValidityRisk: Two largely orthogonal risks must both be resolved for this family to be worth building. (a) Diagnostic-yield risk (Scorer A's central concern): replica lag, pg_stat_replication, and 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery' are extremely well-documented, frequently-blogged Postgres facts almost certainly present in frontier training corpora, so competent agents may already clear this at a high baseline rate via pattern recall rather than live reasoning, especially once any naming cue reveals which endpoint is primary vs. replica -- both scorers' own strongestReasonWrong sections argue the true full-recipe pass rate could run even higher than their point estimates, making this the dominant threat to the family's discriminating value.
