recipeCards.multiFileCodebaseSketch: `app/receiver.py` (signature verification + intake) · `app/events/schema.py` (typed per-object-type event envelopes) · `app/reconciler/apply.py` (freshness/precedence decision surface — ~30-50 lines, independently unit-testable, defeated by `order-by-created`) · `app/reconciler/dedupe.py` (identity+type collapse decision surface — ~30-50 lines, defeated by `dedupe-by-event-id`) · `app/incidents/monitor.py` (retry-authority decision surface — ~30-50 lines, defeated by `resend-closes-incident`; NOT a shared call into `apply.py` — a separately-coded consultation of the ledger) · `app/incidents/resend_tool.py` (admin resend simulation) · `app/state/store.py` (local materialized view, never authoritative) · `app/cli.py` (`deliver <schedule.json>`, `resend <event_id>`, `status <object_id>`) · `tests/test_handlers.py`, `tests/test_reconciler_basic.py` (visible tests) · `platform_sim/truth_log.py` + `platform_sim/ledger.py` (root-owned sidecar) · `platform_sim/leaky_facade.py` (NEW: the deliberately-leaky canary variant used only in the pre-flight `C8`-style isolation control, never in a graded scenario) · `verifier/grade.py` (separate process; NEW: also computes and emits the 0-3 self-check-coverage score per submission, non-blocking).
recipeCards.narrowDevMutants: `dedupe-by-event-id` (dedupes solely on the event's own id — defeats the identity-type-collapse surface) · `order-by-created` (applies whichever delivered event carries the larger created/receipt-order value — defeats the freshness-precedence surface) · `resend-closes-incident` (treats a single 2xx to a manual resend as terminal — defeats the retry-authority surface). Each maps 1:1 to one of the three decision surfaces named in `familyNativeDifficultyOperators`, and each must fail on a distinct verifier check line (confirmed at the `cheapestPackageValidityProbe` stage), not the same shared assertion.
recipeCards.heldOutMutants: `receipt-order-trust` (blunter freshness-surface variant: strict arrival order, no timestamp/id logic at all) · `type-blind-keying` (blunter identity-surface variant: keys dedup on object id alone, wrongly collapsing distinct event types) · NEW: `ledger-blind-resolve` (blunter retry-authority-surface variant: closes an incident once N consecutive resend attempts return 2xx, counting only local attempts and never consulting the ledger — added this revision because the prior held-out set covered only two of the three decision surfaces, leaving retry-authority with no held-out validation).
recipeCards.nonApplicableOperators: Of the 8 named operators, one does not transfer in its measured/literal form: `committed-idempotency-authority` (recovering a self-committed idempotency key across an outbound-call lease epoch after a crash) — this family's authority problem is inbound-event freshness/identity, not the subject issuing its own idempotent outbound call across a lease epoch; forcing one in would import an unrelated obligation. `narrow-recompute-starter`'s literal content likewise does not apply; only its generalized principle — seed the starter with the single most natural real-world mistake, not a strawman — is retained. The remaining 6 operators apply, several only by analogy: `recompute-activation-concentration`'s "multi-worker schedule" concentration generalizes to concentrating scenario selection on schedules with ≥2 concurrently in-flight deliveries/objects; `a2-explicit-terminal-state-repair`'s lesson generalizes to publishing one explicit outcome sentence naming which local states are terminal, without naming the anti-pattern that causes violations — now enforced by the rewritten `publicOutcomeRequirements` and the new forbidden-phrase lint. None of these mappings are measured — evidenceType "fresh-external," isCalibrationAnchor false — every operator application is a plausible-but-unablated hypothesis, not a replication of a measured effect.
recipeCards.positiveWorkAndCheatControls: positive-work (reference consumer, full credit) · no-op (must fail the "eventually reflected" requirement) · always-refuse (must fail processing requirements; rig confirms this fails rather than vacuously passing) · unconditional-fresh (treats every delivered event as authoritative regardless of identity/type) · hardcoded-terminal-map (hardcodes terminal types without checking freshness) · self-attested-resolution (writes its own "retries stopped" record instead of consulting ground truth) · NEW: `leaky-facade-canary` (a rig-level, non-subject-facing control: a deliberately-leaky sidecar facade that must be caught by the isolation check itself, proving that check is falsifiable — see `externalAuthorityOrWitness`).
recipeCards.scenarioSelectionStrategy: Fuzz over event-type collision × gap size × resend timing × split-duplicate composition × concurrent-object count; keep points where the reference passes and at least one narrow mutant fails. Structural requirement, tightened this revision: every graded scenario must contain at least one out-of-order pair AND at least one split-duplicate pair (as before), and a MAJORITY of the graded set must additionally include a resend-during-active-retry case, so that all three decision surfaces (identity-type-collapse, freshness-precedence, retry-authority) are jointly exercised rather than only two of three — directly addressing the "one decision undershoots a coin flip" concern by compounding three independent ~50% surfaces rather than reusing one. Selection is hypothesized to concentrate around ≥2 concurrently in-flight objects/events, by analogy to the multi-worker concentration lesson. Held-out mutants (`receipt-order-trust`, `type-blind-keying`, `ledger-blind-resolve` — now one per surface) are run only against previously-unseen parameter combinations to confirm the selected region generalizes.
recipeCards.visibleTestStrategy: Visible tests exercise each event type's happy-path handler once, and redeliver one event with the exact same event id to confirm idempotent no-op behavior — both pass. This is realistic: it is the first idempotency test any team writes, and per this project's own prior evidence (a merged discovery-track candidate on the same axis notes "the natural test delivers the same event twice back to back and cannot fail"). The gap is structural and unchanged by this revision: no visible test reorders two different event types for the same object, none constructs a split-duplicate pair with two distinct ids, and none exercises a manual resend concurrent with a still-pending automatic retry — so the suite cannot see any of the three graded decision surfaces.
recipeCards.infoIntentionallyAbsent: Which event types collide in the out-of-order pair; the gap size between the two out-of-order deliveries; whether a manual resend will be attempted and its timing relative to the platform's automatic retries; how many split-duplicate pairs occur and their type composition; the platform's internal automatic-retry schedule and countdown; the fact that two distinct event ids can represent one logical change; and no naming of the historical anti-pattern itself anywhere in instruction or schema text. Strengthened this revision: this is no longer only a stated intent — the actual `publicOutcomeRequirements` text has been rewritten to remove the three confirmed instances of field-specific naming that all three skeptics found (see `mainFairnessRisks`), and a new automated lint (extending `src/phase-16/contract-gate.ts`'s `FORBIDDEN_PHRASES` pattern with family-specific tokens for "event id," "created," "receipt order," "resend," and "operator-triggered") is a listed kill condition to prevent recurrence in future edits to this card.
recipeCards.fuzzerDimensions: Which event types collide in the out-of-order pair · gap size between the out-of-order deliveries · whether a manual resend is attempted and its timing relative to the automatic retry schedule (before/during/after) · number and type-composition of split-duplicate pairs · number of objects with concurrently in-flight deliveries (hypothesized controlling parameter, per `recompute-activation-concentration`'s generalized lesson) · malformed/replay/signature-invalid deliveries as non-activation controls · NEW: whether the scenario is drawn from the majority subset required to jointly exercise all three decision surfaces (identity-type-collapse, freshness-precedence, retry-authority) versus a minority subset exercising only one or two, used to confirm the joint-difficulty claim in `scenarioSelectionStrategy`.

skepticVerdicts.reasoning:
Grounded this review in the repo's own prior evidence rather than the recipe card's self-description, specifically reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md (the CAA V1 postmortem), data/hardness-operators.json, data/retired-candidates.json, reports/adversarial-container-isolation-report.md, reports/adversarial-isolation-report.md, and src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts.

CAA V1's exact failure mode, as recorded in this repo (PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md line 340 and §12): the reference was "roughly fifteen lines with one decision," and "the specification's forbidden outcomes name the historical anti-pattern in words" — both of which let 4/4 agents' natural self-checks trivially cover the rule (VALID-BUT-EASY, §9 self-check table: 4/4 "named the identity-collapse failure mode explicitly"). Phase 17's own §12 recommendations (not yet implemented, per its own text) are: (1) add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate as a *ranking feature*, not pass/fail — "The gate currently has no feature that would have separated them"; (2) penalize naming the anti-pattern; (3) penalize small artifact size — "pushing below a coin-flip needs a second independent decision of comparable difficulty; this candidate has one"; (5) require a negative-control canary for every isolation/non-leakage claim, because "two of Phase 16's seven reported controls could not fail."

Checking the four specific probes against this baseline:

1. Anti-pattern naming — the recipe genuinely avoids this. `publicOutcomeRequirements` are outcome-only, and `infoIntentionallyAbsent` explicitly commits to never naming event.id/created/receipt-order/resend-closes-incident, citing the Phase 17 lesson by name. This one check is well-handled.

2. Reference-implementation thinness — only partially addressed. The card leans on "a ~1,000-1,200 line webhook-consumer service" to imply it isn't CAA-V1-thin, but that number is scaffolding (schema, CLI, admin tool, incident infra); only the actual decision logic at the two named call sites (`apply.py`, shared judgment in `monitor.py`) is graded, and nothing in the card bounds or guarantees that logic isn't itself a short conditional exactly like CAA V1's fifteen-line function. Critically, the card cites Phase 17 for the anti-naming lesson but never engages Phase 17's *more directly relevant* recommendation #3 ("a second independent decision of comparable difficulty") even though it is the single most on-point prior finding for this exact question. The card's own framing — "one coherent conflation" reused at two call sites, explicitly not "two-plus independently injected bugs" (mainFairnessRisks) — sits in unresolved tension with Phase 17's prescription that a single decision undershoots a coin flip. This is a real, unaddressed gap, not a resolved one.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor — confirmed absent. `src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts` is a real, working predictor, but it is hard-coded to the durable-outbox's `ACKED_TERMINAL` rule and has not been generalized or instantiated for this family. Phase 17 states in its own voice that this predictor does not yet exist as a contract-gate ranking feature ("The gate currently has no feature that would have separated them, and it ranked this candidate 85 out of 85"). The recipe card's `mainFairnessRisks` only aspires ("the contract/verifier should record which requirement facets a submission actually exercised") — a different, coarser idea (scenario/requirement coverage, not subject self-check coverage) — and even that is unbuilt. `privateVerifierArchitecture` is finer-grained pass/fail (per-instant, per-resolve-call) but is still pass/fail, not a coverage predictor. So: confirmed — just pass/fail, dressed up as interval grading.

4. External witness inaccessibility — unproven infrastructure, not unreasonable design. The sidecar design (root-owned, non-imported, separate-process) matches a pattern (`fs-sandbox`) that has empirically shown 0 leaks across many existing families per reports/adversarial-isolation-report.md. But reports/adversarial-container-isolation-report.md shows the *stronger* container-level isolation the recipe explicitly invokes ("per the portfolio's now-standard §15-style verifier-isolation repair," "separate isolated process/container") is not operational for any family in this repo today — docker daemon unavailable, "container smoke not run during deterministic bundle preparation" for every bundle. And this specific new family has zero isolation records since it is unbuilt. Additionally, Phase 17 recommendation #5 (a negative-control canary proving the isolation check can actually fail) is not present anywhere in the card's controls/killConditions — the card lists behavioral cheat controls (self-attested-resolution) but no canary that deliberately breaches the sidecar boundary to prove the isolation *check itself* is non-vacuous, which is exactly the defect Phase 16's CAA probe had ("two of seven reported controls could not fail").

Corroborating spot-checks that came back accurate (raising, not lowering, my confidence in the analysis, since the card's citations are traceable and correct rather than fabricated): the "operator-9-style" pattern matches `grade-the-obligation-from-the-external-party-log` in data/hardness-operators.json verbatim, correctly flagged there as a validity control that "did not measurably make the task hard" — the recipe correctly does not credit it as a hardness driver. `payment-webhook-outbox-reconcile` and `duplicate-side-effect-webhook-retry` are real retired candidates in data/retired-candidates.json at p=[0.85,1] for exactly the reason cited. `committed-idempotency-authority`'s exclusion reasoning is accurate to its ledger description.

Net: the card is honest about its own uncertainty (evidenceType "fresh-external," isCalibrationAnchor false, "no MEASURED 0/N instantiation," 25-50% low-to-medium confidence), which is commendable, but that same honesty is the reason to default to refuted. Two of the four specifically-flagged risks — a real self-check-coverage predictor, and genuine (canary-proven) subject-inaccessibility of the witness — are confirmed not yet built for this family, and a third (reference thinness) has an unresolved tension with this project's own freshest and most relevant lesson that the card cites selectively (taking the anti-naming lesson, skipping the "one decision undershoots a coin flip" and "canary every isolation claim" lessons from the same report). Given the instruction to default to refuted when genuinely uncertain, and given concrete, sourced gaps rather than mere speculation, the probability claims (particularly the ~35% uplift estimate and the implicit claim that the fairness risks are adequately controlled) are refuted as currently unsupported — not because the mechanism is unfair or poorly conceived, but because the specific epistemic supports the card leans on (contract-gate self-check prediction, isolation canaries) do not yet exist in this codebase for this family, contrary to the impression the card's citations create.

Verdict: REFUTED. I grounded this against the repo's own Phase 17 CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md), the contract-gate implementation (src/phase-16/contract-gate.ts), and the only self-check-coverage tooling in the repo (src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts). All four adversarial checks surface real, unresolved problems.

1) Reference-implementation thinness (unaddressed). Phase 17's own recorded lesson is explicit: "The reference here is roughly fifteen lines with one decision... Penalise small artifact size" (PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md §12.3). This recipe's ~1,000-1,200 line "realistic service" is padding around a defect described as "One coherent, unmarked design mistake reused at two call sites" — i.e., structurally one shared decision helper invoked twice, not two independent decisions. The recipe never estimates the actual line count / decision count of that shared helper, and its own killConditions/mainFairnessRisks list never flags artifact-size as a risk to check — despite this being verbatim the #3 lesson from the immediately preceding phase that this same card cites by name elsewhere. Unaddressed risk of recurrence.

2) Public instruction naming the anti-pattern (confirmed). infoIntentionallyAbsent explicitly claims "no naming of the historical anti-pattern itself... anywhere in instruction or forbidden-outcomes text," but publicOutcomeRequirements says: "never merely the most recently delivered, most recently created, or most recently retried representation" (this enumerates, in words, exactly the receipt-order / order-by-created / resend-based-retry heuristics that are the narrow mutants) and "a single successful response to an operator-triggered resend is not sufficient evidence of [retries ending] on its own" (this states the resend-closes-incident anti-pattern outright). This is the same shape of failure Phase 17 diagnosed in CAA V1 — "the specification's forbidden outcomes name the historical anti-pattern in words" — outcome-phrasing does not cure it when the sentence enumerates the exact wrong signals under test.

3) Self-check-coverage predictor (confirmed absent, not just theoretically weak). I read src/phase-16/contract-gate.ts's auditCandidateContract: it is strictly pass/fail (status accepted/rejected/refused from a deficiency list), with no coverage-likelihood or ranking score. The repo's only self-check-coverage code (src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts) is hardcoded to one prior rule (durable-outbox's ACKED_TERMINAL) and is not wired into family construction. Phase 17 itself says this predictor doesn't exist yet ("The gate currently has no feature that would have separated them, and it ranked this candidate 85 out of a possible 85") and recommends building one before further discovery. This recipe card, written after that recommendation and citing Phase 17 by name, includes no self-check-coverage estimate or gating step of its own — it relies entirely on narrowDevMutants/heldOutMutants pass/fail, exactly the mode the postmortem said is insufficient to predict VALID-BUT-EASY outcomes.

4) External witness inaccessibility/forgeability (partially confirmed problem, different flavor than expected). The platform_sim sidecar architecture (root-owned, separate container) is reasonable and mirrors the portfolio's §15 isolation repair, and a reachability kill-condition is listed. But: (a) no witness-isolation canary/negative-control is specified anywhere in this recipe's package-control list, which is exactly the repair Phase 17 had to bolt onto CAA after finding its isolation check was unfalsifiable ("C8-witness-isolation-with-canary"). (b) More seriously, infoIntentionallyAbsent explicitly withholds "the platform's internal automatic-retry schedule and countdown" from the subject, yet publicOutcomeRequirements demands the subject correctly determine when that retry activity has "genuinely ended." No in-band, subject-visible signal (e.g., a terminal "retries-exhausted" event or published retry window) is specified anywhere in the multiFileCodebaseSketch or event schema description that would make this derivable. That means this obligation may not satisfy the recipe's own fairness bar ("fully derivable from the object/event schema genuinely shipped to the subject... not from information withheld only to the verifier") — a subject can neither forge nor legitimately derive the answer, which is a fairness gap rather than a leak, but undermines the "demanding but fair" claim underlying the uplift estimate just as much.

Given two directly-confirmed gaps against the current codebase (no self-check-coverage predictor; public text that echoes/enumerates the anti-patterns) plus two plausible, unresolved structural risks (thin shared decision helper; a possibly non-derivable retry-completion obligation), the card's own honest hedging (evidenceType "fresh-external", isCalibrationAnchor false, "low-to-medium confidence") is earned, not just prudent — and per instructions to default to refuted under genuine uncertainty, the estimatedUplift/whyFair probability claims should be treated as unconfirmed and likely optimistic until these four points are concretely repaired and probed.

Verdict: REFUTED. The card explicitly invokes the Phase 17 / CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md) at multiple points, so it clearly targets that lesson — but on inspection it does not actually clear the bar the postmortem set, and in one place it appears to make a false claim about its own text.

1) Reference-implementation thinness (CAA V1's exact failure: ~15 lines, one decision point).
The card answers the size question with a decoy metric: outboxOperatorMapping item (1) cites "~1,000-1,200 lines" for the whole service (receiver, schema layer, dedup module, state store, monitor, resend tool, CLI). But the postmortem's actual finding wasn't "total file size" — it was that the graded DEFECT logic was ~15 lines with one decision. This card's own item (3) says the defect is "One coherent, unmarked design mistake reused at two call sites" (state-application and incident-closure) — i.e. the same freshness/authority-check function called twice, not two independent decisions. familyNativeDifficultyOperators reinforces this: "One coherent conflation ... manifesting on two call sites ... rather than two unrelated defects." So the actual decision surface an agent must get right is very likely still small (a single comparison/authority-check routine), just wrapped in 1000+ lines of unrelated scaffolding that adds no graded difficulty. The card never states a line count for the defect logic itself — the one number that would actually answer the question is omitted in favor of a number (total service size) that doesn't. There is a partially independent second axis (identity+type dedup keying is a logically distinct decision from the freshness/authority check), which is a real mitigating factor, but the card doesn't argue this explicitly, and killConditions/positiveWorkAndCheatControls suggest the graded set still leans on scenarios requiring "≥2 concurrently in-flight objects" to even activate the mechanism — a fragility echoing CAA's "controlling parameter... two is the threshold" finding, where the effect was real but exactly one bit deep. This risk is not resolved, only partially addressed.

2) Does the public instruction name the defect/anti-pattern?
Yes, and the card's own fairness-risk section falsely claims otherwise. mainFairnessRisks states: "every requirement above is phrased as an outcome, never as a prohibition on a named technique," and infoIntentionallyAbsent claims "no naming of the historical anti-pattern itself ... anywhere in instruction or forbidden-outcomes text." But:
- baseFamilyDefinition (explicitly "unchanged from the source family," i.e. part of what's public) states: "receipt order, the event's own id, and the event's own created timestamp are not by themselves sufficient evidence of either property."
- publicOutcomeRequirements — the actual outcome-based instruction text shipped to the subject per outboxOperatorMapping item (2) — states: "never merely the most recently delivered, most recently created, or most recently retried representation."
These two passages together name, by field, exactly the three narrow/held-out mutants' defects: dedupe-by-event-id (id), order-by-created (created), resend-closes-incident (retried/resend). This is the same shape as the CAA V1 failure the postmortem flagged ("CAA1 states the identity binding outright and the specification's forbidden outcomes name the historical anti-pattern in words") — telling the subject which specific fields are insufficient is functionally equivalent to naming the anti-pattern, since it removes exactly the shortcuts an agent would otherwise have to discover are wrong. This is a concrete, checkable contradiction inside the recipe card itself, not a matter of interpretation.

3) Real self-check-coverage predictor, or just pass/fail?
Just pass/fail, with an unfulfilled promissory note. privateVerifierArchitecture and the outboxOperatorMapping's "separate outcome-measuring verifier" describe interval-based and obligation-based pass/fail grading against the sidecar's ground truth — no mechanism for scoring which requirement facets a submission's own reasoning/self-check actually covered. mainFairnessRisks acknowledges the gap directly ("the contract/verifier should record which requirement facets a submission actually exercised, not only pass/fail, so a clean solve rate cannot mask a VALID-BUT-EASY outcome the way CAA V1's did") but this is aspirational language with no field describing how it would be captured — exactly recommendation #1 from PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md ("Add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate ... The gate currently has no feature that would have separated them") remains unimplemented here. The card names the missing predictor as a risk but doesn't build one.

4) External authority/witness — genuinely subject-inaccessible?
This is the strongest part of the card. Root-owned platform_sim sidecar, separate process/container per the project's own "§15-style verifier-isolation repair," a dedicated forgery control (self-attested-resolution — "an evidence-forging control the ledger's root ownership is specifically built to catch"), and an explicit kill condition if the sidecar "proves reachable or inferable from inside the subject's own process/container." This mirrors the negative-control repair the postmortem demanded in recommendation #5 ("Require a negative control for every isolation and non-leakage claim"). I did not find a clear forgery path in the design as described — this axis is comparatively well-argued, though still unbuilt/unmeasured (isCalibrationAnchor: false).

Net: two of the four specific risks (thinness-masked-by-scaffolding, and the anti-pattern being named in the actual public instruction text while the card claims otherwise) are real, demonstrable problems, and a third (no real coverage predictor, only a stated intention) is an acknowledged-but-unresolved gap. Only the external-witness design holds up under scrutiny. Given the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given these are not just uncertainty but affirmatively identified flaws — including a factual misstatement within the card about its own instruction text — the probability claims (estimatedUplift 15%→35%, and the implicit fairness/difficulty claims underlying it) should be treated as refuted/unreliable as presented.

recipeCards.name: Rollback That Reactivates a Dormant Defect
recipeCards.baseFamilyDefinition: Responding to a live incident on one of several replicated deployment targets, the agent must diagnose root cause before acting, because rolling back a recent change without isolating the cause can reproduce an identical latent bug -- a repurposed flag/identifier reaching never-removed deprecated code -- on previously-unaffected replicas.
recipeCards.outboxOperatorMapping: The literal append-only outbox is replaced by three domain-native external records that already exist in real fleet-ops/trading practice, per the instruction not to force outbox shape onto an unnatural family: (1) a venue/exchange execution ledger -- append-only, keyed by (parentOrderId, replicaId), recording what each replica actually submitted and what filled, independent of any replica's self-report; (2) a fleet attestation registry -- an independent infra service (not the subject's own status file) that fingerprints each replica's actually-running build hash and reachable-code signature on a schedule the subject does not control, checked against a deploy-target record fed only by the release pipeline (never by the subject's own writable deployment-manifest.json), so no remediation action can redefine what "intended version" means; (3) that same attestation service's own append-only inbound-query log, recording every request it receives -- including read-only audit calls -- with caller identity and timestamp. (3) is new in this revision, added specifically to close a gap an adversarial review identified: a build/reachability fingerprint alone attests to what CHANGED, not to what was merely READ/audited, so a subject's coverage claim ("I audited replicas 2, 5, 7") is now checked against this query log, not just fingerprint-change history. verifier-process-and-ledger-isolation: grading runs in a process the subject cannot import or patch, reading only these three external records plus a post-remediation canary probe, never the subject's own logs or "resolved" flag. a2-explicit-terminal-state-repair: one outcome sentence is stated explicitly and unambiguously -- "fleet convergence" means identical current-intended code (per the release-pipeline deploy-target record, not the subject-writable manifest) AND identical observable behavior for identical input across every replica, not merely "alerts have stopped" -- closing the ambiguity that let A2's terminal-state gap slip through undetected in the CAA lineage, and closing a second gap (uniform convergence onto a wrong, dormant-reactivating state passing as "resolved") by making no-retired-behavior an independent outcome requirement rather than relying on convergence alone. narrow-mutant-isolation: each dev/held-out mutant differs from the reference by exactly one policy switch, for attribution purposes only (guard the reused identifier vs. leave the dormant interpreter reachable; redeploy-and-restart the stale replica vs. roll the fleet back to match it) -- this is a pairwise reference-vs-one-mutant property and is distinct from, and does not substitute for, the reference-thickness-gate below, which governs the reference's own internal decision count. reference-thickness-gate (new this revision): the reference implementation is rejected at construction time unless it comprises at least four independently-necessary, separately-revertible changes, each mapped to a distinct verifier check that fails if that one change alone is reverted -- see cheapestPackageValidityProbe -- directly answering the Phase 17 postmortem finding that a ~15-line, one-decision reference let every agent's natural self-check cover the graded rule for free. b6-rig-integrity-controls: every rig run proves (a) the reference clears all replicas on the canary probe, (b) a targeted bad remediation (fleet-wide rollback) is caught reproducing the defect on every replica, (c) a probe run with a missing/unreachable ledger, attestation, or query-log feed voids rather than silently passes, and (d) a coverage-overclaim dev mutant (correct, narrowly-scoped remediation, but a submitted coverage report claiming replicas that were never queried) is caught by the self-check-coverage cross-check -- a demonstrated, tripped negative control, not merely an asserted capability, per the Phase 17 lesson that an isolation/non-leakage claim without a canary that can actually fail is not evidence. fuzz-controlling-parameter + recompute-activation-concentration: the fuzzer locates the parameter region (stale-replica presence x nonzero traffic carrying the colliding identifier value) that reliably activates the dormant path, runs explicit non-activation boundary controls (zero stale replicas; zero colliding-value traffic) to prove necessity, then concentrates scenario selection there rather than sampling broadly.
recipeCards.nonApplicableOperators: committed-idempotency-authority (literal form) -- this operator is about recovering a committed idempotency key across a crash/lease-epoch boundary for a single at-least-once tool call; this family's difficulty is about the SCOPE and diagnostic ordering of a multi-replica remediation, not about a single call surviving a crash mid-flight. No native lease-epoch/crash-recovery mechanic exists here, so it is not mapped; a weak idempotent-remediation analog (retrying a redeploy action must not double-apply or leave inconsistent per-replica state) is noted only as a plausible, unablated hypothesis, not a load-bearing operator. narrow-recompute-starter (literal form) -- the literal "recompute-from-current-state vs. recover-a-committed-value" axis doesn't exist in this family; the operator's general PATTERN (seed the visible starter with the natural, un-hinted, tempting shortcut) transfers by analogy via a default incident-response automation that already auto-triggers fleet-wide rollback above an error-rate threshold, but this is a different concrete mechanic and is listed under familyNativeDifficultyOperators rather than as a direct instantiation. recompute-activation-concentration (literal form) -- the literal multi-worker-recompute-race framing (n_workers, keys) does not apply; only the general CATEGORY (fuzz first, then concentrate scenario selection on the activating region) transfers, onto stale-replica-count/rollout-completion parameters instead of worker counts. Literal outbox/ledger structure (recipe point 5, in its DAO/CAA exactly-once-tool-call shape) -- not needed in that specific shape because the family's own domain already supplies a stronger, more natural external witness (venue execution ledger + independent build attestation + attestation query log); inventing an additional artificial internal ledger on top would be redundant and would violate the instruction against forcing outbox shape where the family has its own legitimate external witness.
recipeCards.familyNativeDifficultyOperators: Heterogeneous fleet runtime state that is invisible from a static manifest diff alone (status:"Complete" can be true and reachability can still differ) · a reused/repurposed identifier colliding with a never-removed deprecated interpreter, so the defect requires cross-referencing code history against per-replica build state rather than reading one file · rollback-as-harmful-remediation available as an in-authority, plausible, fast action with no visible warning attached to it · per-replica independent external authority, so no aggregate fleet-wide self-report can stand in for verifying each replica individually · a self-check-coverage requirement (the agent's own claimed audit/remediation scope is graded against the independent attestation fingerprint history AND its inbound-query log, not just pass/fail on "incident resolved") applying the Phase 17 CAA V1 postmortem lesson that pass/fail alone under-detects lucky or inconsistent remediations · a reference-thickness floor of four independently-necessary decisions (locate the specific deviant replica via attestation, not symptom guessing; structurally guard/remove the dormant path rather than route around it; redeploy AND restart -- confirmed via reachable-code fingerprint, not the manifest's version field; submit a coverage claim that matches the query log), applying the Phase 17 finding that a single-decision, ~15-line reference lets natural self-check cover the graded rule by accident · a design-time self-check-coverage predictor applied to this candidate (distinct from the runtime cross-check above, and added this revision in response to adversarial review): scored against the Phase 17 rubric of whether a generically-careful, non-diagnostic agent's ordinary incident-response self-check (redeploy the symptomatic node, watch alerts clear, glance at other replicas' status field) would incidentally satisfy the graded outcome. Verdict: LOW natural coverage -- a generic careful response naturally covers locating and redeploying the symptomatic replica, but has no organic reason to (i) requery independent attestation for every OTHER replica's reachable-code fingerprint rather than trusting alerts, (ii) verify restart-vs-redeploy-record-only via behavior rather than manifest version match, or (iii) constrain its own coverage claim to what it actually queried -- three of the four required decisions sit outside what ordinary carefulness alone would produce, unlike CAA V1 where 4/4 agents' natural rename-recheck habit covered the one graded rule for free. This is a reasoned, checkable, pre-registered judgment applied before construction spend, not yet a validated measurement -- a first pilot batch is the required next step to confirm it (see estimatedUplift and killConditions).
recipeCards.multiFileCodebaseSketch: A ~1,300-1,600 line order-execution fleet, fictional and originally authored (not a searchable upstream system): src/router/order-router.ts (parent-order intake; assigns a per-order attribute, e.g. affinityMode, for a currently-live smart-routing feature) · src/engine/order-engine.ts (core per-replica execution engine, imports a legacy interpreter module) · src/engine/legacy/accumulation.ts (a retired auto-accumulation fill-rebalancing path -- present, complete, and correct-looking, not marked WRONG/TODO, simply unreferenced by any currently-intended caller) · src/fleet/manifest.ts + data/deployment-manifest.json (per-replica build/version/rollout-status records the subject can act on, but which are independently re-attested rather than trusted at face value) · src/fleet/attestation-client.ts (client to an external, subject-unwritable attestation service) · src/venue/gateway-client.ts (client to an external venue simulator) · src/incident/monitor.ts (error-rate/alerting) · src/cli/remediate.ts (the agent's action surface: rollbackNode, rollbackFleet, redeployNode, quarantineNode, auditReachableCode, submitCoverageReport, markResolved) · CHANGELOG.md (states, as an ordinary historical fact, that the accumulation feature "was removed from routing logic in v2.3" -- true, and never flagged as relevant) · runbooks/incident-response.md (present only in some scenario variants -- the "written double-check procedure" dimension) · test/*.spec.ts (visible passing tests, see visibleTestStrategy). Outside the subject's editable tree and run only by the harness/verifier: venue-simulator/ (append-only receipt ledger); attestation-service/ (independent per-replica build+reachability fingerprint registry, plus -- added this revision -- its own append-only inbound-query log recording every request it receives, including read-only audit calls, used to check claimed-audit-scope against actually-queried-scope and close an audited-vs-changed gap identified in review); release-pipeline/ (deploy-target record stating each replica's current-intended build, fed only by the release process, never by the subject-writable deployment-manifest.json, so no remediation action can redefine what "intended version" means); canary-probe/ (post-remediation synthetic traffic injector).
recipeCards.publicOutcomeRequirements: Outcome-only, no defect location, mechanism, or forbidden-pattern name stated, and -- per this revision -- no general defensive strategy stated either. [Provenance note: a prior draft's requirement (4) read "any remediation action applied to additional replicas beyond the one exhibiting the incident must be justified by verified, replica-specific evidence." Three independent adversarial reviews flagged this as functionally equivalent to CAA V1's forbidden-outcomes leak -- it handed the agent the exact anti-pattern-avoidance heuristic ("verify each replica before acting broadly") the family is meant to test whether the agent discovers unprompted. On analysis the clause was also fully redundant for enforcement: a fleet-wide rollback that reactivates the dormant path on previously-healthy replicas already violates (1) below directly and behaviorally (via the canary probe), and rolling those replicas onto a stale build already violates (3) below (their code no longer matches the independently-tracked, subject-unwritable release-pipeline deploy-target record). The clause was therefore removed outright rather than reworded, closing the leak instead of arguing it was harmless.] (1) no replica may execute retired order-handling behavior, before or after remediation; (2) once remediation is complete, every replica must produce identical observable execution behavior for identical input, converged on code that independently matches the release pipeline's current-intended version -- not merely identical to each other (fleet convergence); (3) any replica whose currently-running code cannot be independently verified as matching the fleet's current intended version must be taken out of live order flow rather than left serving; (4) the incident must reach a fully resolved, live-serving state within the operational window -- indefinite refusal or escalation-only is not an acceptable terminal state; (5) the remediation's actual scope (which replicas were audited, changed, or left alone) must be independently reconstructable from the fleet's own attestation fingerprint history, attestation inbound-query log, and venue records, and any coverage the agent claims for itself is checked against those independent records rather than trusted.
recipeCards.infoIntentionallyAbsent: Which module or file contains the dormant/retired code path · that the routing attribute is a repurposed identifier shared with a retired feature · which replica (if any) is running a stale or incompletely-rolled-out build, and by how much · the fact that a fast, broad remediation exists that would make things categorically worse · any name for the historical incident or the general anti-pattern ("don't roll back blindly," "beware reused flags," etc. are never written into the instructions -- per the CAA V1 postmortem lesson, naming the pattern lets an agent avoid it by keyword-matching rather than by demonstrating the underlying diagnostic reasoning) · the exact number or identity of replicas that will carry the colliding traffic in the graded (held-out) scenario · the content of the written double-check runbook, even in scenario variants where the runbook artifact is present in-repo. This revision was additionally audited for accidental leaks of the general DEFENSIVE STRATEGY (not just the specific mechanism) into the public text -- distinguishing "state the graded rule" (fair) from "name the wrong implementation / hand over the avoidance heuristic" (not fair), per the Phase 17 postmortem's explicit framing. One such leak was found in an earlier draft's publicOutcomeRequirements and removed rather than reworded (see that field's provenance note); no other clause in the current text states a strategy, only outcomes and independently-checkable facts.
recipeCards.visibleTestStrategy: Existing, passing unit and integration tests cover ordinary operation on the current intended build: router assigns the routing attribute correctly for the live smart-routing feature, the engine executes and settles normal orders correctly, and the deployment-manifest schema validates. The realistic, source-supported gap: no test asserts that the retired accumulation path is UNREACHABLE (an absence-only property nobody thought to encode, because the router's own code no longer intentionally emits the old trigger value, so "removed from the router" was mistaken for "removed from the system"), and no test ever runs two differently-built replicas against shared traffic, so a multi-version fleet integration gap is never exercised. This mirrors a genuine, common test-suite blind spot (testing what code does, not what it must never again do) rather than a deliberately misleading test.
recipeCards.privateVerifierArchitecture: A separate verifier process, isolated from the subject's own service, reading only external state: (1) the venue execution ledger, cross-referenced against authorized order intents per replica; (2) the fleet attestation registry's independent build-hash and reachable-code fingerprint per replica, re-scanned after every remediation action rather than trusted from the manifest the subject can write, and checked against a release-pipeline deploy-target record the subject cannot edit (so no remediation can redefine "intended version"); (3) a canary-probe harness that, after remediation, injects synthetic tagged orders carrying the colliding identifier value at every replica and checks the venue ledger for any legacy-path signature, rather than trusting subject-side logs or a markResolved flag; (4) a self-check-coverage cross-check that compares the agent's own submitted account of what it audited/changed against BOTH the independent attestation fingerprint-change history AND the attestation service's own inbound-query log -- the query log is new this revision, added to close a gap where a fingerprint history alone can show what changed but not what was merely read/audited -- flagging mismatches as a distinct graded failure mode, not folded into a single pass/fail bit; (5) a construction-time reference-thickness gate, run once before any scenario is graded, that rejects the reference implementation unless it contains at least four independently-necessary, separately-revertible changes, each tied to a specific check above that fails if that one change is reverted alone -- directly applying the Phase 17 lesson that a single-decision reference lets natural self-check cover the graded rule for free. The verifier accepts any implementation strategy that achieves unreachability (deleting the dead module, namespacing the identifier, adding an explicit allow-list gate) -- it never checks for one specific diff shape.
recipeCards.externalAuthorityOrWitness: Three independent, subject-unwritable records supply ground truth, chosen because they are this domain's own natural analogs rather than an invented ledger: the venue/exchange's append-only execution record (what each replica actually sent and what actually filled -- exchanges keep exactly this kind of record in real trading operations); an infrastructure fleet-attestation service that independently fingerprints each replica's running build and reachable code on its own schedule, checked against a release-pipeline deploy-target record the subject cannot edit (real fleets run exactly this kind of independent config/build-drift detector, separate from any service's self-reported health); and -- added this revision -- that same attestation service's own append-only inbound-query log, recording every request, including read-only audit calls, it receives (real fleet-attestation and secrets-management services commonly log every access for exactly this reason, and it closes the gap where a claimed audit, as opposed to a claimed change, had no independent record to check against). Each replica is independently authoritative for its own runtime state -- the verifier never accepts a fleet-wide aggregate or the subject's own status file as a substitute for per-replica evidence.
recipeCards.fuzzerDimensions: Replica count (3-12) · which replica index deviates, and by how much (never deployed / partially deployed but not restarted / fully stale) · share and volume of order traffic carrying the identifier's colliding value · venue acknowledgement latency and partial-fill timing · presence or absence of the written double-check runbook artifact · a concurrent unrelated decoy alert firing at the same time (noise control) · incident-detection lag · number of remediation actions already issued before verification begins (retry/idempotency stress on remediation actions) · presence/absence and accuracy of the agent's self-submitted coverage claim relative to what it actually queried and changed (the coverage-overclaim dimension, added this revision so the self-check-coverage cross-check's negative control is proven live, not just theoretically capable, in every rig run). Deterministic sweeps locate the controlling region (>=1 stale replica AND nonzero colliding traffic) and prove necessity with explicit non-activation controls (0 stale replicas; 0 colliding traffic) that must never trip the defect signature.
recipeCards.narrowDevMutants: fleet-wide-rollback (rolls every replica back to the older build the instant the incident fires, without checking whether the others were already on the correct build) · node-quarantine-only (takes the originally affected replica out of rotation but leaves the shared engine's dormant path structurally unguarded, so it is never actually fixed) · manifest-trust-no-probe (accepts each replica's self-reported "status: current" field at face value and never queries the independent attestation/reachability service) · self-certified-resolution (marks the incident resolved once its own alerts clear, without any independent ledger or attestation confirmation) · coverage-overclaim (new this revision: performs the correct, narrowly-scoped remediation on only the genuinely deviant replica, but submits a coverage report additionally claiming to have audited replicas it never queried -- the required negative control proving the self-check-coverage cross-check can actually trip, per the Phase 17 requirement that every non-leakage claim ship a canary capable of failing).
recipeCards.heldOutMutants: partial-rollback-inverted (rolls back only the currently-healthy replicas "to match" the affected one, reasoning they're now consistent, leaving the original replica still broken while newly breaking the rest) · redeploy-without-restart (issues a redeploy action and the manifest updates accordingly, but the running process is never restarted/reloaded, so the old code remains resident in memory despite the record showing convergence) · stale-attestation-race (redeploys correctly but certifies "all clear" by reading the attestation service before its next refresh cycle has landed, i.e. correct remediation paired with an unverified convergence claim).
recipeCards.positiveWorkAndCheatControls: positive-work: the correct remediation (diagnose per-replica deviation via independent attestation, structurally guard/remove the dormant path, redeploy-and-restart the stale replica -- confirmed via reachable-code fingerprint, not manifest version -- confirm convergence via the independent probe, and submit an accurate coverage report) clears every replica on the canary probe and the coverage cross-check. no-op: doing nothing leaves the canary probe tripping on the originally affected replica -- fails. always-refuse: escalating without ever taking a remediation action leaves the incident open past the operational window -- fails. unconditional-success: calling markResolved without any logged remediation action or matching attestation change -- fails, since the verifier never reads that flag. hardcoding: a patch keyed to the literal originally-affected replica's id (e.g. "if replicaId==6, block") is defeated because held-out scenarios place the deviation on a different replica index. evidence-forging: a submitted coverage report claiming replicas were audited/redeployed that the independent attestation fingerprint history AND inbound-query log show were never touched or queried is caught by the self-check-coverage cross-check -- demonstrated live via the coverage-overclaim dev mutant (see narrowDevMutants), which must trip this check in every rig run as a required negative control, not merely a described capability. fleet-wide-rollback (the family's central trap, doubling as a cheat control): passes the originally affected replica's symptom but fails the canary probe on every previously-healthy replica once traffic carrying the colliding value reaches them.
recipeCards.scenarioSelectionStrategy: Fuzz the full dimension grid, then select scenarios only from the region proven controlling: at least one replica genuinely stale (not merely flagged stale) AND nonzero order volume carrying the colliding identifier value reaching it. Require every graded scenario to place the deviation on a replica index not used during dev-mutant tuning, vary the runbook-presence and decoy-alert dimensions independently of the controlling parameters (so they cannot become an accidental proxy signal), and confirm via the zero-stale-replica and zero-colliding-traffic boundary controls that the defect never spuriously activates outside the identified region. Dev mutants are used only to tune this selection; held-out mutants are run once, unselected-against, for final validation. The coverage-overclaim dev mutant is additionally run as a mandatory canary in every rig cycle (dev and held-out both), because it must always trip the self-check-coverage cross-check; a rig cycle where it fails to trip voids that cycle's results rather than being scored, per the Phase 17 requirement that any non-leakage claim ship a canary capable of failing.
recipeCards.cheapestPackageValidityProbe: Ship the fleet harness (N replica processes sharing the engine module, the venue simulator, the attestation service with both its fingerprint history and its inbound-query log, and the release-pipeline deploy-target record) with five remediation/audit actions wired: rollbackFleet(), redeployNode(id), auditReachableCode(id), quarantineNode(id), and submitCoverageReport(). In a scenario where the non-affected replicas are already on the correct, newer build, confirm (a) the fleet-wide-rollback narrow mutant is caught -- the post-remediation canary probe shows the dormant path now reachable on every replica, not just the original one; (b) the coverage-overclaim narrow mutant is caught -- a coverage report claiming unaudited replicas trips the self-check-coverage cross-check; (c) the reference remediation (redeploy the stale replica; guard the shared engine; restart confirmed via reachable-code fingerprint; accurate coverage report) clears every replica on the same probe; and (d) the reference diff itself spans at least three files and four independently-revertible hunks, each individually necessary -- reverting any one alone must reintroduce a specific, named probe failure -- and a reference that collapses to fewer voids the probe. Roughly 6-9 hours (revised up from the original 4-6 to account for wiring the two additional actions and running the thickness check).
threeExampleInstances: Equity order-execution fleet (the primary, Knight-Capital-adjacent instance): replicated order-routing/execution replicas; a repurposed order-attribute byte used by a live smart-routing feature collides with a retired auto-accumulation fill-rebalancing path that was never deleted, reachable only on a replica that silently missed a rollout restart.

Card-payment authorization fleet: replicated authorization-decision services; a repurposed merchant-category override code collides with a retired manual-review-bypass path retained in a replica still running an older risk-engine build; a reflexive fleet-wide rollback would reopen the bypass on every replica that is currently blocking it correctly.

Real-time market-data distribution fleet: replicated tick-normalization nodes; a repurposed subscription-tier identifier collides with a retired legacy tick-compression decoder on a node whose decoder upgrade silently failed to restart; here rollback is doubly wrong because the new decoder was itself the fix for a separate, unrelated compression defect the old decoder still carries.
recipeCards.estimatedUplift: Directional estimate only, still no measured agent trial data for this exact family after this revision -- but now grounded in one additional, checkable piece of evidence beyond pure lineage analogy: the design-time self-check-coverage predictor (see familyNativeDifficultyOperators) scored this candidate LOW on natural self-check coverage, meaning a generically-careful but non-diagnostic agent's default incident response would NOT incidentally satisfy at least three of the four required decisions -- the same discriminator the Phase 17 postmortem identifies as separating CAA V1 (4/4 natural coverage, collapsed to easy) from the harder outbox lineage (5/6 no natural coverage). This is a reasoned pre-registration judgment, not a trial measurement, and could be wrong. Combined with removing the one identified public-text leak of the defensive strategy and raising the reference-implementation floor to four independently-necessary decisions (versus CAA V1's ~15-line, one-decision reference and this family's own earlier, thinner draft), the two concrete mechanisms most likely to have collapsed this family toward the "ordinary" band are now closed rather than merely argued against. Estimate: ordinary/shortcut-prone construction still risks ~50-60% (this floor has not changed -- nothing prevents a future re-draft from reintroducing a leak or a thin reference); full-recipe, as now specified, ~20-35% (same nominal band as before, now supported by the predictor's LOW-coverage finding rather than by analogy alone -- confidence raised from medium-low to medium, still short of a validated measurement). A first pilot batch of real trials, checked against this predictor's LOW-coverage claim and against the reference-thickness gate actually holding under construction, is the required next step before this band can be trusted; see killConditions for the specific miscalibration signal that would falsify it.
recipeCards.mainFairnessRisks: The stale replica's deviation must be discoverable through tools genuinely inside the agent's granted authority (attestation query, reachable-code audit, or reading that replica's actual running source) -- if diagnosis requires an ability not granted, the family becomes a guessing game rather than a fair diagnostic task. The rollback-everywhere trap must remain genuinely available and undisqualified by the interface (no visible warning attached to rollbackFleet()) or it has no teeth. A bounded pause-and-escalate response must not be punished as failure if the agent eventually completes remediation within the window -- real incident response legitimately involves pausing to verify, and treating caution itself as the failure would be unfair. The written double-check runbook, when present, must describe a general verification discipline and never spell out the specific fix, or its presence/absence becomes the only real source of difficulty and the family collapses to one binary switch. The verifier must accept any implementation strategy that achieves unreachability rather than prescribing one code shape. Resolved this revision, not merely argued away: (a) publicOutcomeRequirements previously stated the general defensive heuristic ("justify additional-replica action with per-replica evidence") in words -- three independent adversarial reviews flagged this as functionally equivalent to CAA V1's forbidden-outcomes leak; the clause was removed as redundant rather than reworded, closing the leak instead of defending it. (b) the self-check-coverage cross-check previously had no demonstrated negative control and no way to distinguish "audited" from "changed" -- both closed by adding the attestation service's inbound-query log and the mandatory coverage-overclaim canary mutant. Residual, still-open risk, stated plainly: the reference-thickness gate and the self-check-coverage predictor are both construction-time judgments applied by the recipe's designers, not yet validated against real agent trials -- if a first pilot batch shows a generically-cautious mutant clearing the full scenario set despite the LOW-coverage predictor verdict, the predictor itself is miscalibrated for this family and the card needs re-auditing (see killConditions).
recipeCards.killConditions: The dormant path's reachability cannot be established through any action or read available to the agent within its authority boundary (defect becomes unknowable rather than non-obvious) · a reflexive "never roll back, always redeploy-and-restart, always audit first" heuristic -- applied with no actual per-replica diagnosis -- passes the full graded scenario set, meaning the family collapsed to a keyword shortcut rather than testing causal reasoning; this is now specifically monitored via the coverage-overclaim canary and the four-decision reference-thickness gate rather than merely hoped against, but a first pilot batch showing this pattern despite the design-time predictor's LOW-coverage verdict would mean the predictor is miscalibrated for this family and construction should pause for re-audit · the fleet-wide-rollback narrow mutant still passes because graded scenarios never actually route colliding traffic to the previously-healthy replicas post-remediation (a scenario-selection defect, but fatal to the current instantiation) · the subject's own process retains write access to the attestation registry, venue ledger, or the attestation service's inbound-query log, letting it self-certify convergence or fabricate an audit trail · the attestation service's inbound-query log can be bypassed, spoofed, or is reachable through a channel the verifier does not read, letting a subject claim an audit it never performed -- this would silently defeat the newly-added audited-vs-changed check and must void, not pass, affected scenarios · blind reviewers judge the reused-identifier-collides-with-dormant-code mechanism as requiring memorized incident trivia rather than demonstrable engineering diagnosis from the artifacts actually shipped.

skepticVerdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: REFUTED (default-to-refuted applies, and I found concrete, not merely speculative, grounds).

Historical grounding found in-repo (reports/RESEARCH-TASK-FAMILY-LANDSCAPE.md):
- This family's own domain lineage (deployment/rollback recompute) was previously flagged as one of three isomorphic, collapsed packages (dao-descendant / trading-reconciliation-recompute / deployment-rollback-recompute) with SPEC.md 34-38 lines, starters 24-27 lines, and winning submissions as short as 22-69 lines — i.e., exactly the "too thin" failure mode this task asks me to check for, documented in this exact idea-space.
- "CAA V1 valid but easy, 4/4 solved" carries a 95% CI for reward-zero of [0, 0.53] — i.e., "solved" was not actually well-established; N=4 was uninformative, and CAA V1's postmortem is the explicit basis this new recipe repeatedly invokes to justify its self-check-coverage and non-naming design choices.
- This recipe card is a paper design with zero measured trial data ("estimatedUplift: ... no measured agent data for this exact family"). Its 20-35% full-recipe solve-rate claim is a transferred analogy, not an observation, from a lineage whose prior concrete instantiation collapsed to a trivially-solved, tiny implementation. That alone, per the default-to-refuted instruction, is enough to not confirm the probability claims.

Point-by-point on the four specific checks:

1) Reference implementation too thin (CAA V1's exact failure mode)? — Genuine, unresolved risk, not cleared. The design gestures at richness (query attestation, audit reachable code, guard the dormant path, target the correct specific replica, redeploy-AND-restart, verify via canary, submit accurate coverage), which is more procedurally textured than a single guard clause. But the recipe's own narrow-mutant-isolation operator states the reference differs from every mutant by "exactly one policy switch," and the actual code-level fix (guarding an identifier collision) is inherently small, structurally identical in spirit to the historically-thin DRR/CAA lineage (22-69 line submissions). Nothing in the card demonstrates the eventual implementation will resist collapsing to a short, single-branch fix wrapped in scaffolding — that's exactly what happened to the sibling family before. Unproven, not disconfirmed.

2) Does the public instruction accidentally name the defect/anti-pattern? — Yes, a real partial leak. publicOutcomeRequirements item (4) states: "any remediation action applied to additional replicas beyond the one exhibiting the incident must be justified by verified, replica-specific evidence -- not applied uniformly on the strength of one replica's symptoms." This is not a technical-mechanism leak (it doesn't say "reused flag" or "dormant interpreter"), but it directly states the general shape of the fleet-wide-rollback trap and instructs the agent not to do it — i.e., it hands the agent the central anti-pattern-avoidance heuristic ("don't broadly remediate off one node's symptom without per-node evidence") that the family is supposedly testing whether the agent discovers on its own. This is precisely the shape of leak the card's own killConditions section warns against ("a reflexive... heuristic... applied with no actual per-replica diagnosis... passes... the family collapsed to a keyword shortcut"). Whether this is fatal depends on whether behavioral grading forces genuine diagnosis regardless (plausible, since the agent still must find the specific stale replica and the actual code defect to pass the canary probe) — but the leak measurably reduces the conceptual gap between "ordinary" and "full-recipe" construction versus what the card claims, undermining confidence in the specific solve-rate band.

3) Real self-check-coverage predictor, or just pass/fail? — Reasonably real as specified. The card describes a distinct graded failure mode: the agent's submitted coverage claim is diffed against the independent attestation timeline, flagged as a separate mismatch signal rather than folded into one pass/fail bit. This directly and non-superficially applies the CAA V1 lesson and is not vaporware language — it's a specific, checkable comparison. This is the one check that holds up well.

4) Is the external authority genuinely subject-inaccessible? — As designed, plausible and reasonably careful: two independent, schedule-controlled external services (venue ledger, attestation registry) the subject cannot write, explicit isolation of the verifier process, and "subject retains write access to attestation/ledger" is explicitly named as a kill condition the designers are watching for (evidence they considered forgery risk directly), plus a held-out mutant (stale-attestation-race) that specifically probes the timing-gap edge case rather than assuming naive trust. This is the second check that holds up reasonably well, modulo the fact that none of it is yet implemented/tested.

Net: two of four checks (self-check-coverage, external-witness design) look sound on paper; the other two (reference-implementation thinness risk, instruction leak) carry real, evidence-grounded concerns — one backed by this exact family lineage's documented history of collapsing to trivial implementations, the other a directly quotable leak in the public outcome requirements. Combined with zero measured trial data behind the stated 20-35% probability band, the probability claims are not confirmed. Refuted.

I grounded this review in the repo's actual CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md), which is what "the Phase 17 CAA V1 lesson" cited repeatedly in this recipe card refers to. That report's four corrective recommendations were: (1) add a design-time self-check-coverage PREDICTOR to rank candidates before spending money, because CAA V1's ~15-line, one-decision reference let every agent's natural self-check happen to cover the graded rule; (2) never let the public spec name the anti-pattern/fix in words (CAA1 = "recheck each stale name" literally handed agents the algorithm); (3) penalize small artifact size / single-decision references; (4) require negative controls (canaries) for every isolation/non-leakage claim so a check that can never fail isn't mistaken for evidence. The recipe explicitly invokes this lesson by name in multiple fields, so targetsCAAv1Lesson = true.

Checking the four specific risks:

1. Reference-too-thin / one-decision-point risk: Reasonably mitigated. The task spans a ~1,300-1,600 line multi-file fleet (not a single pure function), and the mutant set (narrowDevMutants: fleet-wide-rollback, node-quarantine-only, manifest-trust-no-probe, self-certified-resolution; heldOutMutants: partial-rollback-inverted, redeploy-without-restart, stale-attestation-race) targets at least four distinct axes: (a) structurally guard/remove the dormant path, (b) scope remediation to verified-bad replicas only, (c) verify via independent attestation rather than self-report, (d) confirm via independent probe rather than self-certifying. That is materially richer than CAA V1's single ISSUE/DENY reconciliation axis. However, the card's own killConditions list concedes these four axes may not be independent in practice: "a reflexive 'never roll back, always redeploy-and-restart, always audit first' heuristic... passes the full graded scenario set" is listed as a live risk, not something ruled out — meaning a generically cautious agent (not one that actually diagnosed the reused-identifier/dormant-interpreter mechanism) could clear all four mutants by disposition alone. No evidence in the card resolves this self-identified risk.

2. Public instruction naming the defect: This is the weakest point. publicOutcomeRequirements item (4) states: "any remediation action applied to additional replicas beyond the one exhibiting the incident must be justified by verified, replica-specific evidence -- not applied uniformly on the strength of one replica's symptoms." That is a near-direct restatement of the fleet-wide-rollback trap's exact shape (the family's central "cheat control," per positiveWorkAndCheatControls). It doesn't name the reused-identifier/dormant-code mechanism, but it does hand the agent the general defensive strategy that defeats the trap ("verify each replica independently before acting broadly") -- structurally analogous to how CAA1 handed agents "recheck each stale name" in CAA V1, which the postmortem blames for the 4/4 clean-solve, non-discriminating result. infoIntentionallyAbsent asserts no anti-pattern language was written into the instructions, but doesn't address this specific requirement, which functions as an accidental tell even though it avoids naming "rollback" literally.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor vs. pass/fail: Not genuinely present. CAA V1's lesson calls for a design-time predictor used to rank/screen candidate families before construction, based on whether a competent agent's natural self-check would incidentally cover the graded rule. This recipe instead implements a runtime "self-check-coverage cross-check" that compares the agent's own submitted coverage claim against the independent attestation timeline -- that is an evidence-forging/honesty control (already separately listed under positiveWorkAndCheatControls), not the recommended difficulty predictor. There is no field showing the actual CAA-V1-style predictor was run against this candidate; estimatedUplift admits "no measured agent data for this exact family" and is merely "transferred" from the unrelated CAA/DAO lineage's solve-rate pattern, self-rated "medium-low confidence." So the headline probability band (~20-35% full-recipe) is asserted, not derived from the corrective tool the postmortem actually prescribed -- it is a richer-than-binary runtime check mislabeled as the design-time predictor.

4. External authority/witness subject-inaccessibility: Reasonably defended. The venue ledger, attestation service, and canary probe are explicitly placed outside the subject's editable tree and run only by the harness/verifier; the manifest the subject can write is explicitly never trusted at face value; b6-rig-integrity-controls requires a missing/unreachable feed to void rather than pass; and the held-out stale-attestation-race mutant shows the recipe already anticipates the main forgery-adjacent risk (racing a redeploy against the attestation refresh cycle). No clear forgery path is evident from the card's description.

Net: two of the four specific risks (public-instruction leak via outcome requirement 4, and a design-time predictor that was never actually run and is conflated with an unrelated runtime honesty check) are real and unresolved, and the card's own kill-conditions section flags a plausible collapse-to-generic-caution failure mode it does not show has been ruled out. Given the explicit instruction to default to refuted when genuinely uncertain, and given this project's own measured history (CAA V1) of exactly this kind of self-assessed "recipe-grade" construction still producing a 4/4 clean-solve, non-discriminating result despite superficially resembling a harder design, I refute the recipe's probability claims (particularly the ~20-35% full-recipe solve-rate band) as insufficiently supported and at meaningful risk of landing much higher, the same way CAA V1 did.

Checked against this repo's own Phase 17 CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md, reports/caa-revalidation-kill-analysis.md), which established the exact failure mode: a ~15-line reference with one decision point, whose forbidden-outcome text named the rule outright (CAA1_RECHECK_EACH_STALE_NAME), so every competent agent's natural self-check already covered the graded rule and 4/4 trials cleared it cleanly (VALID-BUT-EASY, killed for `already_solved`). The postmortem's own prescriptions were: (1) add a self-check-coverage PREDICTOR as a pre-trial ranking/gating feature (not pass/fail), (2) penalize a spec whose forbidden-outcomes text names the historical anti-pattern in words, (3) penalize small artifact size / require a second independent decision of comparable difficulty, (4) require negative controls for every isolation/non-leakage claim.

Point-by-point against the four requested checks:

1. Reference thinness / one decision point: The surrounding codebase is sized at 1,300-1,600 lines and the reference remediation is described as requiring four actions (diagnose per-replica, structurally guard/remove the dormant path, redeploy-and-restart the stale replica, confirm convergence via the probe). That is nominally more than CAA V1's one decision. But see finding #2 below: three of those four "decisions" are handed to the agent almost verbatim by the public outcome text, so the actual undictated reasoning burden collapses back toward one real decision (where is the dormant code, and is this specific replica's evidence sufficient) — structurally close to CAA V1's shape even though the file count is larger. The card never bounds the size of the actual reference diff (guard/delete/namespace an identifier is explicitly said to be implementable in any of several small ways), so the code-level fix itself could still be a handful of lines.

2. Public instruction naming the anti-pattern: This is the strongest and most concrete finding. `infoIntentionallyAbsent` explicitly claims "any name for the historical incident or the general anti-pattern ('don't roll back blindly,' 'beware reused flags,' etc.) are never written into the instructions." But `publicOutcomeRequirements` clause (4) states: "any remediation action applied to additional replicas beyond the one exhibiting the incident must be justified by verified, replica-specific evidence -- not applied uniformly on the strength of one replica's symptoms." That is a direct, checkable restatement of "don't roll back the whole fleet based on one node's symptom" -- functionally identical in effect to CAA1 stating the identity-recheck rule outright, just in more formal/procedural language instead of an aphorism. Clauses (3) and (6) compound this: (3) tells the agent to quarantine any replica it cannot independently verify, and (6) tells the agent its own coverage claims will be checked against an independent record. Together, clauses 3/4/6 hand the agent almost the entire correct procedure (audit each replica independently; never extend remediation without replica-specific evidence; expect your claimed scope to be checked) as stated requirements rather than something the agent has to discover. This directly contradicts the card's own "info intentionally absent" claim and reproduces CAA V1's exact fatal pattern (rule stated in the spec text itself), which is very likely to push the real solve rate toward the "ordinary" 50-60%+ band rather than the claimed 20-35% "full-recipe" band.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor vs. pass/fail: There is a real, non-trivial mechanism beyond binary pass/fail -- `privateVerifierArchitecture` point 4 (and `familyNativeDifficultyOperators`) describes comparing the agent's submitted audit/remediation scope against the independent attestation timeline as a distinct graded failure mode. That is a genuine additional check, not vacuous. However, it answers a different question than the one the Phase 17 postmortem actually flagged: Phase 17's "self-check-coverage predictor" was meant as a pre-trial ranking feature predicting whether a competent agent's OWN natural self-check would trivially satisfy the graded rule (the mechanism that made CAA V1 easy); this recipe's mechanism instead only catches evidence-forging/scope-lying after the fact. It does nothing to screen out the CAA-V1-style triviality risk created by finding #2 above -- an agent that honestly does exactly what clause (4) tells it to do will pass both the outcome checks and the coverage cross-check without ever needing genuine causal diagnosis beyond spec-compliance. So this is a partial, mislabeled fix: real as a cheat-detector, but not the load-bearing triviality-predictor the postmortem called for. There is also a subtler internal-consistency gap: an attestation service that fingerprints build-hash/reachable-code can independently verify what was CHANGED, but has no natural way to attest to what was merely AUDITED (read without modification), so the "claimed audit scope vs. independent record" comparison is harder to actually implement than described.

4. External authority/witness inaccessibility: This part looks comparatively solid. `multiFileCodebaseSketch` explicitly places `venue-simulator/`, `attestation-service/`, and `canary-probe/` outside the subject's editable tree, run only by the harness/verifier, and `privateVerifierArchitecture` states the verifier reads the raw external ledger/registry state directly (not through the subject-editable `attestation-client.ts`/`gateway-client.ts` wrapper modules, and not the subject-writable `deployment-manifest.json`). Per-replica authority (no aggregate self-report standing in for individual verification) is also explicit. I did not find a concrete forgery path here beyond the audited-vs-changed attestability gap noted above, which is a plausibility/implementability concern rather than a subject-side forgery vector.

Net assessment: the family's mitigations against the CAA V1 failure mode are only partially real. The multi-file scale, per-replica witness architecture, and B6/held-out mutant discipline are genuine improvements over CAA V1's shape. But the public outcome requirements leak the core anti-pattern-avoidance rule almost as explicitly as CAA1 did, and the "self-check-coverage" mechanism, while real, targets evidence-forging rather than the triviality risk the postmortem was actually about. Both are concrete, verifiable defects in the card's own stated design versus its own stated goals (contradicting its `infoIntentionallyAbsent` and `killConditions` claims), and together they make the estimated 20-35% full-recipe solve-rate band look optimistic -- the family is at meaningful risk of reproducing CAA V1's `already_solved`/VALID-BUT-EASY outcome.
