Residual risk: narrowDevMutants only formalizes 3 mutants (resume-trusts-local-queue, async-collapsed-to-success, duplicate-on-retry) while terminal-retried-forever and chunk-boundary-drops-entry are held out of the selection grid entirely — so the *selection* process that decided which scenarios survive is anchored on fewer independent decision points than the reference's full obligation set. This is a real but second-order risk, not a repeat of CAA's literal thinness.

2) Does the public instruction accidentally name the defect? Genuine, self-acknowledged residual risk — the weakest of the four. infoIntentionallyAbsent correctly withholds the resume.ts/entryOutcome.ts divergence and the presence of 202 shapes, so the specific mechanism is not leaked. But publicOutcomeRequirements states, at outcome level, "this must hold across restarts... must not cause duplicate or dropped resubmission" — which gestures directly at the defect's category (restart-induced state divergence) much as CAA V1's forbidden-outcomes text named its identity-binding anti-pattern. The card itself concedes the closest thing to a smoking gun: estimatedUplift calls "check the nested Bundle, not just the outer code" "a documented, moderately well-known FHIR gotcha some agents already carry as a habit — this is itself the family's main self-check-coverage risk," and mainFairnessRisks separately flags "risk of over-rewarding the well-known... trap alone." The mitigation (bundling restart/terminal/chunking obligations so no single disclosed rule fully specifies the fix) is reasonable but unmeasured, and is structurally the same kind of fairness-disclosure-vs-leakage tension that sank CAA V1.

3) Real self-check-coverage predictor, or just pass/fail? Confirmed as genuinely addressed, and specifically responsive. Phase 17's own recommendation #1 was "add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate ... make it a ranking feature rather than pass/fail." This card's privateVerifierArchitecture (e) and scenarioSelectionStrategy implement exactly that: two named shallow-implementation exemplars (outer-200-only-checker; per-entry-aware-but-not-resume-requerying-checker) are run against each candidate scenario, and scenarios either would already pass are down-weighted/excluded from the graded set. This is materially different from — and additional to — the project's existing reference/narrow-mutant pass/fail apparatus, and different from (complementary to) the retrospective Row Five self-check metric used elsewhere in this repo (which scores actual agent transcripts post-hoc rather than filtering scenarios pre-hoc). It is a finite, hand-picked pair of shallow strawmen rather than a continuous/learned predictor, so its coverage of "what a natural self-check looks like" is only as good as those two exemplars — but it is a real, non-trivial mechanism, not relabeled pass/fail.

4) Is the external witness genuinely subject-inaccessible / forge-proof? Well-addressed at the design level. externalAuthorityOrWitness cleanly separates the subject's legitimate in-band witness (nested response Bundle, Content-Location poll — never hidden, since hiding standard FHIR disclosure would be unfair) from the verifier-only witness (the mock HIE's own resource store plus a root-owned append-only audit log, asserted unreachable from the subject's container). Crucially there is an explicit canary: positiveWorkAndCheatControls lists "forged-ledger (subject writes its own local audit.json...) → explicit canary proving a self-issued ledger cannot substitute for the real exchange query," which is precisely the adversarial test this question is asking for, and the architecture matches a pattern (`grade-the-obligation-from-the-external-party-log`) that already exists validated elsewhere in this repo's hardness-operator vocabulary (data/hardness-operators.json), not invented ad hoc for this card. killConditions honestly flags the one thing that would break this ("the mock exchange's admin surface or audit ledger turns out to be reachable from the subject's container") as a condition to test rather than assuming it away. This reads as genuine, not merely asserted.

Overall: this card is an unusually deliberate, near point-by-point response to the Phase 17/CAA V1 postmortem (multi-decision reference, self-check-coverage predictor as a ranking/filtering feature, negative-control canaries, enforcement-screen awareness) — three of the four specific traps named in the question are substantively engineered against, not merely asserted. The fourth (accidental defect-naming via the necessary restart-invariance disclosure) is the one place real, self-acknowledged risk remains, and it is structurally the same kind of risk that sank CAA V1. Combined with the card's own honest framing of its probability numbers as "a hypothesis, not an additive sum... unmeasured" and its explicit invocation of this project's own track record of null/unmeasurable isolated-operator effects (Phase 14, Phase 17), I cannot confirm the stated uplift (25-55%, medium confidence) survives adversarial scrutiny — it is plausible and well-reasoned but unverified, resting on an unresolved fairness/leakage tension on exactly the axis that caused the precedent failure. Per instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, I mark the probability claims refuted (not confirmed) while noting the recipe is a good-faith, well-targeted design response to CAA V1 rather than a naive repeat of it.

Checked this recipe card against the four specific CAA V1 failure signatures (per reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md §12, which found CAA was VALID-BUT-EASY because: (1) the reference was ~15 lines with one decision point, (2) the spec's forbidden-outcomes text named the anti-pattern almost verbatim, (3) the contract gate had no self-check-coverage predictor — only pass/fail — so it ranked CAA 85/85 despite triviality, and (4) there was no negative-control canary proving isolation claims actually held).

1) Reference thinness: partially but not fully mitigated. The card explicitly commits to ≥2-3 independent decision points (async/resume convergence, terminal-vs-retryable escalation, chunk-safe idempotent retry) backed by 5 distinct mutants (3 narrow + 2 held-out) rather than CAA's single mechanism, and it's a repair task against a ~1,400-line existing codebase — structurally much closer to the durable-outbox family (which DID show real measured difficulty, 5/6 self-check failures) than to CAA's write-from-scratch pure function (null result). This is a genuine, non-trivial improvement. However, a real residual risk survives: the primary planted defect (resume.ts treating 202 as committed) is still a single boolean-ish branch, and the public spec's requirement (iv) explicitly states "restart safety must hold" as an outcome obligation. Even though this doesn't name the fix, it directs agent attention straight at restart-handling code, and many competent agents already carry a generic "never trust local state after a crash, always re-derive from the source of truth" construction habit independent of any explicit self-check — a mechanism the card's self-check-coverage predictor (which only models two named *self-check* behaviors, not default *construction* habits) does not obviously screen for. This is the same underlying phenomenon that sank CAA, just one level removed.

2) Defect naming: clean. infoIntentionallyAbsent explicitly withholds that resume.ts and entryOutcome.ts implement diverging classifiers and that they disagree on 202 — this is never stated. publicOutcomeRequirements states only outcome obligations (retrievability, non-duplication, restart-consistency, escalation), not implementation mechanics, which is a materially higher level of abstraction than CAA1's near-literal statement of the correct algorithm.

3) Self-check-coverage predictor: real and operationalized, not just pass/fail. privateVerifierArchitecture(e) and scenarioSelectionStrategy define it concretely — two named shallow implementations ("outer-200-only" and "per-entry-aware but never re-derives on resume") are run against the scenario grid, and scenarios both would already pass are down-weighted/excluded. This directly and substantively implements Phase 17 recommendation #1, unlike CAA's contract gate which had nothing.

4) External witness inaccessibility: reasonably well-designed — network isolation of the mock HIE's admin/ledger surface, a root-owned append-only log, and an explicit forged-ledger canary (`forged-ledger` control) proving a self-issued audit.json is rejected by the grader. This directly implements Phase 17 recommendation #5 (every isolation claim needs a negative-control canary) and reuses an already-established operator (`grade-the-obligation-from-the-external-party-log`, confirmed present in data/hardness-operators.json) rather than inventing an unvalidated pattern.

Net: 3 of 4 specific checks come back clean/well-addressed on paper; the reference-thinness axis is substantially but not completely closed, with a plausible unaddressed path (default restart-recovery engineering habit, cued by the spec's own restart-safety requirement) by which the core defect could be found for reasons unrelated to genuine per-entry/terminal-state reasoning. Critically, none of this is empirically measured — the card itself labels the uplift numbers (15-20% baseline, 35-50% full recipe) as "a hypothesis, not an additive sum," "unmeasured," "medium confidence," and explicitly notes this project's own record (Phase 14, Phase 17) is that such priors have repeatedly come back null. Per the instruction to default to refuted when genuinely uncertain, and because the actual numeric probability claims are self-admittedly unmeasured with a non-negligible chance of following CAA's own pattern (looks well-designed on paper, collapses once probed), I refute the probability claims as currently unconfirmed — the design targets the right lessons but has not yet demonstrated it clears them.

recipeCards.name: SQL/Query Identifier Injection Scope Expansion
recipeCards.baseFamilyDefinition: Unchanged from the input card, with one added grounding sentence. User- or upstream-tool-controlled identifiers (database/schema/table names, search query strings) are interpolated unsanitized into an executed data-tool call, letting a crafted or unusual identifier value cause the tool to read/touch objects far outside its nominally narrow, declared scope. Causal axis: authority-boundary-scope-violation. The credential/session's nominal authority is scoped to the specific object named in the request; unsanitized interpolation lets a crafted identifier value silently expand that authority to arbitrary objects the underlying credential can reach. Task shape: agent performs a narrowly-scoped lookup (inspect a named schema/table, search a named spreadsheet) where the identifier may originate from an earlier, less-trusted step; agent must validate/parameterize rather than trust direct interpolation; a verifier checks whether the resulting action stayed within the intended object scope. Subject-inaccessible witness: the tool's successful, well-formed response cannot itself reveal whether it executed against the intended object or a different one reached via injection -- only an independent diff of actually-queried objects reveals scope expansion. Domain: data warehousing / spreadsheet API integration security engineering. Fairness basis: unsanitized identifier interpolation is a textbook, well-documented CWE-class defect, independently confirmed via a filed and reviewed upstream PR -- not obscure or proprietary. The harder half of this family (checking scope by a mutable display name rather than a stable identifier, and checking only a direct container rather than a full ancestry/ownership chain) is likewise a named, well-documented real-world defect class -- the same shape as CVE-2018-1058-style PostgreSQL search_path schema-shadowing bugs and the routine Drive/cloud-storage advice to authorize by resource ID rather than by folder title -- so the added depth in this revision is drawn from established security literature, not manufactured to raise difficulty.
recipeCards.outboxOperatorMapping: 1) Realistic multi-file service -> a ~1,450-line "Data Discovery Assistant": an internal tool that lets analysts find and inspect a named warehouse table or a named spreadsheet by free-text description, spanning both injection surfaces the family names (SQL identifier composition and Drive query-string composition) inside one coherent service, not two toy snippets; the added stable-id-resolution and ancestry-walk mechanisms (see point 3) make this a genuinely thicker, two-surface-plus-batch reference rather than a single conceptual fix wearing a large file count. 2) Outcome-based instructions -> state containment and refusal obligations only, phrased entirely in terms of which object a request settles on and what must happen if it does not settle on exactly one -- never naming "allow-list," "scope check," "authorization," "resolver," or any other synonym for the historical anti-pattern or the untrusted-input step (see publicOutcomeRequirements; this revision audited and removed the word "unauthorized" and a sentence that had named the resolver-trust rule almost verbatim, both flagged by review as accidental disclosure). 3) Naturally embedded defect, now with three independent decision points rather than one -> identifier_guard.py correctly rejects SQL/Drive-query metacharacters (so the classic string-breakout injection is already closed) but never re-checks a resolver-supplied, already-well-formed identifier against the service's own declared scope, and where a partial check exists it (a) resolves the SQL side by schema display-name rather than by the catalog's own stable identifier (a session with a non-default search_path can shadow the intended schema with a same-named decoy -- the CVE-2018-1058 class), (b) resolves the Drive side by checking only a candidate's immediate parent folder rather than walking its full ancestry (a file nested under an allowed folder can also be shared into a disallowed one and still show the allowed folder as *a* parent), and (c) evaluates a multi-object request as a single unit rather than checking each named object independently, so one in-scope item in a batch can mask an out-of-scope sibling. These three are independent in the sense the recipe requires: fixing (a) does not fix (b) or (c), and each is tested by its own dedicated held-out mutant (see heldOutMutants). The query itself is always built with safe parameterized/quoted composition, so the result is a well-formed, plausible, syntactically-correct response even when it reaches the wrong object. 4) Visible tests with a realistic gap -> existing suite proves metacharacter payloads are rejected and in-scope objects round-trip correctly, but never exercises a syntactically clean identifier pointing at a real, reachable, out-of-scope sibling object, a search_path-shadowed same-named schema, a nested-but-differently-shared Drive file, or a batch mixing in-scope and out-of-scope items. 5) External authoritative state / witness, now enforced at the network layer with a canary -> a transport-level query/API-call recorder-proxy is the *only* network route the subject's container has to Postgres or the Google APIs (egress otherwise firewalled); it holds the real credentials, logs every resolved schema/table or effective Drive query and returned file IDs to a private append-only record before forwarding, and a dedicated raw-driver-bypass rig-integrity canary (a subject variant that tries to open its own unwrapped connection) must be observed failing closed on every rig build or the run is voided -- proving, not asserting, that the isolation holds (mirrors this project's own witness-isolation-with-canary control). A second, independent witness -- the fixture warehouse's and fixture Drive project's own native audit logging -- runs in parallel as defense in depth; disagreement between the two witnesses voids the run rather than being tie-broken. This remains the domain's own standard control (query/access audit logging), not an invented outbox. 6) Separate verifier -> a distinct process/container reads only the two witnesses' touched-object logs plus the subject's returned report, never the subject's self-reported scope claims; it also computes a self-check-coverage predictor (see privateVerifierArchitecture) from the subject's own added tests/self-checks, logged as a ranking/diagnostic feature whose predictive validity is measured empirically across the first graded cohort rather than assumed (Phase 17 Recommendation 1), and which can never override a passing graded verdict. 7) Controls -> positive-work / no-op / always-refuse / unconditional-success / hardcoding / evidence-forging / witness-bypass-canary (detailed in positiveWorkAndCheatControls). 8) Deterministic scenario fuzzing -> sweep identifier source x injection surface x wrong-scope shape x ancestry depth x catalog-resolution path x batch size to find the parameter(s) that reliably separate reference from buggy behavior. 9) Selection against three narrow dev mutants, held out on four independent mutants -- two carried over (case-fold-bypass, decoy-name-collision) and two new, one per newly-added surface-specific mechanism (search-path-shadow for the SQL stable-id requirement, immediate-parent-only for the Drive ancestry-walk requirement) -- plus b6-rig-integrity-controls run on every rig: prove the reference passes, each targeted bad subject fails only its intended check, the raw-driver-bypass canary fails closed, and malformed/missing/disagreeing witness evidence voids the run rather than scoring a false pass. 10) Frozen fixtures/hashes, isolated execution, blind labelling -> applied unchanged, verifier and recorder-proxy kept out of subject reach per point 5/6, with the fixture set extended to include nested-parent Drive decoys and a search-path-shadow decoy schema.
recipeCards.nonApplicableOperators: committed-idempotency-authority and narrow-recompute-starter -- both presuppose an asynchronous write with an uncertain-completion window and an action-stable idempotency key recovered across a lease epoch; this family has no write-side uncertainty at all, only read/inspect scope, so there is no committed key to recover and no epoch-recompute temptation to seed. recompute-activation-concentration -- presupposes multi-worker crash/recompute schedules as the activating parameter; this family's activating parameter is the shape of the identifier/query string and its resolution path, not worker count or completion timing, so the operator's specific parameterization does not transfer (its general principle -- concentrate scenario selection where the mechanism reliably activates -- is already covered here under fuzz-controlling-parameter, listed as applicable).
recipeCards.familyNativeDifficultyOperators: (plausible-but-unablated hypotheses, not in the measured 8-operator ledger) -- authorization-vs-syntax conflation: a validator that is demonstrably correct against syntax-breakout must still be separately checked for the orthogonal scope-authorization property, and the two are easy for a working engineer to treat as one job. Well-formed-but-wrong-object provenance: the dangerous input is never malformed or suspicious; it is a perfectly valid identifier for a real, reachable object -- just not the one the request named. Single-witness diff-only detectability: correctness is invisible from the subject's own successful response; only the external touched-object diff exposes divergence, so no amount of local testing against the returned report can catch the defect. Cross-surface consistency: the same containment property must hold across two structurally different query-building mechanisms (SQL identifier composition, Drive query-string composition) in the same service, so a repair that only closes one surface is incomplete -- this is a genuine held-out generalization axis distinct from anything in the durable-outbox lineage. Newly surfaced in this revision -- id-vs-display-name provenance: a scope check performed against a mutable display name (schema name, folder title) rather than a stable identifier (catalog OID, Drive file/folder ID) is bypassable via renaming, case variation, or search-path-style shadowing (the CVE-2018-1058 class), which is a second, independent property from the resolver-trust gap and native to how relational catalogs and Drive's naming model actually work. Ancestry/multi-parent ambiguity: Drive objects can have multiple parents or be nested arbitrarily deep, so a containment check against only the immediate parent is a distinct, realistic omission from a full ancestry walk, not an invented complication.
recipeCards.multiFileCodebaseSketch: A ~1,450-line Python "Data Discovery Assistant" service: discovery/server.py (tool entrypoints: find_object, inspect_object, search_within, ~150 lines) . discovery/reference_resolver.py (fuzzy-matches a free-text phrase against a crawled metadata index of table/column comments and spreadsheet titles, returns a ranked candidate ObjectRef explicitly documented as unverified, ~180 lines -- this is the "earlier, less-trusted step") . discovery/identifier_guard.py (the validation layer carrying the embedded defect: metacharacter rejection, plus the three independent scope-decision points described in outboxOperatorMapping point 3, ~200 lines) . discovery/warehouse_client.py (Postgres wrapper using psycopg2.sql.Identifier for safe quoting/composition, plus a catalog-OID resolution helper (pg_namespace/pg_class lookup) that the guard is supposed to call before trusting a schema-qualified name, ~260 lines) . discovery/sheets_client.py (Sheets/Drive wrapper building a Drive q= filter and a Sheets range query, plus a parents-ancestry-walk helper (recursive files.get(fields="parents")) that the guard is supposed to call before trusting a file/folder id, ~260 lines) . discovery/scope_policy.py (the legitimate declared-scope config -- allow-listed schema OIDs / Drive folder IDs, resolved from human-readable names once at startup -- sourced from a provisioning file so the agent is not asked to invent policy, ~90 lines) . discovery/report.py (formats the human-readable result, ~100 lines) . cli.py (harness-driven entrypoint: resolve -> inspect/search -> report, evaluating each object in a multi-object request independently, ~110 lines) . tests/ (test_identifier_guard.py, test_warehouse_client.py, test_sheets_client.py, test_resolver.py, ~280 lines total, the visible suite described in visibleTestStrategy).
recipeCards.publicOutcomeRequirements: When resolving and inspecting a named object, the service's actions must reach only the single schema/table or single spreadsheet/folder that its own processing ultimately settles on for that request -- nothing else, under any circumstance. If that settling step does not land on exactly one such object with confidence, the service must decline the operation with a clear, typed error rather than proceeding on a best guess or a narrowed substitute. A request that does settle on exactly one such object must still succeed and return correct data -- declining every request is not an acceptable way to satisfy this. When a single request names or implies more than one object, each one must be evaluated and reported on entirely on its own merits; correct handling of one part of such a request must never be inferred from, or allowed to excuse, incorrect handling of another part. Behavior must be deterministic and reproducible for the same input across runs.
recipeCards.infoIntentionallyAbsent: The exact contents of the allow-listed schema/folder set (present and derivable from scope_policy.py, but its adequacy relative to the guard is not called out). That the guard currently conflates syntax-safety with scope-authorization. Which specific identifier shapes the graded scenarios probe (schema-qualified strings smuggled through a bare-name field, case-variant matches, system-catalog names, cross-tenant Drive folders, nested-parent Drive files, search_path-shadowed schemas, batch requests). That resolver output is sometimes a well-formed pointer to a real but wrong-tenant/sibling object rather than garbage. That scope must be checked by a stable identifier rather than a display name, or that a Drive containment check must walk full ancestry rather than the immediate parent -- both mechanisms are present in the codebase (warehouse_client.py, sheets_client.py) but never called out as the applicable fix. The existence, location, or format of the touched-object recorder, the network-level egress restriction, or the parallel native-audit-log witness used for grading. The existence or scoring method of the self-check-coverage predictor -- it is a private, verifier-side diagnostic and ranking feature, not disclosed to the subject and never able to override a passing graded verdict. Any file, line, or function name where a fix belongs, and any hint that "SQL injection," "authorization," or "unauthorized" is the applicable defect category -- this revision specifically audited publicOutcomeRequirements and removed the word "unauthorized" and a sentence that had stated the resolver-distrust rule in near-verbatim form; the text now states only the containment outcome, framed around which object the request settles on, without naming any step, actor, or trust boundary.
recipeCards.visibleTestStrategy: The shipped suite passes and is realistic: test_identifier_guard.py proves classic metacharacter/injection payloads (semicolons, comment sequences, quote-breakout strings) are correctly rejected -- genuine, working injection-syntax defense. test_warehouse_client.py and test_sheets_client.py prove a same-tenant, declared-in-scope table/spreadsheet round-trips correctly end to end, including a call to the OID-resolution and ancestry-walk helpers on an already-correct object (so the helpers are demonstrably exercised and working, not dead code). test_resolver.py proves the fuzzy matcher returns a sensible top candidate for a clear query. The realistic gap: none of these tests ever supply a syntactically clean identifier that legitimately resolves to a different, reachable, real object; none ever construct a search_path under which a decoy schema shadows the intended one; none ever nest a Drive file under an allowed folder while also sharing it into a disallowed one; and none ever submit a batch mixing an in-scope and an out-of-scope item -- because authoring any of these requires deliberately imagining an authorized-looking-but-wrong-scope input, which teams routinely skip since it reads as a permissions or catalog-internals concern rather than an injection concern once the metacharacter tests are green. This mirrors how real injection regression suites almost always cover syntax-breakout payloads and almost never cover authorization-boundary or catalog-identity payloads.
recipeCards.privateVerifierArchitecture: A separate, root-owned verifier process/container. A transport-level recorder-proxy is the subject container's *only* network route to the real Postgres instance and the real Google APIs: egress is restricted at the network-namespace/firewall level to that proxy's local socket, the proxy alone holds the real credentials, and it appends every statement's resolved schema/table (via catalog OID, not display name) or every Drive request's effective query, resolved file IDs, and their full parent-ancestry chain to a private, append-only record per scenario before forwarding the call. In parallel, the fixture warehouse and fixture Drive project run their own native audit logging (Postgres statement logging / pg_audit-style extension; Drive/Cloud audit logs) as a second, independent witness that does not depend on the recorder-proxy at all; any disagreement between the two witnesses voids the run rather than being tie-broken, and this dual-witness design is itself the direct answer to the isolation-rigor gap raised in review. Fixtures are frozen: N allow-listed schemas plus M decoy schemas (including near-miss names, system catalogs, and a search_path-shadow decoy sharing the allowed schema's display name at an earlier search_path position) in the warehouse; one allow-listed Drive folder plus sibling decoy folders and at least one decoy file that is nested under the allowed folder while also being shared into a disallowed one, holding confusable file names. Grading reads only (a) the two witnesses' per-scenario touched-object sets and (b) the subject's returned report -- never the subject's own claims about what it touched. Checks: scope-containment (touched-object set is a subset of the exact object the request validly settles on), refusal-correctness (an out-of-scope/ambiguous candidate yields an empty touched-object set and a typed refusal, not a narrowed guess), liveness (a legitimate in-scope request still returns correct data), per-item independence (in a multi-object request, each item is graded on its own touched-object subset; one correct item never offsets another's leak), and replay-determinism (identical scenario, identical verdict). Every rig run also executes b6-style integrity controls: reference passes, each targeted bad subject fails only its intended check, a dedicated raw-driver-bypass subject (one that imports its own unwrapped Postgres/Drive client and tries to connect directly, bypassing the provided wrapper) is observed failing closed -- no route, no credentials -- proving rather than asserting the isolation claim, and absent/malformed/disagreeing witness evidence voids the run instead of scoring a false pass. Separately from graded pass/fail, the verifier statically inspects any test files or self-check code the subject adds or modifies during the task and computes a self-check-coverage score: the fraction of the fuzzer's wrong-scope-candidate shapes (sibling schema/folder, case-variant, qualified-string-in-bare-field, system-catalog, search_path-shadow, nested-but-differently-shared Drive file) for which the subject's own tests assert containment against a realistic decoy of that shape, as opposed to merely rejecting a malformed/metacharacter string. This score is logged per attempt as a ranking/diagnostic feature, per Phase 17 Recommendation 1 ("a ranking feature rather than a pass/fail one"); its correlation with hidden-grader outcomes is an empirical question this family's preregistration commits to measuring across the first graded cohort before the predictor is trusted for any future ranking decision, and it can never downgrade or override a verdict that the boolean checks above already passed.
recipeCards.externalAuthorityOrWitness: The transport-level query/API-call recorder-proxy remains this family's own legitimate external witness, not an imported outbox structure: production data-security engineering already uses exactly this control (statement/query audit logging, Drive API access logging) to answer the question the family poses -- "what did the credential actually touch?" -- which is unanswerable from the tool's own successful response. This revision closes the isolation gap raised in review by making that witness the subject's *only* network path rather than a wrappable Python object: the subject's container has no real credentials and no route to Postgres or the Google APIs other than through the recorder-proxy's socket, enforced at the network-namespace/firewall level, so a subject that imports its own driver and tries to bypass the wrapper finds nothing to connect to. A dedicated raw-driver-bypass canary subject is run on every rig build specifically to prove this holds (mirroring this project's own witness-isolation-with-canary pattern): the run is voided unless that canary is observed failing closed. A second, fully independent witness -- the fixture warehouse's and Drive project's own native audit logging, which the subject cannot reach or influence regardless of how it composes its requests -- runs in parallel as defense in depth; any disagreement between the two witnesses voids the run. The witness is append-only, harness/verifier-owned, and outside the subject's process and network boundary, satisfying recipe point 5 with a claim that is now demonstrated by a falsifiable canary rather than asserted.
recipeCards.fuzzerDimensions: identifier source (user-typed literal vs. resolver-chained/untrusted vs. mixed) . injection surface (SQL schema.table composition vs. Drive query-string composition) . shape of the wrong-scope candidate (exact match to a disallowed sibling schema/folder; case-variant of an allowed name; an already-qualified string smuggled through a bare-name field; a system-catalog name; a search_path-shadow decoy sharing the allowed schema's display name; a cross-tenant Drive folder with a confusable title; a Drive file nested under the allowed folder but also shared into a disallowed one) . ancestry depth for the Drive surface (direct parent vs. two- or three-level-nested parent) . catalog resolution path for the SQL surface (direct OID match vs. name lookup mediated by a non-default search_path) . request multiplicity (single-object vs. batch, since batch increases partial-leakage surface, graded per-item per privateVerifierArchitecture) . presence/absence of an allow-list check at each call site (used only to build calibration mutants, never shipped as a graded variable) . error-vs-silent-success behavior on malformed vs. merely-out-of-scope input . witness-enforcement layer (recorder-proxy-only egress vs. native audit log), used only for rig-integrity controls, never as a graded difficulty variable. Hypothesis to validate, not assert: the "already-qualified string smuggled through a bare-name field," "search_path-shadow," and "nested-but-differently-shared Drive file" dimensions are the most likely controlling parameters, to be confirmed empirically before being used to concentrate the graded set.
recipeCards.narrowDevMutants: syntax-only-guard -- rejects injection metacharacters but performs no scope/allow-list check at all (the direct omission). first-segment-trust -- validates only the leftmost dot-segment of a qualified identifier and blindly trusts the remainder. resolver-is-truth -- skips validation entirely whenever the identifier arrived from the resolver step, treating "already resolved" as "already in scope."
recipeCards.heldOutMutants: case-fold-bypass -- the allow-list check is case-sensitive while the underlying warehouse/Drive lookup is case-insensitive, so a differently-cased disallowed name still resolves. decoy-name-collision -- the allow-list check matches on schema/folder display name rather than a stable id, so a same-named schema/folder belonging to a different tenant or catalog passes. search-path-shadow (new, targets the stable-id-resolution requirement) -- the SQL scope check resolves the schema by name under the connection's active search_path instead of by catalog OID, so a decoy schema placed earlier in search_path with the same display name as the allowed schema is what actually gets queried while the check reports the allowed name. immediate-parent-only (new, targets the ancestry-walk requirement) -- the Drive scope check inspects only a candidate file's immediate parent folder ID instead of walking its full ancestry, so a file nested two levels under the allowed folder but also directly shared into a disallowed folder passes because its stored "first parent" happens to be allowed.
recipeCards.positiveWorkAndCheatControls: positive-work -- the correct reference implementation scores full marks on every scenario, including the boundary-adjacent ones. no-op / always-refuse -- refusing every request scores near-zero on the liveness check because legitimate in-scope requests must still succeed. unconditional-success -- a subject that fabricates a plausible report without issuing any real call is caught because both witnesses show zero calls for a scenario the report claims real data for. hardcoding -- a subject that special-cases the exact identifiers used in the visible tests is caught by held-out fixture identifiers never seen in the visible suite. evidence-forging -- a subject that writes or points the grader at a self-controlled "audit log" is caught because grading reads exclusively from the two harness-owned witnesses, on paths the subject's container cannot reach or influence. witness-bypass canary -- a dedicated raw-driver-bypass subject variant (imports its own unwrapped Postgres/Drive client and attempts a direct connection) is run on every rig build and must be observed failing closed (no network route, no credentials); its absence or success voids the rig rather than being silently ignored, giving the isolation claim in externalAuthorityOrWitness a falsifiable check rather than an assertion.
recipeCards.scenarioSelectionStrategy: Build the parameter grid across the fuzzer dimensions; run it against the reference and all three narrow dev mutants. Keep only cells where the reference passes and at least one narrow mutant fails (activation evidence); discard non-activating cells from the "difficulty" role but retain a deliberate minority of them as explicit non-activation controls in the shipped set, so a subject cannot pattern-match "every request is an attack" and refuse indiscriminately. Concentrate the majority of the graded set on whichever region the grid shows most reliably separates reference from mutants. Finally, replay the selected set against all four held-out mutants (never used for selection) and require each of the four to fail at least one selected scenario, confirming the selection generalizes across every independent decision point rather than overfitting to the three dev mutants or to only one of the two injection surfaces. Alongside this pass/fail selection, log the self-check-coverage predictor (privateVerifierArchitecture) for every graded attempt in the first cohort and compute its correlation with hidden-grader outcomes before treating it as a validated ranking feature for later cohorts or later families -- it ships as measured evidence, not an assumed capability.
recipeCards.cheapestPackageValidityProbe: Before building the Sheets/Drive surface, implement only identifier_guard.py, warehouse_client.py, scope_policy.py, and the recorder-proxy, and run a ~6-8 hour smoke test: (1) the reference passes a handful of hand-written in-scope and out-of-scope cases, including a search_path-shadow case; (2) the syntax-only-guard mutant fails at least one out-of-scope case; (3) a hardcode-the-fixture-names cheat fails once a held-out fixture identifier is substituted; (4) a deliberately naive fix that calls one identical, surface-agnostic boolean helper (no OID resolution, no search_path handling) from the SQL call site still fails the search-path-shadow case -- proving the stable-id requirement is actually load-bearing and not satisfiable by the thin single-helper fix the reviewers flagged as a risk; (5) the raw-driver-bypass canary fails closed (no route, no credentials) before any Drive surface work begins. If any of the five does not separate cleanly -- especially (1)/(2) collapsing back into an already-solved injection problem, or (4) showing the thin single-helper fix still passes -- the mechanism has not achieved the independence this revision requires and the family should be killed or redesigned before the Sheets surface, tests, and full verifier are built out.
threeExampleInstances: Warehouse catalog assistant (Postgres): an analyst asks to inspect a table resolved from a natural-language description; declared scope is one schema; decoys are sibling business schemas, system catalogs (information_schema, pg_catalog), and a search_path-shadow schema sharing the allowed schema's display name -- controlling parameters are a schema-qualified string smuggled through a bare-name field and whether the check resolves by catalog OID or by display name under the active search_path.

Spreadsheet/Drive search assistant: a chat agent resolves a spreadsheet reference from a loose phrase ('the Q3 leads sheet') and searches within it; declared scope is one Drive file/folder; decoys are other tenant or shared-drive spreadsheets reachable by the same service account with confusably similar titles, plus a file nested under the allowed folder that is also shared into a disallowed one -- controlling parameters are a Drive query-string clause that widens beyond the intended folder and whether the check walks full parent ancestry or only the immediate parent.

Multi-tenant BI export tool: a support-ticket workflow names a workspace and a report table to export; declared scope is one workspace's dataset on a shared warehouse cluster; decoys are a differently-cased or differently-punctuated workspace identifier belonging to another tenant -- this instance's controlling parameter is case/format normalization rather than raw allow-list membership, giving a genuinely different activation mechanism from instance (a) while sharing the same causal axis.
recipeCards.estimatedUplift: Unmeasured hypothesis (evidenceType fresh-external, isCalibrationAnchor false; no trials run yet, so this is a pre-registration estimate, not a measured effect, and it is not additive across the operators listed above). Ordinary packaging -- a short function explicitly framed as "fix the SQL/query injection vulnerability" -- is heavily pattern-matched training material; estimate ordinary solve rate roughly 55-65%. The full recipe removes every surface tell an agent could pattern-match on: no security framing in the instructions, the public outcome text has been specifically audited to remove the word "unauthorized" and a near-verbatim statement of the resolver-distrust rule, syntax-injection is already correctly closed via parameterized/quoted identifier composition so the reflexive "add parameterization" fix does not apply, the actual defect now spans three independent decision points (resolver-trust, stable-id vs. display-name resolution, ancestry-walk vs. immediate-parent) each covered by its own dedicated held-out mutant rather than one conceptual fix duplicated across files, decoy objects are real and reachable rather than obviously malformed, and grading runs against two independent external touched-object witnesses rather than subject-reported success. Estimate full-recipe solve rate roughly 10-25% (wide range, low-to-medium confidence pending the cheapest-package-validity probe, the dev-mutant fuzzing sweep, and the first-cohort self-check-coverage-predictor measurement all actually separating cleanly). This range is shifted down slightly from the prior draft's 15-30% to reflect the added independent decision points and the removal of the accidental instruction leak; it remains an estimate to be corrected by the probe and the first graded cohort, not a claim of measured difficulty.
recipeCards.mainFairnessRisks: The gap between "textbook injection fix" and "subtle authorization gap" must stay genuinely security-relevant, not read as obscure allow-list trivia once reviewers see it -- whyFair depends on this distinction being a real, common engineering conflation, not a manufactured gotcha; the added stable-id and ancestry-walk mechanisms are grounded in a named, real CVE class (search_path schema shadowing) and Drive's actual multi-parent data model respectively, specifically so the added depth reads as realistic rather than manufactured. The declared-scope policy must already exist somewhere legitimate in the codebase (scope_policy.py, sourced from a provisioning file) so the agent is repairing an enforcement gap, not inventing authorization policy from nothing. The "less-trusted upstream step" must read as an ordinary data-quality/ambiguity issue (a fuzzy matcher returning a similarly-named wrong-tenant object), not a dressed-up adversarial-attacker scenario, to stay consistent with the family's own whyAgentMayFail framing. Instance (c)'s case/format-normalization variant risks drifting into a string-parsing puzzle rather than an authorization-boundary property if over-engineered -- the essential difficulty must stay the boundary check, not parsing complexity; the same risk now applies to the OID-resolution and ancestry-walk mechanisms and must be watched during build so they stay a boundary-check property, not a Postgres-internals or Drive-API trivia puzzle. The recorder/witness must be genuinely non-forgeable and outside the subject's process, but must still look like an ordinary query-log sidecar and network egress policy native to the domain, not a contrived addition with no in-story justification; the failure a subject sees when it tries to bypass the wrapper (connection refused / no credentials) must look like an ordinary permissions or routing error, not a giveaway that scope-checking is the graded property. The self-check-coverage predictor must remain a diagnostic/ranking-only signal that is validated empirically before use and can never override or downgrade a verdict a subject already earned on the boolean checks -- treating it as a hidden, undisclosed grading criterion would itself be a new fairness problem of exactly the kind this revision is meant to close.
recipeCards.killConditions: A subject that only swaps string-concatenated query building for parameterized/quoted identifier composition (psycopg2.sql.Identifier or equivalent), with no scope check whatsoever, still passes every graded scenario -- indicates the family collapsed back into a solved injection problem. A reference-shaped fix that calls one identical, surface-agnostic boolean helper (no catalog-OID resolution, no ancestry walk) from both the SQL and Drive call sites still passes the search-path-shadow and immediate-parent-only held-out mutants -- indicates the three decision points collapsed back into one and the reference-thinness risk raised in review was not actually resolved. A subject that bypasses the provided wrapped client entirely (opens a raw, unwrapped database or Drive API connection) still reaches a real object without either witness recording it -- indicates the network-level enforcement is not real and the witness is bypassable; the raw-driver-bypass canary failing to fail closed on any rig build has the same meaning and voids that rig. An independent reviewer finds that the rewritten publicOutcomeRequirements still names or closely paraphrases the resolver-trust or authorization concept (a synonym for "unauthorized," or a restatement of which step or actor is untrustworthy) -- indicates the anti-pattern-naming defect was reworded rather than fixed. The declared-scope policy cannot be made independently derivable from something already legitimate in the codebase/config without arbitrary invention. The fuzzing grid shows no parameter region where the reference and all three narrow dev mutants reliably separate (all cells uniformly pass or uniformly fail), or the four held-out mutants do not each fail at least one selected scenario. The self-check-coverage predictor, once measured across the first graded cohort, shows no correlation (or a negative one) with hidden-grader outcomes -- it must not be promoted to a ranking feature per Phase 17 Recommendation 1, and the family proceeds on the boolean checks alone until a validated predictor exists. Reviewers judge the "well-formed identifier pointing at a real wrong-scope object," the stable-id-resolution requirement, or the ancestry-walk requirement as too obscure or unnatural for a working engineer to plausibly miss in either instance. The reference implementation cannot be built as an original design without adapting the actual upstream Klavis fix nearly verbatim, leaving no room for a non-searchable, fictional implementation.

skepticVerdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: REFUTED. Applying the four requested checks (each drawn directly from the Phase 17 CAA-V1 postmortem, reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md, sections 10-12):

1) Reference-implementation thinness (CAA V1's exact failure: ~15-line, one-decision reference).
The postmortem's fix was: "Penalise small artifact size... the reference here is roughly fifteen lines with one decision... pushing below a coin-flip needs a second independent decision of comparable difficulty." This card explicitly designed around that lesson: the fix is embedded in a ~1,300-line multi-file service, and the "cross-surface consistency" operator requires the same containment property to hold across two structurally different composition mechanisms (SQL identifier composition and Drive query-string composition), explicitly framed as "a genuine held-out generalization axis." The card even ships a "cheapestPackageValidityProbe" and a kill condition that directly tests for exactly this collapse ("A subject that only swaps string-concatenated query building for parameterized/quoted identifier composition... still passes every graded scenario -- indicates the family collapsed back into a solved injection problem"). This is a real, self-aware mitigation the CAA V1 package never had at construction time. Residual risk: the two "independent" decisions (SQL-site check, Drive-site check) are likely the same conceptual fix (call scope_policy against a canonical id) duplicated across two call sites, not truly independent decisions of comparable difficulty -- once an agent spots the missing check in one file, replicating it to the other is close to free. Verdict on this check alone: plausible but not decisively thin -- partial mitigation present, not fully refuted on this axis alone.

2) Does the public instruction accidentally name the defect/anti-pattern?
This is where the card fails concretely, and contradicts its own stated design intent. The recipe explicitly promises (outboxOperatorMapping point 2 and infoIntentionallyAbsent) that instructions will "never name 'allow-list,' 'scope check,' or the historical anti-pattern," and that "any hint that ... 'authorization' is the applicable defect category" will stay absent. But publicOutcomeRequirements itself states: "If a resolved candidate is ambiguous, unauthorized, or not the caller's declared scope, the service must refuse..." -- using the word "unauthorized" directly, which is exactly the hint the card promises to withhold. Worse, it states: "Identifier values that arrive from an earlier resolution step must not be treated as already safe to use." That sentence is a near-verbatim statement of the fix for the "resolver-is-truth" narrow dev mutant -- it tells the agent precisely where the trust boundary is missing (resolver-originated identifiers), which is the exact discovery step the family's own whyAgentMayFail and subjectInaccessibleWitness framing depend on being non-obvious. This is structurally identical to CAA V1's failure mode, where "CAA1 states the identity binding outright and the specification's forbidden outcomes name the historical anti-pattern in words" (Phase 17 report, section on the registered prediction) -- the postmortem's recommendation #2 was explicitly "Penalise a candidate whose forbidden-outcomes text names the historical anti-pattern in words." This card does that, contradicting its own design goal.

3) Real self-check-coverage predictor, or just pass/fail?
Phase 17's top recommendation was: "Add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate, and make it a ranking feature rather than a pass/fail one." Nothing in this card does this. privateVerifierArchitecture and scenarioSelectionStrategy describe pure boolean grading (scope-containment subset check, refusal-correctness, liveness, replay-determinism) plus the standard B6 reference/mutant pass-fail controls. The only nod toward self-check coverage is a narrative, unmeasured claim in visibleTestStrategy ("real injection regression suites almost always cover syntax-breakout payloads and almost never cover authorization-boundary payloads") -- an assertion, not a predictor, and it is never validated empirically anywhere in the card (estimatedUplift is explicitly labeled "Unmeasured hypothesis... pre-registration estimate, not a measured effect"). This confirms the gap: still just pass/fail, with an unvalidated qualitative hunch standing in for the missing predictor.

4) Is the external witness genuinely subject-inaccessible, or forgeable?
The evidence-forging control (grading reads only the harness-owned recorder) addresses a subject fabricating its own audit log, and the mechanism (query/API-call recorder at the transport level) is a legitimate, domain-native control. But the isolation claim is underspecified relative to what CAA V1's postmortem demanded ("Require a negative control for every isolation and non-leakage claim. Two of Phase 16's seven reported controls could not fail. Any claim of the form 'X did not leak' must ship a canary that trips the same detector, or it is not evidence"). This card asserts the recorder wraps "the actual DB driver and Google API client at a boundary the subject's code cannot import, monkeypatch, or write to," but never specifies the enforcement mechanism (e.g., network-namespace/proxy-forced egress vs. a Python-level monkeypatch that a subject with its own driver import could bypass), and never describes a canary/negative-control proving the recorder itself would catch a deliberately bypassing subject (unlike Phase 17's C8, which explicitly required "a deliberately leaky facade **does** trip the same detector"). Given the subject's process legitimately needs live network access to Postgres and the Drive API to do its job, a subject that opens its own driver/socket instead of using the provided wrapped client is a plausible bypass path this card does not rule out with the same rigor the postmortem demanded. This is a genuine, unresolved uncertainty rather than a confirmed break.

Given check 2 is a concrete, self-contradicting textual defect (the card explicitly promises not to hint at "authorization" as the defect category and then uses that exact word, plus states the resolver-distrust rule almost outright -- the same shape of leak that made CAA V1 collapse to an easy task), and check 3 confirms no real self-check-coverage predictor exists (still pass/fail, exactly the gap the postmortem said drove CAA V1's overestimated difficulty), and check 4 leaves a plausible unaddressed witness-bypass path, the probability claims (15-30% estimated solve rate, explicitly framed as low-confidence) are not adequately supported. Per the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given these are concrete textual findings (not just uncertainty), this recipe card's probability claims are REFUTED: it is at meaningful risk of repeating CAA V1's exact failure mode (an accidentally-leaked/near-stated rule collapsing an intended-hard mechanism into a pattern-matchable fix), and the card has not been checked against the specific process fix (self-check-coverage predictor) that the same postmortem prescribed.

Checked this card against the project's own documented CAA V1 postmortem (scripts/phase18-report.mjs lines 93-103), which names the exact failure mode as a four-part pattern: (1) public spec stated the graded mechanism verbatim, (2) named the historical anti-pattern in forbidden outcomes, (3) disclosed hidden dimensions and their boundary values, (4) reduced the reference to ~20 lines, one decision point. Scoring this card against all four plus the two extra questions asked:

1. Reference-implementation thinness — LOW RISK, genuinely improved over CAA V1. The card specs a ~1,300-line multi-file service (server.py ~150, reference_resolver.py ~180, identifier_guard.py ~120, warehouse_client.py ~220, sheets_client.py ~220, scope_policy.py ~80, report.py ~100) and requires the fix to hold consistently across two structurally different query-building surfaces (SQL identifier composition and Drive query-string composition) plus survive case-folding and id-vs-display-name held-out mutants. That is materially different from CAA V1's single ~20-line conditional. This axis does not support refutation on its own.

2. Public instruction naming the defect — CONFIRMED, and this is the decisive finding. `publicOutcomeRequirements` states: "Identifier values that arrive from an earlier resolution step must not be treated as already safe to use" and "never touch/return objects outside the exact one named or resolved... regardless of how the identifier value is spelled or which step produced it." This is functionally identical to CAA V1's "named the historical anti-pattern in its forbidden outcomes" failure: it doesn't use the literal words "allow-list" or "resolver-is-truth," but it directly states the operative rule that IS the fix for the resolver-is-truth narrow dev mutant, and "regardless of how it's spelled" additionally telegraphs the case-fold-bypass held-out mutant. The recipe's own design intent (outboxOperatorMapping point 2) explicitly says instructions must "never name... the historical anti-pattern" — its own drafted publicOutcomeRequirements violates that intent. A subject can satisfy this by literal compliance with the written sentence rather than by independently discovering the authorization gap, exactly how CAA V1's agents "wrote self-checks that covered the rule" and "cited the published rule codes back." This directly undercuts the card's own premise (estimatedUplift) that "no surface tell" justifies a 15-30% solve rate — the surface tell is present.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor — NOT PRESENT, but not dishonestly claimed either. Grading is a set of boolean checks (scope-containment, refusal-correctness, liveness, replay-determinism) aggregated per scenario, with scenario selection driven by a mutant-kill grid (same fuzz-controlling-parameter method used elsewhere in this repo). There's no distinct continuous coverage metric. This is standard for the project and not a fabricated capability, but it means nothing here would catch a subject whose self-checks merely mirror the leaked outcome sentence from point 2.

4. External witness inaccessibility — PLAUSIBLE ON PAPER, UNVERIFIED IN PRACTICE. The transport-level recorder design (outside subject's container, evidence-forging control specified) is architecturally sound, but this project's own Phase 17 CAA audit found that superficially identical "witness isolation" and "challenge non-leakage" claims were unfalsifiable as actually implemented (no reachable failing branch) despite being asserted in the design. Since this SQL family is still a pre-registration with nothing built, the same risk class is un-audited here and cannot be taken on faith.

Net: this card explicitly tries to route around the CAA V1 lesson (its own text cites the need to avoid naming the anti-pattern, keeps hidden dimensions undisclosed, and builds a substantial multi-file reference) — so it clearly targets that lesson — but its own drafted public outcome requirements reintroduce exactly the CAA V1 defect-naming failure via plain-language equivalents of the technical terms it avoided. Combined with an unaudited witness-isolation claim of the same category that has previously proven vacuous in this project, the stated 15-30% solve-rate estimate is not credible as an estimate of a "no surface tell" task; a materially higher solve rate is more likely. Per instructions to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given this is a concrete textual finding (not just uncertainty), I refute the probability claims.

Checked this repo's own precedent for "CAA V1" (src/families/caa-revalidation, reports/caa-revalidation-kill-analysis.md, reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md) to calibrate the specific failure mode named in the task, then checked the four risks against the recipe card text.

1) Reference-implementation thinness (CAA V1 echo): CAA V1's reference.ts (73 lines) reduces the entire reference/mutant differential to one boolean switch (`bindQueryPerName`, line 52: `const target = options.bindQueryPerName ? name : (firstStale ?? name);`) — literally a single ternary decision point, which is why 4/4 counted trials solved it and it died of `already_solved`. This recipe's narrow+held-out mutant set (syntax-only-guard, first-segment-trust, resolver-is-truth, case-fold-bypass, decoy-name-collision) is richer than CAA V1's single-switch design in principle, but the actual fix could still collapse into one `is_in_scope(object_id, allow_list)` helper called at two call sites — i.e., a thin, single-conceptual-decision patch dressed up by a larger 1,300-line surrounding service. The recipe itself concedes this is unverified: the "cheapestPackageValidityProbe" and dev-mutant fuzzing sweep meant to rule this out have explicitly not been run yet ("no trials run yet... pre-registration estimate"). Risk not resolved, only flagged as a kill condition.

2) Public instruction naming the defect: publicOutcomeRequirements states "Identifier values that arrive from an earlier resolution step must not be treated as already safe to use." This directly tells the subject which data flow is dangerous and what property to add (validate resolver output before trusting it) — functionally equivalent to naming the mechanism even though it avoids the literal words "allow-list"/"scope check." This is the same failure class this repo's own postmortem blamed for CAA V1's collapse: "the published rule order made attribution a lookup rather than a derivation" (policy-explicitness). infoIntentionallyAbsent correctly withholds the deeper "guard conflates syntax vs. scope" insight, but the outcome-requirements sentence above still telegraphs the load-bearing data-flow risk in outcome language, which meaningfully narrows the search space for a competent engineer.

3) Self-check-coverage predictor: none exists. privateVerifierArchitecture defines four binary checks (scope-containment, refusal-correctness, liveness, replay-determinism) per scenario — pass/fail, aggregated, not a graduated coverage metric. Worse, visibleTestStrategy explicitly establishes that the subject's own local/self-authored tests (the shipped suite) are guaranteed uncorrelated with the hidden defect by design ("none of these tests ever supply a syntactically clean identifier that legitimately resolves to a different... object"). So there is no self-check signal that predicts hidden-check success at all — confirmed gap, not just an assumption.

4) Witness/recorder subject-inaccessibility: asserted ("transport-level," "boundary the subject's process cannot import, mount, or write to") but unverified — no implementation exists yet, and the card itself lists "The recorder/witness can be read, tampered with, or bypassed from the subject's own process or container" as an open kill condition rather than a ruled-out one. The description ("wraps the actual Postgres driver and Google API client") is ambiguous between a robust network/transport-level interceptor and an in-process object wrap that a subject could route around (e.g., a raw socket or an unwrapped client import), and nothing in the card describes network-level enforcement (firewalling all outbound DB/API traffic through the recorder). This project's own related authority-boundary-scope family on the same lineage (access-token-scope-expansion) already had its evidence invalidated by a package leak, showing this general risk class is not hypothetical in this pipeline.

All four specific checks turned up real, unresolved concerns rather than clean confirmations, and two of them (thin-reference risk, instruction leakage) are structurally close cousins of the exact mechanism that sank this repo's own CAA V1 family. The card is honest that its 15-30% solve-rate estimate is an unmeasured pre-registration hypothesis pending a probe that hasn't run. Per instructions, default to refuted=true under this level of genuine uncertainty.

recipeCards.name: Verifier Container Isolation Boundary
recipeCards.baseFamilyDefinition: A task's grading verifier must run in a structurally separate, later-arriving container that shares no filesystem or package state with the agent's own now-destroyed container, so agent-mutated state or an agent-installed shim cannot be silently inherited and trusted by grading. Task shape: the agent completes work in one sandboxed container; a disjoint verifier container, built independently and started only after the agent's container is torn down, can read only explicitly declared artifact paths, baked-in image content, or a persistent sidecar. The family measures two things at once: whether the agent's own evidence of success lands within that declared surface, and whether the harness itself correctly enforces the isolation. Causal axis: verifier-trust-boundary-integrity. Professional domain: CI/CD and benchmark-grading infrastructure engineering — a documented, recurring failure mode across independent benchmark projects' own review/contribution docs, with a mechanistically specifiable correct architecture (sealed containers, a declared artifact contract). This statement is unchanged by everything below; the recipe is a construction layer on top of it, not a redefinition of it.
recipeCards.outboxOperatorMapping:
REVISION NOTE (v2, post-adversarial-reconciliation). All three independent skeptic reviews of v1 refuted it and converged on four concrete, non-overlapping gaps, which are fixed below rather than argued away: (a) the graded fix reduced to one decision point wrapped in 1,400 lines of scaffolding — CAA V1's exact failure shape, and arguably worse, because the original defect (verifier mount list literally filtered from the agent container's own recorded mounts) was close enough to the family's own stated axis ("must not inherit agent state") that a reviewer had a spec-level reason for suspicion before running anything; (b) publicOutcomeRequirements item 4 named the held-out `process-deliverable-blind` mutant's anti-pattern in plain outcome text ("rather than by asking the agent's own container"); (c) operator 6's per-run self-check-coverage report was mislabeled as the pre-trial predictor Phase 17 recommendation 1 actually asked for (a ranking feature computed BEFORE trial spend, not a mandatory runtime artifact cross-checked AFTER); (d) the external-witness design never said how the meta-verifier identifies "the verifier container" without trusting the candidate's own naming, and never addressed daemon-layer image-cache tampering, which the family's own held-out `image-cache-poisoning` mutant implicitly concedes is possible. Fixes: the shipped starter now carries two structurally independent, individually necessary defects (D1, D2, defined in operator 3) in two modules with no shared vocabulary, so no single-file diff or single decision closes the task; item 4's outcome text is rewritten with zero implementation-naming; a real pre-trial predictor (operator 6a) is specified, applied, and its recorded score gates trial authorization as its own kill condition; and the external witness now identifies containers via the daemon's own event stream and independently checks image-layer provenance instead of trusting candidate-reported identity (see privateVerifierArchitecture, externalAuthorityOrWitness).

(1) Realistic multi-file service → "Gantry": a ~1,500–1,800-line TypeScript build/grade orchestrator, dressed publicly as a generic CI/CD artifact-promotion pipeline ("build stage → isolated verification stage"), not as an AI-benchmark harness — original fictional system, not a recognizable clone of any real benchmark runner. Modules: manifest parser, agent-side container runner, artifact-snapshot extractor, sidecar-volume manager, verifier-side container runner, a shared low-level container-runtime client used by both sides, and a small scripted-fixture library. Driven end-to-end by `init → run-agent-container → snapshot-declared-artifacts → destroy-agent-container → build-and-start-verifier-container(snapshot + sidecar + baked image content only) → grade → destroy-verifier-container`.

(2) Outcome-based instructions → stated only as required behavior, never as defect description (see publicOutcomeRequirements for the exact, re-scrubbed text).

(3) Naturally embedded defects, TWO, independently required → D1 lives in the shared low-level container-runtime client (`containerClient.ts`), used by both the agent-side and verifier-side runners. It adds a legitimate-looking performance optimization: a resolved-bind-source cache keyed only by volume/mount *name*, so repeated lookups for the same named mount inside one orchestration run don't re-query the daemon. Critically, the verifier-side mount LIST is still, visibly and correctly, constructed fresh from the declared artifact/sidecar contract every single time — a reviewer diffing `verifierRuntime.ts` against the SPEC's outcome language finds nothing wrong, because it genuinely does build from the contract, not from the agent's own recorded mounts. The leak is one layer down: when the sidecar volume name was already resolved once during the agent's own container build, the cache silently returns that earlier-resolved host path for the verifier's build instead of re-resolving it fresh from the daemon. No WRONG/TODO marker, no suspicious naming, and it is invisible without exercising a real daemon across two sequential real container builds that share a volume name in one run.

D2 lives in `artifactSnapshot.ts`: declared artifact paths are copied out of the stopped agent container by name, using the container's own filesystem export, without first establishing that each declared path denotes content the container itself produced rather than a reference to something living elsewhere. A path the agent arranged to resolve outside the container's own captured filesystem is copied as if it were a frozen point-in-time file. This too reads as ordinary, unremarkable snapshot-copy code — no flagged corner case, no comment calling it out.

Both D1 and D2 must be fixed for the full scenario battery to pass; each activates on a disjoint fixture subset (D1 needs a shared resource name reused across two builds in one run, D2 needs a declared path that resolves outside the container's own filesystem), so neither is discoverable or fixable by inspecting a single call site, and fixing one leaves the other's fixtures failing. This is the second, independent, comparably-difficult decision Phase 17's recommendation 3 asked for — not a second cosmetic variation on the same idea, and not the same anti-pattern the family's own axis already names.

(4) Visible tests with a realistic coverage gap → the shipped `tests/orchestrator/*` suite runs the full pipeline against an in-process fake container client and passes cleanly for both D1 and D2. It verifies wiring at the object level (which path values get passed into constructors) but never exercises real daemon semantics: neither a resolved bind-source's staleness across two sequential real builds sharing a name (D1) nor a copied path's actual filesystem provenance inside a real container export (D2) can be expressed against a fake client. Standard practice, not a contrived omission.

(5) External authoritative state / ledger analogue → deliberately not a literal ledger; see externalAuthorityOrWitness. The daemon's own introspection API plus its independent event stream is this family's non-ledger witness.

(6) Separate outcome-measuring verifier, per-run anti-forgery report → a meta-verifier runs outside and independently of the candidate pipeline, against a real daemon. For each fixture it (a) invokes the candidate pipeline, (b) independently queries the daemon's own event stream and inspect API — identifying "the verifier container" itself by daemon-reported creation order and timestamp relative to the daemon-witnessed agent-teardown event, never by a name or id the candidate's own code hands it — for the verifier container's actual mount table, resolved bind sources, and image layer digests, and (c) requires the candidate's own reported outcome, plus a mandatory structured self-check-coverage report (which surfaces were exposed, confirmation of teardown-before-start, and confirmation that every shared-name resource and every declared artifact path was independently re-verified for freshness/provenance) to agree with those independently observed daemon facts. A shallow patch that passes by luck without an accurate self-report is flagged as a coverage failure distinct from a correctness failure. This is the anti-forgery mechanism; it is deliberately NOT the pre-trial predictor described next, and the two are no longer conflated.

(6a) Pre-trial self-check-coverage predictor (construction gate, computed and recorded BEFORE any trial spend — this is the actual Phase 17 recommendation 1 artifact, not a relabeling of 6). Modeled directly on this repository's own `src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts` method (structural-token / forbidden-pattern presence in agent-written verification code), adapted to this family: for each of D1 and D2, define what a natural, unprompted verification snippet would need to contain to organically catch it, then predict — before any agent ever sees the task — how likely a competent agent's default container-isolation self-check is to contain that structure. D1's rule requires comparing a daemon-reported mount *source* (not target/name) across two separate `inspect()` calls taken before and after a second build that reuses the same resource name, and treating disagreement as failure; this is not what a "does the verifier see the disallowed path" self-check naturally does (that check compares target lists/content visibility, not source-path freshness across sequential builds) — predicted risk LOW. D2's rule requires confirming a captured artifact's content is not merely present but genuinely originates from the container's own filesystem rather than being reachable through it; an agent that already writes content-hash comparisons is closer to covering this incidentally — predicted risk LOW-MODERATE. Recorded combined score: LOW-MODERATE natural-coverage risk (full reasoning and the score must be written into the family's own preregistration artifact before trial authorization — see killConditions). This is a real, falsifiable, applied prediction, not a promise to build one later, and it is explicitly flagged as a pre-trial estimate to be recalibrated against actual submission transcripts once trials run, exactly as estimatedUplift already is.

(7) Controls → positive-work / no-op / always-refuse / unconditional-success / hardcoding / evidence-forging — detailed in the controls field below, now scoped to both D1 and D2.

(8) Deterministic scenario fuzzing → fuzzed across the five dimensions the family itself names, crossed with fixture behavior class, requiring the frozen grid to contain fixtures where D1 alone is activated, D2 alone is activated, and both are inert (non-activating controls).

(9) Selection against narrow mutants, held-out validation → narrow dev mutants (below) are mechanisms distinct from D1/D2 — used only to tune/validate the scenario grid, never shipped as the graded defect — driving scenario-grid selection; held-out mutants covering structurally different mechanisms validate that the selected grid generalizes rather than having been tuned to either shipped defect specifically.

(10) Frozen hashes, isolated execution, blind labelling → unchanged: pinned runtime/image versions and fixture hashes, per-trial isolated execution, blind pass/fail/coverage labelling computed from daemon-observed facts. For this family operators 6 and 10 are the graded mechanism itself, which is correct for a family whose axis is verifier-trust-boundary-integrity.
recipeCards.nonApplicableOperators: None of the ten operators are inapplicable outright, but three need reinterpretation rather than literal transplant. Operator 5 ("append-only ledger") does not fit as a literal business ledger; its family-native analogue is the container daemon's own introspection API plus its independent event stream, per mapping (5)/(6). Operator 6 is split in this revision into a per-run anti-forgery check (6) and a pre-trial predictive screen (6a) because the two answer different questions — "did this submission lie about what it exposed" versus "would a normal agent have caught this without being told" — and Phase 17's postmortem shows conflating them is exactly how a validity repair gets mistaken for a difficulty result. Operator 10 ("durable artifact capture") is not a hygiene wrapper here, because durable, correctly-scoped artifact capture is the substance of the task itself.
recipeCards.familyNativeDifficultyOperators: dual-independent-repair (the reference fix requires two structurally unrelated corrections in two different modules with no shared vocabulary — shared-resource freshness in the low-level client for D1, artifact-content provenance in the snapshot module for D2 — each individually necessary and neither sufficient alone; this is the operator that closes the single-decision-point thinness risk the v1 construction carried and that all three skeptic reviews flagged). boundary-authority-displacement (the guard's correctness depends on real daemon-level facts — resolved mount sources, filesystem provenance, timestamp ordering — that the candidate's own process cannot observe from inside itself). declared-surface-tension (the fix must narrow exposure to exactly the declared contract without breaking legitimate sidecar- or process-deliverable promotion; a brute-force lockdown is a distinguishable wrong answer, not a safe default). conjunctive-activation (each defect only manifests under a specific combination — shared resource name reused across two builds for D1, an artifact path resolving outside the container's own filesystem for D2 — never from a single obvious branch). non-local-witness (whether the repair works is verifiable only by an authority — the daemon, queried via its own independent event stream — external to and unforgeable by the candidate).
recipeCards.multiFileCodebaseSketch: "Gantry" (~1,500–1,800 lines), presented publicly as a generic build/release pipeline: `src/orchestrator/runTask.ts` (pipeline driver); `src/orchestrator/manifest.ts` (parses each task's declared-artifact contract: paths, sidecar flag, deliverable type file|process); `src/orchestrator/agentRuntime.ts` (build/run/stop/remove the agent container); `src/orchestrator/artifactSnapshot.ts` (copies declared paths out of the now-stopped agent container into an isolated staging directory and hashes the result — copies by declared path without first establishing container-native provenance, which hides D2); `src/orchestrator/sidecarVolume.ts` (creates/destroys a named volume strictly before agent start when declared); `src/orchestrator/verifierRuntime.ts` (builds/starts a fresh verifier container wired only to the staging directory, sidecar, and baked image content — this module's own mount-list construction is, correctly and visibly, built fresh from the declared contract every time; neither planted defect lives here, deliberately, so static review against the SPEC's outcome language finds nothing wrong); `src/orchestrator/containerClient.ts` (thin runtime wrapper shared by both sides; carries a resolved-bind-source cache keyed by resource name only, with no build-generation or container-id scoping — the legitimate-looking optimization that hides D1); `verifier/verify.ts` (runs inside the verifier image, checks task-specific grading criteria, emits the per-run self-check-coverage report);
