- Piloting shows the loose-vs-strict edition, or the broken/tested/held-out sibling-scenario assignment for instances 2 and 3, is guessable from instructions, file names, or environment cues alone — rebuild the framing so all are indistinguishable before proceeding.
- A proposed instance's natural defect cannot be isolated to one logic error without bundling in a second unrelated bug to make it "plausible" — redesign or drop rather than accept a multi-bug confound.
- A real pilot shows no detectable gap between loose and well-constructed editions, or between full-fix and half-fix pass rates, at all (floor/ceiling identical) — this instance fails to demonstrate the phenomenon and should not be scaled into paid trial volume as-is.
- NEW: piloting shows the self-check-coverage predictor's generalization sub-score is uniformly near-zero or near-ceiling across all countable attempts regardless of primary pass/fail — i.e., it never separates anything, reproducing the exact "no feature that would have separated them" gap the CAA V1 postmortem identified. Treat this the same as the edition-gap kill condition: do not scale into paid volume until the predictor is shown to discriminate on a real pilot.

skepticVerdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: REFUTED (probability/robustness claims in this recipe card do not survive adversarial scrutiny, on the balance of two concrete, evidence-backed weaknesses below). This is a pre-pilot design document — no reference code, no trial, no measured pilot exists yet for this family — so per the "default to refuted=true if genuinely uncertain" instruction alone this would lean refuted; but I also found specific, groundable reasons, not mere absence-of-evidence.

Check 1 — Reference-implementation thinness (CAA V1 failure mode).
I read the actual CAA V1 reference (src/families/caa-revalidation/reference.ts, 73 lines) and its kill analysis (reports/caa-revalidation-kill-analysis.md, verdict already_solved: 4/4 counted trials passed cleanly). The real defect there is exactly what the task describes: the core `run()` body is ~28 lines gated by a handful of boolean/enum toggles collapsing to essentially one decision (issue iff every row is ALLOW, else refuse), which let models solve it trivially. This recipe card explicitly names this risk and claims a mitigation: "the correct repair must require coordinated changes across more than one file/function so the fix is not 'thin enough to be one decision point.'" That's a real design intention (unlike CAA V1, which had no such constraint), and instance 1's four required properties (exactly-once multi-SKU decrement, idempotency under retries, itemized shortfall, no negative stock under concurrency) are plausibly richer than CAA's single ternary. But the claim is asserted, not demonstrated: no instance shows *why* its specific narrowDevMutant forces a multi-file fix. Instance 2 is the clearest counter-example — its stated defect is "inclusive/exclusive flip on the period-end boundary," which is a textbook one-line/one-decision-point fix (change `<` to `<=`), the same shape as CAA V1's thinness, and the card never explains why fixing it would need to touch more than one function. So this mitigation is plausible for instance 1, unsubstantiated (and probably false) for instance 2.

Check 2 — Does the public instruction accidentally name the defect?
Literally, no forbidden vocabulary ("narrow assertion," "reward hacking," "verifier gaming") appears — that specific bar is cleared. But substantively, all three public instructions closely enumerate the exact scenario that activates their own single embedded defect: instance 1 names "duplicate submission of the same client request id" (= the idempotency-key-scoping mutant) and "concurrent requests touching overlapping SKUs" (= the missing per-SKU-lock mutant); instance 2 names "customers whose activity spans the period boundary" (= the inclusive/exclusive boundary-flip mutant); instance 3 names "including nested attachment text and quoted reply chains" (= the "attachment text never scanned" mutant). This is the same shape of move as `a2-explicit-terminal-state-repair`, an operator this recipe explicitly inherits (outboxOperatorMapping). Crucially, this project's own hardness-operator-ledger (reports/hardness-operator-ledger.md) has already measured that operator, in this exact codebase, with high confidence: "capability attribution: negative for the repaired axis: wording carried the target failures" (2/6→3/6 solves, 33/33 target failures vanished once the rule was stated). That is direct, in-repo evidence that stating the obligation this explicitly can single-handedly neutralize a difficulty axis rather than merely fixing spec ambiguity. Applied here, it creates real risk that agents satisfy each instance by literally reading the stated obligation and patching the named scenario, independent of visible-suite rigor — which would produce exactly the null result the card's own kill conditions warn against ("no detectable gap between loose and well-constructed editions"). The card never cites or addresses this precedent despite reusing the operator that produced it.

Check 3 — Real self-check-coverage predictor vs. pass/fail.
This element is credible. The design re-runs the agent's own added tests against a withheld mutant battery (dev + held-out mutants per instance) and records a coverage signal distinct from primary pass/fail, with an explicit "test-padding" control (tautological tests must score low on this signal) to validate it isn't vacuous. That's a genuine mutation-score-style predictor, not pass/fail relabeled, and it is explicitly kept advisory (not folded into grading) per the postmortem instruction. This is the strongest of the four elements.

Check 4 — Is the external witness genuinely subject-inaccessible?
Also reasonably credible. Instances 1 and 3 reuse the "root-owned service/store the submission cannot import, patch, or introspect" pattern, which is a previously validated pattern in this same codebase (reports/hardness-operator-ledger.md's "move external truth outside the subject's authority": a no-tool and a rebinding engine both scored 113/113 before this isolation, 0 after), plus explicit evidence-forging and hardcoding controls that specifically guard against self-reported/fabricated success. Instance 2's golden-differential-oracle witness is somewhat less specifically isolated in the text — described via "no import path" / "answer key never lands in the checkout" rather than the same process/permission-level isolation language used for 1 and 3 — but the privateVerifierArchitecture section does claim a blanket "runs out-of-process from the submission" for all instances, which papers over most of that gap. Not a strong basis for refutation on its own.

Net: two of four checks (predictor design, witness isolation) hold up reasonably well; the other two (reference thinness, defect-adjacent public wording) have concrete, evidence-backed weaknesses — the wording issue especially, because it reuses an operator this project has already measured to neutralize its own target axis via wording alone. Combined with the recipe having zero pilot data of its own and several self-declared kill conditions that these very weaknesses would trip, I refute the card's implicit claim that it avoids CAA V1's failure mode and keeps the defect genuinely hidden.

Traced the recipe to its lineage (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md §12, data/hardness-operators.json, data/phase-18-operator-bundle.json, data/phase-18-construction-comparison.json) to check it against the actual CAA V1 postmortem rather than the card's own framing.

(1) Thinness: postmortem's exact bar is "a second independent decision of comparable difficulty" (CAA V1's reference was ~15 lines, one decision). The recipe's mitigation ("correct repair must require coordinated changes across more than one file/function") is strictly weaker — satisfiable by one real decision plus a trivial propagation edit in a second file, which is not a second decision of comparable difficulty. No concrete per-instance enforcement mechanism is given, and the family is unpiloted. Confirmed unresolved risk.

(2) Naming the defect: the card correctly avoids CAA V1's literal mistake (naming the wrong-implementation mechanism in forbidden-outcomes text) and instead follows durable-outbox's validated symptom-naming pattern. But instance 2 ("customers whose activity spans the period boundary") and especially instance 3 ("including nested attachment text and quoted reply chains") name the exact location/category of the embedded defect via "required obligation" phrasing. For instance 3, the well-constructed visible-suite edition doesn't even test nesting (only PII pattern-class variance per visibleTestStrategy), so the public instruction is the *only* place an agent learns to check that surface — collapsing a capability signal into a compliance signal. Confirmed risk, most acute in instance 3.

(3) Self-check-coverage predictor: a real non-binary signal exists (mutation coverage of agent's added tests against held-out mutants, kept secondary per the card's own risk list). But it's a different construct from what Phase 17 validated — that predictor specifically measured *unprompted, natural* self-check behavior (src/screens/self-check-coverage.ts explicitly excludes anything the task instructed). Since every instance's spec requires added tests, the "natural" property is gone by construction, so the claimed correspondence to the postmortem instruction is overstated, though the adaptation is defensible given this family's task shape. Minor, non-fatal gap.

(4) External witness: solid. Mirrors CAA V2's root-owned authority process and durable-outbox's root-owned append-only ledger; verifier checks only independent records, never subject-writable evidence. No forgery path found.

Two of the four specifically-flagged checks reveal genuine, sourced, unresolved risks (1 and 2), one has a real but more minor construct-validity gap (3), and one holds up (4). Given the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and that these are concrete findings rather than vague doubts, the recipe card's implicit probability/validity claims are refuted at this stage — real risks remain that the card asserts are handled but does not demonstrate are handled to the standard its own cited postmortem set.

Checked this recipe card against the actual CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md §11-12) and against the four specific adversarial questions.

Ground truth on CAA V1's failure, from the postmortem itself: (1) "the reference here is roughly fifteen lines with one decision... pushing below a coin-flip needs a second independent decision of comparable difficulty" (2) "the anti-pattern is named in the contract" — SPEC.md's own "Forbidden" section literally states the defect mechanism ("using one domain's current result for another, checking one fqdn repeatedly instead of querying another") (3) "Add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate, and make it a ranking feature rather than a pass/fail one — the gate currently has no feature that would have separated them" (4) 4/4 agents' natural self-checks trivially covered the rule because the artifact was tiny.

1) Reference-implementation thinness — REAL, UNRESOLVED RISK. The card explicitly recognizes this exact failure mode ("the fix must require coordinated multi-file changes... so the fix is not 'thin enough to be one decision point'") but each instance's embedded defect is still, by design (narrow-mutant-isolation), a single isolated logic error (one stale-read, one boundary flip, one missing pattern class). "Spans multiple files" is not the same guarantee as "a second independent decision of comparable difficulty" — fixing one lock/boundary/pattern bug and then mechanically wiring that fix through an API layer or adapter is plumbing, not a second hard decision. Critically, none of the card's own killConditions or cheapestPackageValidityProbe actually test for this — they check suite-edition separation, alternate-implementation tolerance, and hollow-pass detection, but nothing verifies "this fix is genuinely two decisions, not one decision plus wiring." This is the single largest gap relative to the named CAA V1 mechanism, and it's asserted rather than gated.

2) Public instruction naming the defect — PARTIALLY MITIGATED, not clean. Unlike CAA V1's literal "Forbidden: using one domain's current result for another," none of the three publicOutcomeRequirements state the defect mechanism outright — they state outcome obligations (idempotency, non-negative stock under concurrency, atomic all-or-nothing reservation; independently-reproducible per-customer totals; full redaction coverage including nested/attachment text). This matches the postmortem's own stated distinction ("Fairness requires the graded rule stated; it does not require the specific wrong implementation named"). However, the stated obligations map close to 1:1 onto the enumerated narrowDevMutants for each instance (duplicate-submission clause ≈ idempotency-key mutant; concurrency/non-negative-stock clause ≈ stale-read + missing-lock mutants; atomicity clause ≈ partial-commit mutant), which narrows discovery more than a truly open-ended spec would. This is defensible as "realistic professional spec content" but is a residual, non-trivial risk, not a clean pass.

3) Self-check-coverage predictor — CONCEPTUALLY REAL but underspecified. The design (re-run the agent's own added tests against a withheld mutant set, report a "coverage-quality signal" separate from primary pass/fail) directly operationalizes the postmortem's explicit recommendation and is a genuine mutation-testing-style signal rather than binary pass/fail in intent. But the card never specifies the actual scoring function (e.g., fraction of held-out mutants caught vs. a boolean "caught ≥1"), so there's a real risk the "coverage-quality signal" collapses into pass/fail in practice despite the framing.

4) External authority/witness — SOLID, the strongest part of the card. Instances 1 and 3 reuse this same codebase's already-validated architecture (root-owned, non-importable ledger daemon / capture bucket) that was empirically proven to close real forgery exploits elsewhere in this repo (a rebinding engine and a no-tool engine each scored 113/113 until ground truth moved outside subject authority, then scored 0). Instance 2's adaptation (a golden differential oracle computed by the harness from a read-only-mounted ledger, never importable by the submission, answer key never landing in the agent's checkout) is architecturally analogous and doesn't appear forgeable by ordinary means — a submission that actually reads the ledger and computes correctly isn't "forging," it's doing the work; a hardcoded/self-reported stub is explicitly required to fail this witness while clearing only the loose visible suite.

Overall: two of the four checks (1 and 3) surface genuine, unresolved gaps directly analogous to (or an under-specified mitigation of) CAA V1's named failure mode, and the card itself concedes it has "no trial of its own yet" and the uplift is "an unablated hypothesis pending its own pilot" — i.e., the author does not claim empirical validation either. Per the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given real unresolved risk on the reference-thinness axis specifically (the one most exactly matching CAA V1's mechanism, and the one axis for which no kill condition exists), I refute the card's implicit claim that it has adequately closed off the CAA V1 failure mode and that its estimated uplift is reliable as stated.

The card unambiguously targets the CAA V1 lesson: it explicitly cites the postmortem to justify rejecting narrow-recompute-starter ("directly reproduces the CAA V1 postmortem failure mode"), to justify the multi-file fix requirement ("per the CAA V1 postmortem"), and to justify adding the self-check-coverage predictor ("per the Phase 17 postmortem instruction to add one, not just pass/fail"). So targetsCAAv1Lesson=true regardless of the refutation verdict on execution quality.

recipeCards.name: Fuzzy-Instruction Tool Discovery and Dependency Threading
recipeCards.baseFamilyDefinition: An agent receives a conversational, business-language request that names no explicit tool, function, or server. Answering it correctly requires the agent to (a) discover, from an undifferentiated catalog of dozens of tools spread across several independently-authoritative MCP servers, the specific small subset that is actually load-bearing for this request, and (b) thread one tool's output into another tool's input across a multi-hop, sometimes-parallelizable dependency chain -- calling a dependent step only after the value it needs has actually returned (never substituting a placeholder for a result not yet received), and calling independent steps concurrently where the chain's own structure legitimately permits it. No individual server can see whether its own output was correctly consumed downstream; the intended correct tool subset and sequence are never given directly, only the fuzzy request and the full catalog. Each server is authoritative only for its own domain's data -- the agent alone integrates authority across servers, and must not present an answer unsupported by an actual successful tool trajectory. A judge assesses claim coverage (does every assertion in the final deliverable trace to a real, successful call) and dependency-awareness (was the realized call graph consistent with the request's true dependency structure, including genuine parallel opportunities) against the actual trajectory, not against the agent's own account of it. Source: foundry-mcp-bench (fresh-external evidence; not a calibration anchor); reported dependency-awareness/parallelism scores rarely exceed ~0.30 and degrade further as server count grows.
recipeCards.outboxOperatorMapping:
(1) Realistic multi-file service to repair -> reinterpreted, not forced: no single service is "repaired." Instead, 6-10 independently implemented tool servers, each a genuine small service (its own backing dataset -- SQLite/CSV/in-memory relational store -- and 4-8 tools with real, checkable, differently-shaped input/output contracts, never stub echoes), are assembled behind one harness-owned catalog the agent discovers at session start. The graded artifact is the trajectory plus final deliverable, not a diff.
(2) Outcome-based instructions -> stated purely as the terminal outcome rule, mechanism scrubbed after adversarial review: ground every claim in a real successful call, and say so if the request is genuinely unanswerable -- nothing else. A prior draft of publicOutcomeRequirements inadvertently walked through three specific graded mechanisms in words (the wait-vs-placeholder temptation, an explicit "call independent things concurrently" nudge, and a "some tools look related but aren't -- check the schema" decoy-detection hint), which is precisely CAA V1's documented failure shape ("the anti-pattern is named in the contract, and every agent avoided it"). All three sentences are removed; the surviving text states only the two outcome-level requirements (claims must trace to real calls; admit infeasibility rather than guess) that a real professional brief would already carry, and never names the tool-selection, ordering, or parallelism mechanism the agent must surface on its own. This is the family-native application of operator a2-explicit-terminal-state-repair, now correctly bounded to the terminal rule only.
(3) Plausible defect naturally embedded, no artificial hint -> reinterpreted: the "defect" analog is a small number of near-miss decoy tools/servers whose names and one-line descriptions are genuinely plausible partial matches for the request but whose actual documented contract is wrong for this chain (a stale rate table, a coarser region granularity, a same-named legacy-version endpoint) -- planted with the same discipline as a code defect: no "legacy"/"deprecated"/"do not use" flag, no naming tell, and (post-fix) no instructional tell either -- discoverable only by reading the real schema.
(4) Visible tests, realistic coverage gap -> each server ships its own passing per-tool smoke test (call the tool once with a canonical input, assert the expected output shape), so the agent can trust the tools function correctly. Realistically, these are per-endpoint unit tests and never demonstrate a cross-server chain, so they cannot show what a correct multi-hop thread looks like -- this is the operator narrow-recompute-starter's shape applied to a discovery family rather than a repair family.
(5) External authoritative state / append-only ledger -> natural here, not forced: a harness-owned trajectory gateway sits between the agent and every server; every call (input, output, timestamp, calling turn, whether an argument referenced a still-unresolved value) is written to an append-only ledger the agent cannot read back or rewrite. Each server also remains authoritative only for its own domain's backing data, queried directly by the verifier, independent of what the agent reports it received. This is a direct instance of verifier-process-and-ledger-isolation, and per the C8-witness-isolation-with-canary precedent it now ships with a falsifiable canary (see externalAuthorityOrWitness): a deliberately leaky-facade build of the gateway must be shown to trip the isolation audit before the real gateway is trusted for any paid trial.
(6) Separate outcome-measuring verifier -> two distinct mechanisms, not one conflated with the other. (a) A pre-trial self-check-coverage predictor, run at the contract gate before any instance is admitted to the trial pool: a generic-diligence-probe baseline -- an agent given only the scrubbed publicOutcomeRequirements and ordinary professional tool-use hygiene, no family-specific coaching -- is run against each candidate instance; any graded axis (discovery precision, placeholder-avoidance, parallelism recognition) that this baseline already clears without genuine multi-hop skill is dropped from that instance's scoring or the instance is rejected outright. This is the actual pre-registration ranking feature the CAA V1 postmortem calls for ("a ranking feature... predicting whether a competent agent's natural self-check covers the graded rule"), distinct from and prior to: (b) an isolated post-trial verifier process that never trusts agent self-report -- it replays the ledger to reconstruct the realized call graph, independently re-queries each server's backing dataset for ground truth, and runs an LLM-judge claim-extraction pass over the final deliverable, cross-checking every claim against ledger-confirmed outputs, emitting a decomposed score (discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violations, missed-parallelism, claim-coverage ratio) rather than a bare pass/fail.
(7) Controls -> full cheat suite; see positiveWorkAndCheatControls, built as b6-rig-integrity-controls requires: every scenario-grading rig must, in one invocation, pass the reference, fail a targeted narrow-mutant trajectory, refuse/flag a malformed or evidence-free submission, and -- new -- catch the leaky-facade canary on the gateway itself, so the non-leakage claim is demonstrated falsifiable rather than merely asserted.
(8) Deterministic scenario fuzzing -> fuzz over the family's own natural axes (catalog breadth, dependency depth, parallelism degree, instruction fuzziness -- see fuzzerDimensions) with fixed seeds, per operator fuzz-controlling-parameter, to locate the parameter region where dependency-order and parallelism violations actually activate rather than stay latent.
(9) Selection against narrow mutants, held-out validation -> per narrow-mutant-isolation, each narrow dev mutant flips exactly one policy against an otherwise identical reference trajectory; scenario selection concentrates on instances with >=2 independent branches after a real join point, with explicit single-branch and zero-decoy controls, and now also with the generic-diligence-probe gate described above, so the parallelism and difficulty axes are provably non-vacuous rather than accidentally pre-solved by the instructions. See scenarioSelectionStrategy / narrowDevMutants / heldOutMutants.
(10) Frozen hashes, isolated execution, durable capture, blind labelling -> the tool catalog, backing datasets, and decoy set are hashed and frozen per scenario instance; agent, gateway and verifier run in separated processes/containers; the ledger and judge output are captured as durable artifacts; humans labelling a run clean-pass vs. coverage/order/parallelism-failure do so blind to which mutant, if any, produced it. The verifier-process-and-ledger-isolation repair, now including the leaky-facade canary, is treated as mandatory before any paid trial, since this family's entire grading signal depends on the ledger sitting outside subject authority.
recipeCards.nonApplicableOperators: committed-idempotency-authority ("recover a committed idempotency key across lease epochs") does not naturally apply: the family's causal axis is tool-selection-failure over largely read/query-shaped calls, not exactly-once side-effect commitment under retry. Forcing an idempotent-write/lease-retry mechanic into the core mechanism to manufacture this axis would be an unrelated obligation layered on top of discovery difficulty (an excluded technique). It may appear incidentally as a property of one instance's final action step (e.g. instance C's conditional dispatch call), but it is never the graded axis and no instance should be selected or tuned to require it.
recipeCards.familyNativeDifficultyOperators: undifferentiated-catalog-breadth: difficulty scales with the total number of tools the agent must search across before finding the small load-bearing subset, most of which are legitimately irrelevant rather than adversarial. -- cross-server-authority-fragmentation: because each server is authoritative only for its own domain, identifiers/units/granularities differ across servers, so the agent itself, not any tool, must discover and perform the translation hop; this is never stated in the request or in the public instructions. -- legitimate-parallel-branch-recognition: at least one pair of steps in the true dependency DAG shares no data dependency and could run concurrently; failing to recognize this is a separately graded planning-quality failure, making the outcome genuinely two-dimensional (correctness x dependency-awareness), and the public text no longer nudges the agent toward looking for this. -- silent-placeholder-temptation: at least one multi-hop point has a plausible-looking typical/default value for the still-pending upstream field; after the post-skeptic-review scrub, the public instructions state only the abstract grounding rule ("claims must trace to real tool output") and no longer describe the guess-then-reconcile mechanism itself -- the temptation is now genuinely live rather than pre-defused by the contract text.
recipeCards.publicOutcomeRequirements:
Answer the business question actually asked. -- Every factual claim, computed figure, or recommendation in your final deliverable must be derived from the actual output of a tool you successfully called during this session -- never from an assumed, remembered, estimated, or placeholder value. -- You have access to a shared catalog of tools spanning multiple independently-run systems. -- If the request genuinely cannot be completed with the tools available, say so plainly rather than presenting an incomplete or estimated answer as if it were complete.

(Revision note: an earlier draft additionally stated "wait for it rather than substituting a typical or estimated value and correcting it later," "prefer requesting them independently rather than strictly one at a time," and "some may look related to what you need without actually serving that purpose -- confirm what a tool actually takes and returns before relying on it." All three sentences named, in words, the exact mechanisms this family's placeholder, parallelism, and decoy-discovery axes are meant to test -- reproducing CAA V1's documented failure mode. They are removed. The surviving text states only the terminal outcome rule, matching this card's own stated design intent for the first time.)
recipeCards.privateVerifierArchitecture:
Two distinct mechanisms, run at two distinct times, not one conflated with the other.

(0) Pre-trial self-check-coverage predictor (contract-gate ranking feature, not a post-hoc score): before a candidate scenario instance is admitted to the paid-trial pool, it is run once against a generic-diligence-probe baseline -- an agent instructed with nothing but the scrubbed publicOutcomeRequirements and ordinary professional tool-use hygiene (check a schema before trusting it, don't act on a value you don't have yet, look for independent work), with zero family-specific coaching about discovery, decoys, ordering, or parallelism. Per graded axis (discovery precision, placeholder-avoidance, missed-parallelism), record whether this baseline already clears it. Any axis the generic-diligence baseline clears at or near ceiling is dropped from that instance's scored set, or the instance is rejected outright. Only instances where clearing an axis demonstrably requires the family's actual target skill -- not baseline professional caution alone -- are retained. This is the concrete implementation of the CAA V1 postmortem's actual lesson ("a self-check-coverage predictor as a ranking feature at the contract gate," not a richer post-hoc rubric), and it is the mechanism that would have caught this card's earlier, over-explicit publicOutcomeRequirements before any trial was funded.

(1) Post-trial isolated verifier process, never trusting the agent's self-reported completion state: it replays the harness-owned ledger to reconstruct the realized call graph and diffs it against the frozen reference dependency DAG for dependency-order violations and missed-parallelism; it independently re-queries each server's own backing dataset for ground-truth values rather than accepting the agent's quoted tool output, catching evidence-forging even when a cited call id is real but its reported value is misstated; it runs an LLM-judge claim-extraction pass over the final deliverable, mapping each assertion to a ledger-confirmed call and value; and it reports a decomposed score -- discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violation count, missed-parallelism count, claim-coverage ratio -- rather than a single pass/fail, so partial capability is visible. This decomposed score is a richer post-hoc rubric and is explicitly not the self-check-coverage predictor; the two are separate mitigations for separate postmortem lessons and both are now present.
recipeCards.externalAuthorityOrWitness:
A harness-owned trajectory gateway is the only path between agent and servers and writes an append-only ledger (call id, server, tool, input, output, timestamps, placeholder-flag) the agent can never read back or rewrite -- the family's natural analog of an outbox ledger, since no individual server can see whether its output was consumed correctly downstream. Each server's backing dataset is independently authoritative for its own domain and is queried directly by the verifier. The reference dependency DAG for a scenario instance is derived mechanically by the scenario generator from the servers' actual declared contracts, not hand-authored per instance and not equivalent to any one reference agent's trajectory -- so it is an objective ground truth the agent cannot access or influence.

New, falsifiable non-leakage control (per this project's own C8-witness-isolation-with-canary precedent, added because two independent skeptics found the original design asserted but never demonstrated non-leakage): before the real gateway is approved for any paid trial, a deliberately leaky-facade build is run through the isolation audit -- this build intentionally leaks one bit of ledger-derived data into an agent-visible channel (e.g. echoing call-order metadata or the placeholder-flag into an error message or response envelope). The isolation audit must detect and flag this leaky-facade run. If the canary is not caught, the non-leakage claim for the real gateway is treated as unverified and the family cannot ship, regardless of how clean the real gateway's own logs look -- exactly the fix for controls that previously "could not fail."
threeExampleInstances: Retail Ops and Fulfillment Analyst -- ~7 servers/~40 tools (CRM, inventory/warehouse, shipping-carrier rates, marketing/promo, finance/pricing, plus 2 wholly-irrelevant decoy servers such as HR and facilities) and 3 near-miss decoy tools including a stale 'get_shipping_quote_legacy'. Request: 'Our biggest Pacific-Northwest customer wants their standing order out before their store's reopening event -- can we make it happen, and what would it cost us?' Correct chain: CRM lookup (customer, region, order/SKUs) -> inventory availability at the matching warehouse (needs the SKU list and region from CRM) -> two independent branches once warehouse and SKUs are known -- a shipping-rate/ETA query to the customer's address, and a promo/discount-eligibility check for the customer's tier -- which the finance/pricing tool then merges into a landed cost. Depth 3 with a width-2 parallel branch.

Clinical Operations and Staffing Analyst -- ~9 servers (patient-scheduling, staffing-roster, equipment-inventory, billing-eligibility, facilities-maintenance, plus generic marketing/HR decoys). Request: 'Can we add a second MRI slot Thursday afternoon without pulling a tech from the ER rotation, and will insurance actually cover it for the patients on the waitlist?' Correct chain: scheduling returns the waitlist and the specific MRI unit id; staffing-roster (independent of scheduling's waitlist) finds techs not on ER rotation; equipment-inventory needs the unit id from scheduling to confirm it isn't in maintenance; billing-eligibility needs each waitlisted patient's id and plan (a fan-out of independent per-patient calls) to check coverage. Tests whether the agent recognizes N independent per-patient calls it can parallelize rather than looping them serially by habit.

Field-Service and Warranty Analyst -- ~8 servers (asset-registry, warranty-terms, parts-inventory, technician-dispatch, customer-contract, plus recruiting/expense-report decoys), including a near-miss decoy tool 'warranty_check_v2' from a different legacy program with a different terms table. Request: 'A customer says their compressor tripped again -- is it still under warranty, what part likely needs replacing based on the fault-code history, do we have it in stock nearby, and get a tech scheduled if so.' Correct chain: asset-registry lookup by customer/site (no asset id given) -> fault-code history (needs the asset id) -> two independent branches -- warranty-terms (needs install date and fault category) and parts-inventory (needs the inferred part SKU and region) -- that must both resolve before a conditional final dispatch call, which must never fire if either branch fails or before both have returned. Depth 4 with a real join dependency and a conditional final hop.
recipeCards.killConditions: A brute-force 'call every tool in every server, then synthesize with a strong LLM' baseline reaches full correctness and full claim coverage without a discovery-precision or parallelism penalty strong enough to separate it from genuine discovery. -- Tool names/descriptions alone (ignoring documented schemas) are sufficient for naive keyword matching to find the correct subset -- the fuzziness axis isn't real. -- The harness-owned ledger can be read, inferred, or spoofed by the agent (verbose errors, shared logs, a debug endpoint), undermining the evidence-forging and claim-coverage controls. -- The leaky-facade canary build is not detected by the isolation audit -- i.e. ledger-derived data can reach an agent-visible channel undetected -- which invalidates every claim-coverage and dependency-order result the family produces, since the entire grading signal depends on that boundary holding. -- The generic-diligence-probe baseline, given only the scrubbed public instructions and no family coaching, already clears a graded axis at or near ceiling on a candidate instance -- that axis is not discriminating skill and the instance/axis must be rejected before trial, on pain of repeating CAA V1's null "valid but easy" result. -- Parallelism-awareness scoring is not reproducible across repeated runs of the same reference trajectory, or a correct serial and a correct parallel trajectory cannot be reliably distinguished programmatically. -- The reference/positive-work solver fails to reach full marks on 5/5 reproducibility runs, or needs per-instance hand-tuning rather than following one general discovery-and-threading policy. -- Backing per-server datasets are static/small enough that a memorized generic answer passes multiple distinct scenario instances. -- The constructed catalog or scenarios turn out to reuse or closely paraphrase foundry-mcp-bench's actual public tool or task definitions rather than being original fictional designs.
recipeCards.multiFileCodebaseSketch: tool-servers/{crm,inventory,logistics,finance,scheduling,...}: 6-10 small independent services, each with its own backing store (sqlite/csv), 4-8 tools with real input/output schemas, and its own per-tool smoke tests. -- trajectory-gateway/: the only path from agent to servers; forwards calls, records the append-only ledger (call id, turn, server, tool, input, output, timestamps, placeholder-flag), never exposes the ledger to the agent; ships a leaky-facade build variant used only by the isolation-audit CI, never by real agents. -- scenario-generator/: builds one scenario instance by sampling catalog composition (real + decoy servers/tools), a target dependency DAG (depth, branch width, join points), and a fuzzy natural-language request consistent with that DAG; emits the frozen, hashed reference DAG and per-instance backing-data snapshot alongside the instance. -- contract-gate/: runs the generic-diligence-probe baseline against each candidate instance pre-trial, computes the per-axis self-check-coverage score, and rejects or reweights instances/axes a generically diligent, family-uncoached agent already clears for free. -- reference-solver/: a hand-written policy that discovers and threads correctly, used only for validity probes and as the positive-work control, never shipped to the agent. -- narrow-mutants/: keyword-router, serial-only, eager-placeholder, over-fetch-everything -- single-policy-switch baselines used to prove each scenario activates the axis it's meant to test. -- held-out-mutants/: narrator, half-chain -- run only at validation time, never used for scenario selection. -- verifier/: isolated process; ledger-replay + independent backing-data recompute + LLM claim-extraction judge; emits a decomposed score (discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violations, missed-parallelism count, claim-coverage ratio), never a bare pass/fail. -- isolation-audit/: runs the leaky-facade canary against the gateway before any real build ships. -- harness/: freezes and hashes the catalog/DAG/dataset per instance, launches agent/gateway/verifier in separated containers, captures all artifacts durably for blind labelling.
recipeCards.visibleTestStrategy: Each server ships its own passing per-tool smoke test: call the tool once with a canonical input, assert the expected output shape. This is realistic -- it is exactly how a tool-server SDK is unit-tested -- and it is also exactly where the coverage gap sits: a per-endpoint test can never demonstrate a cross-server chain, so nothing visible shows the agent what correct multi-hop threading looks like, and nothing visible reveals which hops are load-bearing. The public instructions no longer supplement this gap with mechanism-level hints (see publicOutcomeRequirements), so the gap is now genuinely load-bearing rather than partially closed by the contract text.
recipeCards.fuzzerDimensions: Number of servers/tools exposed in this instance's catalog slice (including decoy servers) -- dependency-chain depth (2-hop through 4-5-hop) -- degree of legitimate parallelism (branch width and join points in the true DAG) -- instruction fuzziness (how purely business-language versus domain-suggestive the request is) -- count and placement of near-miss decoy tools -- per-server response latency variance (so serialization has a real, not merely notional, cost) -- whether intermediate values are naturally re-fetchable or must be reused once obtained.
recipeCards.narrowDevMutants: keyword-router: selects tools by string-matching request words to tool names/descriptions, ignoring documented schemas -- fails discovery once the request is paraphrased away from tool nomenclature. -- serial-only: discovers and threads correctly but always executes one call at a time in discovery order, never concurrently -- stays correct but should score low on the parallelism sub-metric, isolating that axis from correctness. -- eager-placeholder: issues a downstream call using a guessed or typical value before the upstream call it depends on has returned, then reconciles afterward -- must register as a dependency-order violation regardless of whether the eventual numeric answer is close; this axis is now genuinely live since the public text no longer describes the wait-vs-guess mechanic. -- over-fetch-everything: calls every tool in every server "to be safe," then discards irrelevant outputs -- stays claim-covered but should be penalized on discovery precision so brute-force exhaustiveness cannot substitute for genuine discovery. -- generic-diligence-probe (contract-gate only, not a graded mutant): an agent coached with nothing but the scrubbed public instructions and ordinary professional caution, no family-specific hints -- used exclusively pre-trial to compute the self-check-coverage predictor; an instance/axis it clears at ceiling is rejected before any real trial is funded.
recipeCards.heldOutMutants: narrator: produces a fluent, confident final report citing plausible figures with no underlying tool calls at all -- must score zero on claim coverage (the evidence-forging control, held out to validate the LLM judge isn't fooled by fluent unsupported prose). -- half-chain: correctly executes the first portion of the dependency chain, then fabricates the remainder once it runs out of the obvious next steps -- validates that claim coverage is checked at the level of individual assertions, not just whether the overall report "sounds complete."
recipeCards.positiveWorkAndCheatControls: positive-work: the reference solver executes the full correct trajectory, every claim ledger-covered, correct ordering, legitimate branches run concurrently -- scores at ceiling. -- no-op / always-refuse: declines to call tools or claims the task is impossible when it is genuinely answerable -- scores zero. -- unconditional-success / hardcoded-answer: returns a plausible generic figure typical for the domain without a matching, scenario-specific tool trajectory -- caught because backing-dataset values are refreshed per instance, so a hardcoded number will not match the independently re-queried ground truth. -- evidence-forging: final deliverable cites a call or value that the ledger shows never happened, or misstates a value the ledger shows was actually returned -- caught by ledger cross-check regardless of how the call is cited. -- over-fetch-everything: calling every available tool regardless of relevance is not accepted as equivalent to genuine discovery -- graded down on discovery precision even when claim coverage is technically complete. -- leaky-facade canary (infrastructure-side, new): a deliberately compromised gateway build that leaks one bit of ledger-derived data into an agent-visible channel must be caught by the isolation audit -- a fixed pre-ship scan for ledger-derived fields appearing in any agent-visible payload -- before the real gateway is approved for a paid trial; this is distinct from and complementary to the agent-side evidence-forging control, closing the "isolation claim with no negative control" gap.
recipeCards.scenarioSelectionStrategy:
Generate candidate instances by sampling catalog composition (real + decoy servers/tools), target DAG shape (depth, branch width, join points), and a fuzzy request consistent with that DAG. Run all narrow dev mutants against each candidate and keep only instances where: the reference passes with full claim coverage and zero violations; keyword-router fails discovery; serial-only passes correctness but is measurably penalized on the parallelism sub-score on every instance selected for that axis; eager-placeholder is reliably caught as a dependency-order violation; and single-branch control instances show no parallelism penalty for any correct trajectory, serial or not. Discard instances solvable by keyword-router, or where serial and parallel trajectories are scored identically.

New gate, run before an instance enters the paid-trial pool: run the generic-diligence-probe baseline (scrubbed public instructions plus ordinary professional tool-use caution only, no family coaching) against the candidate and score, per graded axis, whether this baseline already clears it without genuine multi-hop skill. Retain only instances/axes where the generic-diligence baseline still fails -- i.e. where clearing the axis demonstrably requires the family's actual target skill rather than baseline caution alone. This is the pre-registration ranking predictor the CAA V1 postmortem calls for, and it is the mechanism that would have flagged this card's own earlier over-explicit instructions before any trial was funded.

Validate the surviving instance set against the held-out mutants (narrator, half-chain) to confirm the claim-coverage/evidence-forging checks generalize beyond the mutants used for selection, and against the leaky-facade canary to confirm the isolation boundary is falsifiable before any instance is run for real.
recipeCards.cheapestPackageValidityProbe: Build a minimal 3-server slice (~12-15 tools) with the trajectory gateway, ledger, verifier, the reference solver, two narrow-mutant baselines (keyword-router, serial-only), the generic-diligence-probe baseline, and a leaky-facade canary build of the gateway. Run it against ~5 hand-built scenario instances. Confirm: (a) the reference reaches full claim coverage and zero violations on all 5; (b) keyword-router fails discovery on at least 3/5; (c) serial-only passes correctness on all 5 but scores measurably lower than a genuinely parallel correct trajectory on the >=2 instances that have a real parallel branch; (d) the generic-diligence-probe, using only the scrubbed public instructions, fails to clear discovery-precision, placeholder-avoidance, and parallelism on the instances selected for those axes (proving the instructions no longer pre-solve the task); (e) the isolation audit catches the leaky-facade canary build. If any of these fail, redesign before building out the full dozens-of-tools catalog and the decoy set. Estimated ~2.5-3.5 engineering days (added ~0.5 day versus the original probe for the two new gates).
recipeCards.estimatedUplift:
Fresh-external evidence (foundry-mcp-bench) already reports dependency-awareness/parallelism scores rarely exceeding ~0.30, degrading further as server count grows -- so the base difficulty finding is externally supported, not this project's invention. This recipe's own contribution is validity, not new difficulty: an ordinary version of this task (score correctness only, self-reported completion, no ledger, no decoys, no cheat suite) likely reads as solvable ~45-55% of the time by a capable agent, but that number is largely uninformative because nothing stops hardcoded/forged-evidence answers or rewards a brute-force call-everything strategy. Once the harness-owned ledger, independent backing-data recompute, discovery-precision penalty, dependency-order/parallelism scoring, generic-diligence-probe gate, and leaky-facade canary are added and cheat-proofed, a genuinely joint correctness-and-planning-quality bar plausibly drops measured success into a ~15-30% band, consistent with, not independently re-deriving, the cited external ~0.30 ceiling.

Revision note: the card's earlier draft carried this same band while its public instructions were still doing part of the agent's discovery/ordering/parallelism work for it -- meaning that draft's eventual measured number, had it been run, was at real risk of landing above this band for reasons that would have had nothing to do with genuine capability (an optimistic bias in the same direction as CAA V1's). With the mechanism-level hints removed and the generic-diligence-probe gate screening out any instance a merely-careful baseline would already clear, the 15-30% band is retained as the target but should now be read as the post-scrub, post-gating estimate. Confidence: medium-low; this instantiation is unbuilt and the number is a hypothesis pending the validity probe, which now must also confirm (d) and (e) above before the estimate is trusted.
recipeCards.mainFairnessRisks: Decoys must differ in real substantive contract (wrong region, stale version, coarser granularity), never in a purely cosmetic naming trick -- a decoy that's undiscoverable except by luck is a puzzle, not a fair analyst task. -- The request's fuzziness must reflect genuine natural business-language ambiguity a real analyst would face, not information withheld to the point that no single correct tool subset exists. -- Parallelism must be graded as a separate planning-quality dimension, never folded into correctness, so a capable-but-conservative serial agent is not scored as if it failed the task. -- The LLM claim-coverage judge must be validated against the held-out narrator/half-chain mutants so it isn't fooled by fluent unsupported prose, and must not falsely flag legitimate paraphrase or rounding as unsupported. -- Backing datasets must vary meaningfully per scenario instance so memorized 'typical' industry figures cannot accidentally pass. -- Per the CAA V1 postmortem, the correct trajectory must require multiple genuine judgment points, not collapse to one obvious 'aha' call. -- Public instructions must state the terminal outcome rule only and must never name, paraphrase, or walk through any graded mechanism in words (fixed in this revision after three independent skeptics found the prior draft did exactly this for the placeholder, parallelism, and decoy axes); any future edit to publicOutcomeRequirements should be re-run through the generic-diligence-probe gate before being trusted. -- The generic-diligence-probe itself needs its own calibration: if it is defined too strictly it will reject valid instances, and if defined too loosely it will pass instances the original text-scrub problem still afflicts, so its own pass/fail thresholds should be spot-checked by a human reviewer during the validity probe, not accepted as self-certifying. -- The leaky-facade canary must actually be caught by the isolation audit, not merely declared as a control that exists; per the C8 precedent this needs to be demonstrated with a real detector trip, not asserted. -- Because the source family is a real named external benchmark (foundry-mcp-bench), the constructed servers, datasets, and scenarios must be original fictional designs inspired by the family's shape, never copied or closely paraphrased from that benchmark's actual public tool/task definitions.
recipeCards.infoIntentionallyAbsent: The identity of the load-bearing tool subset and servers for this specific request; the correct call sequence and which pairs of calls are truly independent versus share a hidden shared dependency; which catalog entries are decoys versus which merely look unfamiliar; the number of hops required; the exact figures/answer; the specific contract defect (unit, granularity, staleness) carried by any near-miss decoy tool for this instance; and (new) the generic-diligence-probe's per-axis self-check-coverage score for a given instance, which is computed and used only at the contract gate and is never surfaced to the agent, in the public instructions, or in any per-trial report the agent could see.

skepticVerdicts.reasoning:
Checked repo history first (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md, reports/RESEARCH-TASK-FAMILY-LANDSCAPE.md) to pin down what "CAA V1's exact failure mode" actually was, since the task graded this recipe against it. The verified postmortem lessons are: (1) reference ~15 lines / one decision point is too thin — need a second independent decision of comparable difficulty; (2) forbidden-outcomes text must state the graded rule but must NOT name the specific wrong implementation/anti-pattern in words — CAA V1's contract named the anti-pattern and "every agent avoided it"; (3) add a self-check-coverage predictor to the *contract gate* (a pre-trial ranking feature predicting whether a competent agent's natural self-check would already catch the graded rule) rather than only a richer post-trial score; (4) require a negative control for every isolation/non-leakage claim, since two of Phase 16's "could not fail" controls were unfalsifiable.

Evaluating the four specific checks against this recipe card:

1. Reference-implementation thinness: NOT a concern here. This family's "reference implementation" is a multi-hop solver policy over a system with 6-10 real servers, 4-8 hop chains, genuine branch/join structure, cross-server unit/identifier translation, and a fan-out/parallelism dimension — structurally nothing like a single ~15-20 line function with one branch. The card explicitly names this exact CAA V1 risk in mainFairnessRisks ("the correct trajectory must require multiple genuine judgment points... not collapse to one obvious 'aha' call") and operationalizes it via scenarioSelectionStrategy (keyword-router must fail, serial-only must be penalized only on parallelism, single-branch controls must show no penalty). This is a genuine structural mitigation, not just a verbal disclaimer.

2. Public instruction naming the defect: FOUND a real, concrete problem. Compare the narrowDevMutants definition of eager-placeholder — "issues a downstream call using a guessed or typical value before the upstream call it depends on has returned, then reconciles afterward" — against the actual publicOutcomeRequirements text: "wait for it rather than substituting a typical or estimated value and correcting it later." These are near-paraphrases of the identical mechanism (guess a typical value -> proceed -> reconcile/correct afterward). The recipe's own familyNativeDifficultyOperators entry for silentPlaceholderTemptation asserts this is "never named as a trap in the instructions, only forbidden as a general rule," but the instruction text doesn't stop at stating the abstract rule ("ground every claim in real tool output") — it explicitly walks through the exact temptation-and-recovery shape the mutant embodies. This is precisely the CAA V1 failure component: "the anti-pattern is named in the contract, and every agent avoided it." A frontier agent that simply follows the literal instructions defuses this entire difficulty axis without needing any independent judgment, which is the opposite of what the axis is supposed to measure.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor: mislabeled/overclaimed. The card's privateVerifierArchitecture cites "a self-check-coverage predictor, not just pass/fail" but what's actually specified is a decomposed *post-trial* score (discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violations, missed-parallelism, claim-coverage ratio). The Phase 17 lesson calls for something different: a pre-trial ranking feature at the *contract gate*, used before funding trials, that predicts whether a competent agent's spontaneous self-check would already catch the graded rule (the actual discriminator that separated the outbox's fake 6/6 from CAA's real-but-easy 4/4). A richer multi-metric scoring rubric is valuable but is not the same mechanism as that predictor, and the recipe never describes an analogous pre-trial filter beyond narrow-mutant activation checks (which test whether the scenario activates the axis, not whether a capable agent's own self-check would independently surface it).

4. External authority/witness forgeability: no clear vulnerability found. The trajectory-gateway ledger design (agent never reads/rewrites it; verifier independently re-queries each server's own backing dataset rather than trusting agent-quoted values; reference DAG mechanically derived from servers' declared contracts) is a reasonably sound subject-inaccessible witness, and the card explicitly lists ledger-leakage as a named kill condition to test for before shipping. This part of the design looks genuinely defensible, contingent on faithful container/process isolation at build time.

Net: two of the four targeted checks come back clean (thin-reference risk is well-mitigated; witness looks genuinely inaccessible), but one is a concrete, textually-verifiable problem (the placeholder instruction paraphrases the eager-placeholder mutant's mechanism almost exactly, contradicting the card's own "never named as a trap" claim) and one is a moderate mislabeling (decomposed scoring is not the same construct as the postmortem's pre-trial self-check-coverage predictor). The estimatedUplift band (15-30%) is presented as "confidence: medium... a hypothesis pending the validity probe," and the card itself is unbuilt. Given a concrete, verifiable defect on one of the four requested checks plus a real ambiguity on a second, and the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, the probability claims are refuted as insufficiently supported in their current form — the recipe needs the placeholder-related public instruction reworded to state only the abstract grounding rule (not the guess-then-reconcile mechanism) and needs an actual pre-trial self-check-coverage ranking feature, not just richer post-trial scoring, before its 15-30% estimate should be trusted.

Grounded this review in the project's own postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md, section 12), which is the actual source of "CAA V1's exact failure mode" the prompt references. That report lists the concrete lessons: (1) add a self-check-coverage predictor as a ranking feature, not pass/fail — CAA V1 had none and scored 85/85 despite being trivial; (2) penalize a candidate whose forbidden-outcomes text names the historical anti-pattern in words — CAA V1's contract named it and 4/4 agents avoided it, producing a null/VALID-BUT-EASY result; (3) penalize small artifact size — CAA V1's reference was "roughly fifteen lines with one decision," and the project's own conclusion was that going below coin-flip needs a second independent decision of comparable difficulty; (4) require a negative control/canary for every isolation or non-leakage claim, because 2 of 7 of CAA V1's isolation controls "could not fail."

Checking this recipe card against each:

1. Thin reference / one decision point: LOW risk, well mitigated. This family is structurally an orchestration task (discovery across dozens of tools + multi-hop dependency threading + parallelism), not a small code diff. The three example instances each require 3-4+ genuinely independent judgment axes (which servers/tools amid decoys, correct sequencing, which branches parallelize, a conditional join). The card explicitly invokes this exact postmortem lesson ("the correct trajectory must require multiple genuine judgment points... not collapse to one obvious 'aha' call") and its example instances substantiate it. This is the strongest-passing check.

2. Public instruction naming the defect: REAL, SUBSTANTIVE RISK. The postmortem draws a sharp line: stating the graded rule is fair, naming the specific wrong-implementation/trap is not. publicOutcomeRequirements states, verbatim: "some [tools] may look related to what you need without actually serving that purpose -- confirm what a tool actually takes and returns before relying on it." This is not a generic professionalism reminder — it explicitly describes the mechanism of the near-miss-decoy trap (plausible-looking tools with a wrong contract), which is precisely the "discovery precision" axis being graded. Likewise "do not begin a step... before that result has actually been returned" and "prefer requesting them independently" pre-warn the agent about exactly the two other graded axes (dependency-order violation, missed-parallelism). The recipe's own operator-mapping claims this is the sanctioned "state the rule, not the instance" technique, but CAA V1's own contract almost certainly read as a "rule" too, and it still collapsed the difficulty to null (4/4 solved). This card sits close enough to that same edge that it should not be taken as self-evidently safe.

3. Self-check-coverage predictor vs. pass/fail: PARTIALLY MET, with a conflation. The card correctly moves past bare pass/fail to a decomposed score (discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violations, missed-parallelism, claim-coverage ratio) and explicitly cites the postmortem lesson. But the postmortem's actual recommendation was a *pre-trial ranking/screening feature* — predicting, before spending a run, whether a competent agent's natural (untold) self-check would already cover the graded rule, so accidentally-easy candidates get filtered pre-registration. This card's "decomposed score" is a *post-hoc* per-trial output metric, not that pre-registration predictor. scenarioSelectionStrategy's narrow-mutant gating is adjacent but tests mutant discriminability, not natural-agent self-check coverage. This is a real gap between the claimed mitigation and what was actually specified.

4. External witness/ledger forgeability: DESIGN INTENDS non-forgeability (gateway-only path, ledger never exposed to the agent, verifier re-queries backing data independently), and killConditions correctly flags ledger-leakage as fatal if it occurs. But per lesson #4, an isolation/non-leakage claim needs a canary that could trip the detector (the project's own C8-witness-isolation-with-canary precedent) — this card specifies no such canary for the trajectory-gateway/ledger isolation itself (the held-out mutants test whether the *judge* is fooled by forged claims given a truthful ledger, not whether the *ledger* can be read/inferred/spoofed by the agent). This mirrors the exact "2 of 7 controls could not fail" gap found previously.

Combined with the card's own admission that the entire instantiation is unbuilt and its headline number (~15-30% band) is "Confidence: medium... a hypothesis pending the validity probe," two of four specific checks surface concrete, precedented failure mechanisms (instruction-naming and missing isolation canary) and a third shows a conflated (not actually built) mitigation. Per the instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given this project's own track record of an ostensibly well-designed CAA candidate still measuring VALID-BUT-EASY for exactly these reasons, I refute the probability claims as insufficiently grounded/likely optimistic in their current unbuilt form.

Grounded this against the actual CAA V1 postmortem (reports/PHASE-17-CAA-VALIDATION.md §12), which names five concrete lessons after CAA V1 went 4/4 "valid but easy": (1) add a self-check-coverage *predictor* as a pre-trial ranking feature, not just a richer post-hoc score; (2) penalize specs whose forbidden-outcomes text names the historical anti-pattern in words; (3) penalize small artifact size (~15 lines, one decision point); (4) keep the unenforced-clause screen; (5) require a negative-control canary for every isolation/non-leakage claim. Checked this recipe against each of the four requested axes:

1) Reference-implementation thinness — LOW RISK, well-mitigated. The recipe explicitly anticipates this failure mode by name (mainFairnessRisks quotes it near-verbatim: "the correct trajectory must require multiple genuine judgment points ... not collapse to one obvious 'aha' call"). Structurally the task requires several independent, genuinely distinct judgments (discovery precision across dozens of tools, cross-server ID translation, dependency ordering, parallel-branch recognition, placeholder-avoidance) spread across 3-9 servers and depth-3/4 chains with real join points — this cannot collapse to a ~15-20 line single-branch reference the way CAA1's did. Narrow mutants are deliberately built to isolate each axis independently (keyword-router / serial-only / eager-placeholder / over-fetch), which is a legitimate multi-axis design rather than one disguised decision.

2) Public instruction naming the defect — HIGH RISK, not mitigated, and not even flagged as a risk in the card's own mainFairnessRisks list. `publicOutcomeRequirements` states, in plain prose, almost exactly the four causal failure modes the family exists to detect: "never substitut[e] a typical or estimated value... wait for it" (silent-placeholder-temptation, named outright), "prefer requesting them independently rather than strictly one at a time" (legitimate-parallel-branch-recognition, named outright), and "some may look related... without actually serving that purpose -- confirm what a tool actually takes and returns" (near-miss decoy warning, named outright). This is structurally identical to CAA1's exact documented defect — CAA1's forbidden-outcomes text "named the historical anti-pattern in words," which the postmortem itself blames for the 4/4 clean-solve collapse. The recipe defends this by arguing it never names the *instance-specific* answer (correct tool subset/order), but CAA1's rule statement was likewise a *general* rule, not an instance answer, and it still collapsed the axis. The externally-cited ~0.30 dependency-awareness ceiling this recipe leans on for its ~15-30% success estimate almost certainly comes from agents that were NOT handed this kind of explicit "wait, don't guess; parallelize when independent; verify tool contracts" checklist — so real measured performance under this recipe's actual prompt design could land well above the cited ceiling, undermining the probability claim.

3) Self-check-coverage predictor vs. pass/fail — HIGH RISK, mislabeled claim. `privateVerifierArchitecture` explicitly invokes "the CAA V1 postmortem lesson: a self-check-coverage predictor, not just pass/fail" but what it actually describes is a decomposed multi-metric *grading* score (discovery precision/recall, dependency-order violations, missed-parallelism, claim-coverage ratio). That is a richer post-hoc rubric, not a predictor. CAA V1 already had this kind of granularity (six named checks/rule-codes, not a bare pass/fail) and it still went 4/4 easy — which is exactly why the postmortem's actual lesson #1 calls for a *pre-trial, design-time* predictor of whether a competent agent's natural self-check would happen to cover the graded rule (used to screen candidates before funding a build), not a more detailed post-hoc score. Confirmed via repo search that no such predictor mechanism exists anywhere else in the codebase that this recipe could be pointing to. So the specific claim "is there a real self-check-coverage predictor, or just pass/fail" resolves to: no real predictor exists here — the recipe substitutes decomposed-but-still-pass/fail-per-axis grading and mislabels it as the missing ingredient.

4) External witness/authority forgeability — LOW-MODERATE RISK, reasonably designed but with a minor gap. The ledger is written only by a harness-owned gateway process the agent cannot read or write (architecturally sound, consistent with this project's previously-used verifier-process-and-ledger-isolation pattern), and the verifier independently re-queries each server's own backing dataset rather than trusting agent-reported values or the agent's account of the ledger — this defeats simple evidence-forging (confirmed via the narrator/half-chain held-out mutants and the evidence-forging control). Ledger-spoofability is explicitly listed as a kill condition to test before shipping. The one gap versus the letter of lesson 5 is that there's no explicit canary analogous to Probe V2's "deliberately leaky facade" test demonstrating that if the gateway/ledger itself were compromised, the detector would catch it — the current controls test agent-side forgery, not infrastructure-side witness leakage. This is a real but secondary gap, not close to axis 2/3 in severity.

Net: two of the four specifically-flagged risks (public instruction over-explicitness, and the mislabeled self-check-coverage predictor) are substantive and closely reproduce CAA V1's actual documented failure signatures rather than being resolved by this recipe's design. Given the task's instruction to default to refuted=true under genuine uncertainty, and given these are not marginal doubts but concrete, textually-grounded matches to the exact postmortem language, the recipe's probability claims (the ~15-30% success band, and its framing as "consistent with" the external ~0.30 ceiling) are not well supported as stated and should be treated as refuted pending a redesign that (a) strips or weakens the explicit behavioral checklist in publicOutcomeRequirements down to only what a real professional would need stated, and (b) adds an actual design-time self-check-coverage prediction step distinct from richer post-hoc scoring. The recipe does explicitly target CAA V1's lessons by name (privateVerifierArchitecture and mainFairnessRisks both quote the postmortem), so targetsCAAv1Lesson is true even though the targeting is only partially successful.

recipeCards.name: Multi-Day State Carryforward Drift
recipeCards.baseFamilyDefinition:
Unchanged, restated for reference: "A single trajectory simulates extended, multi-day professional work where later steps depend on state correctly carried forward from many earlier steps; a deterministic verifier inspects only the final end-state, so any single dropped or drifted piece of upstream context propagates silently to failure." Task shape: a long chain of dependent operations over simulated extended time in a rich, multi-component environment; the agent plans and executes without intermediate checkpoint feedback, and some steps require genuine cross-domain expert judgment. Causal axis: long-horizon-planning-execution-monitoring. Domain: cross-domain terminal professional work (office/scientific/engineering/sysadmin). Authority boundary: the agent's authority is scoped to the full multi-step task; the verifier is binary against the fully carried-forward final state with no partial credit for locally-correct-looking intermediate steps. Subject-inaccessible witness: no intermediate checkpoint signal is available during execution; whether earlier state was correctly carried forward is only knowable at the final verifier. Natural scenario dimensions: number of dependent stages simulated; richness of the multi-component environment; required domain expertise; execution time budget. Why agents may fail: reported gaps attribute failure to long-horizon planning, execution monitoring, and error recovery, with a documented ~27-point score jump from extending the time budget alone. Why fair: full scope and rules are communicated up front; difficulty comes from sustaining correct execution over many steps, not hidden information. None of this is altered by the construction recipe below -- the recipe only supplies HOW to build, verify, and validate an instance of this already-defined family.

RECONCILIATION NOTE (post three-skeptic review, all three refuted): all three skeptics independently converged on the same two concrete, checkable gaps -- (1) the self-check-coverage "predictor" was a runtime, agent-writable annotation count that the private verifier also consulted for diagnostics, which is the exact self-declared-evidence pattern the verifier architecture claims never to trust, and is gameable by padding annotations; (2) the tool-mediated system-of-record's non-leakage/tamper-resistance was asserted, never proven with a negative control, unlike this repo's own Phase 17 C8-witness-isolation-with-canary precedent. Two skeptics additionally flagged reference/mechanism thinness (repeated single-field substitution; no numeric floor on graded-fact count) and the public brief stating the grading mechanics (supersession + no-intermediate-feedback) nearly as directly as CAA1 named its anti-pattern. All four are fixed by construction below, not argued away: the predictor is rebuilt as a construction-time-only, non-agent-touching archetype battery (see privateVerifierArchitecture, scenarioSelectionStrategy); a store-forgery mutant and a leaky-variant canary are added (see narrowDevMutants #7-8) with matching killConditions; a numeric minimum-fact floor plus a mandatory multi-fact synthesis requirement replace single-field substitution as the graded mechanism (see familyNativeDifficultyOperators, threeExampleInstances); and the public outcome text is rewritten to state only ordinary domain accuracy expectations, with the meta grading-mechanics sentence moved to infoIntentionallyAbsent.
recipeCards.outboxOperatorMapping:
Mapping of the 10-point recipe onto this family (point 3 is reframed rather than applied literally -- see nonApplicableOperators). Revisions from the post-review hardening pass are marked [HARDENED].

1. Realistic multi-file environment -> a realistic multi-subsystem workplace environment the agent operates across simulated days: an inbox/event feed, a set of professional tool-scripts, and a running state record the agent maintains, spanning enough files and subsystems (scheduling, records, comms, finance-or-lab-or-infra system) that no single file holds the whole task.

2. Outcome-based instructions -> [HARDENED] the brief states only the required end-of-horizon deliverables and ordinary domain accuracy/currency expectations, phrased exactly as a real professional assignment brief would phrase them (see publicOutcomeRequirements). It no longer states the meta grading rule ("later information supersedes earlier information," "you receive no intermediate feedback; only end state is evaluated") -- that sentence was flagged by two independent skeptics as functionally equivalent to CAA1's outright statement of its own tested mechanism. It is removed from public text and moved to infoIntentionallyAbsent: the agent must discover it operationally from the environment's day-gating and the absence of any response to submissions, exactly as a real employee discovers it, not from a labeled rule.

3. Plausible defect naturally embedded -> reframed (see nonApplicableOperators): ordinary plot-native corrections and updates delivered at specific simulated days through normal in-fiction channels, never flagged as wrong, exactly the "stale-state" mechanism already in this repo's mechanism ledger rather than a software defect.

4. Visible tests with a coverage gap -> a day-end self-check tool that verifies per-day submission completeness and schema validity only, never cross-day consistency. [HARDENED] It now exposes no diagnostic signal beyond bare completeness/schema pass-fail -- the earlier draft's "provenance annotation count" is removed entirely (see visibleTestStrategy) because it was agent-writable and therefore gameable/self-declared.

5. External authoritative state / append-only witness -> [HARDENED] a day-gated event feed plus a tool-mediated system-of-record store that the agent can only extend through defined professional actions, enforced as a hard sandbox boundary (read-only mount / separate process, not convention) rather than an asserted convention -- see externalAuthorityOrWitness. This isolation claim now ships with a negative control (narrowDevMutants #8): a deliberately-writable canary build that the same detector must be shown to catch, per this repo's own Phase 17 postmortem recommendation #5.

6. Separate verifier over external outcomes -> an isolated verifier reads only the system-of-record store and the agent's produced deliverable artifacts, never the agent's own running notes, chat narration, self-declared status, or any field of its own state/ files, with no exception (see privateVerifierArchitecture).

7. Positive-work / no-op / always-refuse / unconditional-success / hardcoding / evidence-forging / [HARDENED] store-tamper / isolation-canary / substitution-is-insufficient controls -> see positiveWorkAndCheatControls and narrowDevMutants.

8. Deterministic scenario fuzzing -> fuzz stage count, event placement day, fan-out, environment richness, time budget, and [HARDENED] synthesis-density and overlap-count (see fuzzerDimensions) to find the region where a plausible-but-incomplete agent fails specifically on carryforward and nothing else.

9. Preregistered narrow mutants + held-out validation -> [HARDENED] now eight dev mutants (added store-forgery/tool-bypass and a construction-time-only leaky-variant canary) rather than six -- see narrowDevMutants and heldOutMutants. Additionally, before any instance is selected, a NEW construction-time-only, pre-trial gate runs: a small fixed library of generic, domain-agnostic self-check archetype scripts (completeness-only; same-day-only; final-day full-recency; changed-since-last-touch), zero LLM calls, against the frozen reference trajectory and the frozen event feed, and separately against each narrow dev mutant's final state. This produces a per-instance ranking of which archetype tier is the cheapest one that still catches every narrow mutant without flagging the reference -- directly implementing Phase 17 postmortem recommendation #1 ("add a self-check-coverage predictor to the contract gate, and make it a ranking feature rather than pass/fail"). It never touches any live agent's own submitted artifacts or narration, resolving the exact contradiction three skeptics identified in the prior draft (a verifier that claims never to trust self-declared evidence, then computing a "predictor" from the agent's own annotated state). An instance where a cheap generic archetype already catches every mutant is flagged high-risk-of-being-easy and is redesigned or dropped (killConditions #10) -- the paper-equivalent of the gate that ranked CAA 85 out of 85 before a dollar was spent.

10. Frozen hashes, isolated execution, durable capture, blind labelling -> the event-feed script and system-of-record schema are frozen and hashed before any trial; each attempt runs in its own isolated environment instance; full transcripts, final artifact state, and the system-of-record diff are captured as durable evidence; failing runs are labelled blind to condition. [HARDENED] Every isolation/non-leakage claim in this card now additionally ships with a negative control before it counts as evidence (narrowDevMutants #8, killConditions #9), per Phase 17 postmortem recommendation #5 -- the exact repair for the two Phase 16 CAA controls (witnessIsolated, challengeNonleakage) that had no reachable failing branch.

Mapping of the 8 measured local operators onto this family (as native analogs, not literal reuse), with hardening notes:
